News.title: Mum & kids found dead with head injuries were discovered after desperate calls by concerned family – as dad ‘fled UK’
News.content:
A MUM and her two children were found dead with head injuries after desperate calls by heir concerned family.

Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, and her daughters Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, were found dead by cops in a house in Great Denham, near Bedford, on July 7.



The husband, Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, 45, is suspected of their murder.

He fled the country and was arrested in South Africa earlier this month.



Prosecutors in the UK have authorised murder charges against him.

An inquest has now heard that all three victims died from head injuries.

Coroner Emma Whitting opened and adjourned an inquest into their deaths at a hearing in Ampthill, Bedfordshire, today, July 28.

The mother died from “head injuries” and the children’s cause of death was given as “blunt force head injuries,” according to statements from the coroner’s officers.



Sam Silk, from the coroner’s office, told the inquest a cousin of Nothabo had contacted Bedfordshire Police on July 6 after they had become concerned for the family’s welfare.

The cousin told officers she usually spoke to the mother every day but had not heard from her for several days.

Inquiries revealed the children had not attended school that day and initial welfare checks carried out by the police at an associated address found it was unoccupied.

Cops then went to the £1.3million family home on Carnoustie Drive in the early hours of July 7 where the bodies were discovered.

The inquest has been adjourned to a date to be determined.



The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has started an investigation into the “contact” officers had with the mother and her children before their deaths.

Bedfordshire Police made a “mandatory referral” to the IOPC on July 7.

A spokesperson for the watchdog said: “We also received a voluntary conduct referral concerning a police constable on 8 July.”

Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, a British citizen of Zimbabwean heritage who goes by the name of Mark, was arrested in Johannesburg, South Africa, on July 10 on an unlicenced firearms charge.

He later appeared in court accused of illegally possessing firearms.

Courts in South Africa will now determine whether a British extradition request meets the legal requirements to send him back to the UK.

Prosecutors in England have authorised the three murder charges.

News.title: Heartbroken friend shares worst fear after North Carolina woman Elizabeth Waddell, 44, vanished from vacation Airbnb
News.content:
THE worried friend of missing American tourist Elizabeth Waddell still has hope they will be reunited after she vanished on a vacation in the Caribbean.

Waddell, 44, a physical therapist from Cary, North Carolina, has been missing since July 22, when she disappeared during a trip to Grenada.



Her final moments were captured on surveillance footage, according to Grenada police, who said cameras showed Liz entering the water at Grand Anse Beach at around 11:51 am.

Investigators said the footage showed her swimming beneath a jetty about 13 minutes later – but she was never seen returning from the water.



Police have also received eyewitness accounts from people who saw her swimming in the area.

Authorities said they will not release the surveillance video publicly at this stage but could do so later if they believe it would assist the investigation.

Elizabeth Waddell AIRBNB DISAPPEARANCE Devastated friend reveals red flag after American vanished on vacation

Commissioner Randy Connaught confirmed during a press conference that the FBI is assisting, particularly with reviewing the video evidence.

As the search continues, Liz’s loved ones are facing the devastating possibility that she may have drowned, while still desperately hoping she somehow made it out of the water.



Amanda Romano-Harmon, who has known Liz and her family for nearly 25 years, said the family is struggling through the emotional toll of the search.

“We’re trying to take it moment by moment right now,” Amanda told The U.S. Sun.

“It’s quite, you know, emotional and fatiguing, as you can imagine.”

Amanda said she understands Liz could not have survived in the water for this long.

“I hope she got out of the water,” the heartbroken friend said.



“I don’t think the Navy Seals could withstand the water for this long, treading that kind of water.”

Amanda stressed that she does not want to speculate about what happened and is still holding onto hope that Liz may be found alive.

“I mean, it would be speculation,” she said.



“I hope she got out of the water. I hope that there wasn’t an undertow or anything that was too strong that day.”

She added, “The bay is pretty shallow and the conditions supposedly were calm that day.”

Liz, an adventurous traveler, was visiting the island with her friend Heather when she disappeared during what was supposed to be a dream three-week getaway.

“She has the adventure bug, and she’s a free spirit and she’s very curious,” Amanda said.

According to Amanda, Liz had gone outside in her swimsuit with a towel while Heather finished an online course at their Airbnb overlooking the bay.



“She was in a swimsuit and had a towel,” she said.

“The Airbnb overlooked the bay. And so she went out. And I guess she was going to hang out there until Heather finished her online coursework.”

When Heather later looked outside and could not see Liz, she went searching for her.

She found only Liz’s towel left behind on the pier, while her phone and other belongings remained inside the Airbnb.

“She went out to walk about and see if she could find her, and all she found was her towel that was on the pier,” Amanda said.



“She went back to the Airbnb, realized Liz didn’t have her phone or any of that with her, it was all in her room, and got worried.”

Liz was reported missing to Grenada police, who launched a search involving multiple agencies and local volunteers.

Amanda also pushed back on reports circulating online that Liz had gone swimming at 8 pm, insisting it was around 1pm.

“She was out in broad daylight in the middle of the afternoon,” she clarified, adding that it was a popular spot for tourists to go swimming.

Amanda said family and friends have traveled to Grenada to help with the search, while authorities and locals have been working to find answers.



“They’ve checked all the hospitals on the island, they’ve checked places that they visited prior the week that they were there on the island,” she said.

“They’re checking places that she kind of had on her list of where she wanted to go while she was visiting the island.”

The Coast Guard has been involved, with divers searching the area for several days.

Amanda said local tour operators have also joined the effort.

“They’ve had divers out for a few days, and even one of the glass bottom boat excursion companies there, their boat operators just took the boats out and have been searching for her as well,” she said.



“We’re grateful for that.”

Police are also investigating an unconfirmed report that someone may have seen a woman matching Liz’s description.

“We have an unconfirmed tip that we received that somebody possibly saw someone who looked like her on Friday night in front of a grocery store,” Amanda said.

“Again, that is unconfirmed. And police are pulling surveillance for that.”

Before the trip, Amanda said Liz had been excited to explore Grenada with Heather.



The pair regularly traveled together, choosing different islands to experience local culture, food and scenery.

“She was really looking forward to exploring Grenada and seeing their cultures and everything and just being immersed with the people,” Amanda said.

“She was definitely interested in the food scene.”

Now, her friends and family are pleading for information that could help bring her home.

“Liz, we’re searching,” Amanda said in a message directly to her friend.



“We’re doing everything we can. We’re throwing everything we can at it.

“If you can hear us, know that we’re looking for you and we want to bring you home, just come home to us.”

To watch Amanda’s full interview about her friend Liz, visit The U.S. Sun’s YouTube channel.

News.title: Two teen girls ‘raped in alleyway’ as cops launch manhunt and share CCTV of person they want to speak to
News.content:
TWO teenage girls have allegedly been raped in an alleyway – sparking an urgent police manhunt.

Investigators have released CCTV of a person they wish to speak to as part of a probe into the sexual attack in Blackpool Town Centre.



Local cops were called at 2:36am on July 25 to a report of an alleged double rape.

Two girls, both in their late teens, had allegedly been raped by a man in an alleyway off Deansgate in Blackpool.



The alley runs between Edward Street and Topping Street.

The area was cordoned off by Lancashire Constabulary over the weekend as detectives and forensic officers scoured the scene for evidence.

Sharing a CCTV clip of a man they want to talk to, local police said: “Do you recognise the man in the video?”

Cops added: “We want to speak to him as part of our investigation into a rape in Blackpool.

“An investigation was launched by detectives, and both girls are being supported by officers.

“If you recognise the man in the footage or you were in the area at the time or have information which can help the investigation, please contact 101 – quoting log 0195 of 25th July.”

News.title: Fury as Burnham insists Labour’s plan to stop dinghy migrants is WORKING despite 900 crossing in his first week as PM
News.content:
LABOUR’S plan to stop small boat crossings is working, Andy Burnham has insisted despite a fresh influx.

The PM admitted there was more to do but pointed to a drop in numbers comp-ared with this time last year.



Some 13,007 migrants have made the perilous journey from France this year — down 45 per cent on 2025.

But the recent heatwave has seen a spike in crossings, with almost 900 leaving the beaches in Mr Burnham’s first week.



Responding to the latest crossings, he said: “The Home Secretary has brought forward a very rigorous plan in relation to this.

“And let’s remember, the numbers can fluctuate but overall boat crossings are down, down quite significantly year on year.

“So that does suggest that the plan is working.”

He wants illegal migrants to go through “all relevant and necessary checks” amid fears hostile states are smuggling in spies via Channel crossings.

Mr Burnham said: “The public wants to see control being exerted, and while we’ve made progress, there is more to do, and I recognise that completely.”

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has struck a new deal with French authorities to halt crossings from their beaches.



UK taxpayers have paid Paris over £1billion for help stopping the boats, with limited results.

Tory Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp blasted: “We’ve seen well over 1,000 illegal immigrants cross in just the last few days.

“Shabana Mahmood’s deal is not working.

“I witnessed today the French doing nothing to stop a migrant boat and even helped by handing out lifejackets.

“The only thing protecting our borders is the weather.”

News.title: Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd must NOT be freed early ‘as he’s a risk to women’, his victim’s family tell Burnham
News.content:
SPEEDBOAT killer Jack Shepherd must not be freed early, his victim’s family have told the PM.

Charlotte Brown’s father Graham branded Shepherd a “risk to women” after he admitted assaulting an ex.



Graham’s daughter Charlotte died aged 24 after being taken on a high-speed boat trip by an intoxicated Shepherd during a first date on the Thames in 2015.

Shepherd, 38, pleaded guilty to vicious attacks against a former partner, who he met in the same flats when he was released on licence.



Graham told The Sun: “I’ve always said Shepherd remains a risk to women. This proves it beyond doubt.

“He has no respect for women at all.



“Shepherd is currently in prison.

“I just hope he is not freed under the Government’s early release scheme as he will always be a risk to females.



“I would directly appeal to the Prime Minister to re-examine the early release scheme to ensure offenders like Shepherd who pose a threat to females are not released early.”

Last week, Andy Burnham paused the introduction of reforms that would have seen offenders — including those who have assaulted women — released after serving as little as 33 per cent of their sentence.

News.title: Meghan & Harry’s global privacy tour is back in full swing, keeping a low profile while revealing kids’ eating habits
News.content:
COULD it be? Surely not? Oh my God, it is.

“A global icon, a philanthropist, a humanitarian, a woman known around the world for her heart, her voice . . . ” Blah blah blah.



You could be forgiven for thinking that, at the very least, Mother Teresa had risen from her grave.

But no, it’s the Duchess of Sussex (“Oh, call me Meghan”) making a guest appearance as a judge on MasterChef Australia.

And guess what? In a happy, ahem, coincidence, her husband Prince Harry just happens to make a video call in to the studio while she’s filming.



“What’s going on? Have I interrupted something?” he asks, as though he didn’t already know that his wife was appearing on one of Australia’s biggest shows.

“We wish you were here,” she gushes, before informing the millions of viewers, “He’s in Canberra now, with the veterans.”

Yes, buckle up folks, Meghan and Harry’s worldwide privacy tour is back in full swing.

We didn’t see images from their recent meeting with the King, perhaps because Buckingham Palace forbade it.

But in the past fortnight, we have seen photos of their children (well, the back of their heads) visiting Princess Diana’s childhood home of Althorp in Northants, as well as a slew of intimate shots from their recent family holiday in Portugal.



One was a back shot of Meghan standing on a beach in a swimsuit (can you imagine the fuss from the Sussex camp if a paparazzo had taken and printed such an image?), another showed Harry playing with the kids in the pool, and a photo giving the exact location of a favoured restaurant.

Curiously specific for a couple so fervent about their security. Unless, of course, they’re planning never to return there again.

And now, courtesy of Meghan on MasterChef, we know that “being from the UK, [Harry] loves a lot of meat, potatoes, cream sauces” and “can handle a really good curry”.

Also that Meghan herself likes both savoury and sweet food (revelatory) and, when her kids ask for dessert, she tells them: “If you can pick it, you can have it.”



I feel I know more about this family’s movements, likes and dislikes than those of some of my closest friends.

Which would be fine if, simultaneously, they were not constantly hammering home the message that they just want to be left alone by the ghastly media.

But Meghan and Harry, it would seem, just want to have their home-baked cake of immense privilege and eat it too.

On MasterChef Australia, that contradiction might pass unnoticed, but for many in Britain, it continues to grate.



Mind you, in the two shots of Meghan and Harry’s video call, I note that Australia’s Network 10 took the opportunity to run a trailer caption underneath for a forthcoming series.

It read: “The Traitors”.

Enough said.

HENRY NOWAK’S killer Vickrum Digwa reportedly arrived at high- security HMP Frankland “shaking with terror”.

I tried to muster sympathy for his plight, but found there was none.



SLAM THAT DOOR REMEMBER the “Ed Stone”? It was the 8ft tall limestone tablet upon which then-Labour leader Ed Miliband carved his six election pledges in 2015. It was “lost” (reportedly destroyed) the same year, along with his chance of becoming Prime Minister. But replicas exist – one at the home of Tory donor David Ross, another at the Ivy restaurant in London’s Chelsea. Suffice to say, it was an object of ridicule that haunts our new Foreign Secretary to this day. Wait until someone tells Donald Trump about it. Something also tells me that the same finger of fun-filled fate is awaiting the “No 10 North” front door prop that was hastily transported to Manchester for Andy Burnham’s photo op last week. Watch this space. I start the bidding at £100 . . .

Where’s the rest of your outfit Margot?

MARGOT ROBBIE went shopping in Paris this week wearing what the fashionistas might call a “slip” ensemble.

My mum would have called it a “nightie”, swiftly followed by: “And you’re not going out in it.”

But it’s the latest trend and everywhere I go there are young girls wearing them.

The urge to run up and say: “You appear to have forgotten the rest of your outfit” is overwhelming. And, yes, I’m aware that makes me sound very, very old.



Bill idiot fire chasers for rescues AS if the “danger tourists” who travel to war zones for social media likes aren’t bad enough, we now have a new branch of idiocy to deal with. Mountain rescuers in Wales had to send out a helicopter to extract two “wildfire chasers” who became stranded after trying to get drone footage of an active blaze. “Incidents such as this require the commitment of personnel and resources that could otherwise be available for genuine emergencies, while also exposing team members to unnecessary risk,” says a spokesman. Let’s hope they send them the bill.

A “TRAVEL consultant” has successfully sued her employer for disability discrimination, after a request to switch on her camera during a remote Zoom training session made her feel “super anxious”.

She was granted sick leave in October 2023 and has not returned to work for the Holiday Extras call centre since.

Sigh. Where to start?

Does she post on social media? Does she go out with friends? Does she leave the house to go shopping?

If the answer to any of the above is “yes”, then she sure as hell can switch on the camera during a remote meeting.

And the employment tribunals facilitating this nonsense are slowly killing enterprise.



TAX TO TEMPT RICH

MEMO to Gary Lineker and all the other “patriotic millionaires” who say they want to pay more tax: No one is stopping you.

The address to write to is: HM Treasury, London SW1A 2HQ.

The reality, of course, is that very few do.

The “Cut My Tax” website has researched voluntary donations over the years and it makes fascinating reading.



In 2014 and 2015, the yield was a big fat zero, and in 2023, 38 people donated just over £28,000 in total.

In fact, aside from 2020 when five generous souls donated nearly £1.2million between them, the amounts over the past decade have been pretty paltry.

“It seems that a number of people who are supposedly desperate to pay more tax are in reality only keen to force other people to pay more tax,” says the accompanying article. Quite.

So why the reticence? Well, one imagines the super-wealthy would happily pay extra tax if they knew it wasn’t just being dropped into a black hole of government misspending.

One imagines that dementia care, cancer treatments, children’s mental health etc would be popular for targeted donations. While the Chagos Islands “deal”, migrant hotels, botched projects like HS2 and giving foreign aid to countries with space projects might be less so.



So perhaps the way forward is to set up a website where, just like those charitable donation boxes in supermarkets you drop green tokens in, multi-millionaires can choose from several worthy recipients.

Something tells me those donations would soar.

Meanwhile, one assumes that Gary et al’s cheques are in the post.

EDUCATION Secretary Lucy Powell is the latest Labour bigwig to bang on about her values being shaped by her working-class roots.

The claim, as well as the poor grammar and spelling of the post announcing her appointment, has attracted ridicule because she got into Oxford and her mother was a headteacher.



Remember Hyacinth “Bouquet” (spelled Bucket) from Keeping Up Appearances, the hit sitcom about a woman with aristocratic pretensions who lived in a suburban semi?

Perhaps it’s time for a reboot with Hyacinth “Bucket” (spelled Bouquet) called Playing Down Appearances?

News.title: Baked Britain on brink of longest dry spell since 1976 as most parched part of UK revealed after 43 days without rain
News.content:
THE home of British horticulture is now the driest place in the UK after going 43 days without a drop of rain.

The parched spell at Wisley in Surrey, home of the Royal Horticultural Society garden, began on June 17.



The mercury has topped 30C on 12 days since, turning the ­gardens to scorched dust.

If rain holds off for 48 hours the rainless period will equal the national drought record of 45 days set in 1976.



Trees at Wisley have begun to lose leaves and grass is frazzled. Staff caring for the hundreds of rare and valuable plants say they have never experienced a summer like it and have begun rationing water.

Environmental horticulture head Mark Gush said: “The previous record at Wisley was 36 days without rain in 1976.



“So we’ve already broken a 50-year record and that’s really significant. It now looks like we’re about to break the national record.”

Wisley visitor Paul Parkinson, 65, from Wimbledon, South West London, said: “I was 15 in 1976 and I don’t think even that was this dry.

“We have a hosepipe ban now, but it just doesn’t seem like the Government have planned for this very well.

“There is no thought being put into resilience in the water system.”



Paul Rutter, 73, of Fareham, Hants, said: “I haven’t seen grass like this since 1976.”

His wife, Angie, 70, said: “It got hot in 1976, but nothing like this.”

Parts of the South West went 45 days without rain in July and August in 1976. But this summer has seen three heatwaves already — and another is due with temperatures set to hit 35C in parts of the South East tomorrow.



And after record-breaking temperatures in May and June, England recorded just seven per cent of its average July rainfall.

Wisley is not the only place to have gone weeks without rain.

Herstmonceux in East Sussex has had 39 dry days, Heathrow in West London has notched up 37, while parts of Hampshire, Suffolk, Bedfordshire, Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire have all topped 30.

Reservoir levels are at dangerously low levels amid a 30 per cent rise in demand.

Eight water firms — Anglian, Southern, Thames, South East, Affinity, Welsh, South West and Cambridge — have imposed hosepipe bans on 23million customers. Last year, only four did.



North Wales and the Upper Severn has declared a drought, while many regions from Cornwall to Lincs are one step below that.

The Met Office’s Will Lang said: “There are signs of more changeable weather into early August, which may bring rain to some areas.

“However any rainfall, particularly across southern parts, is unlikely to be widespread or substantial.” The heat has seen wildfires, dried-up ponds and wetlands and animal rescue centres full of hedgehogs and foxes with heatstroke.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Farms are harvesting early and say yields will be lower than usual. Paul Tompkins of the National Farmers’ Union, said: “The intensity and longevity of the hot, dry weather is taking a toll.”

The UK Health Security Agency has issued an amber heat-health alert for the East Midlands, East of England, South East and London.

News.title: Bizarre moment a dozen nude men run down town’s main street as cops say they’ve ‘exposed themselves’ to a fine
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a group of naked men are caught running down a busy street, landing them in hot water.

Bizarre footage shows the men running down one of Australia‘s most loved dining strips on the Gold Coast.



The dozen or so men were seen spilling out of a pick-up truck on the corner of Breaker Street.

Shouts of “go, go!” could be heard as they raced along the high street in nothing but their birthday suits.



In chilly conditions, the group reportedly sprinted all the way down Tedder Avenue – which is lined by high-end restaurants – and back again.

People heading out for dinner could do nothing but stop and stare as the pack of naked men went tearing past them.



The person who captured the incident from their balcony can be heard saying: “What the hell are they doing?

“They’re nudie running!”



“Everyone was standing up in the restaurant having a look,” one witness told Nine News.

“The most action Main Beach has ever seen!”

Another said: “‘Are we really seeing this?’ But it was very entertaining, and very quick.

“I just gathered it must have been a buck’s night.”

Queensland Police said they were aware of the incident but had yet to receive an official complaint.



Wilful exposure carries a fine of $345 (£180) in Queensland, while public nuisance can see offenders charged over $500 (£260).

Acting Chief Superintendent Brett Jackson said authorities would investigate if it “comes into our knowledge that something has occurred and caused distress to someone”.

“That behaviour isn’t what we want to see on the Gold Coast and it won’t be tolerated,” he added.

News.title: Woman given £12million payout after vital organ accidentally removed in 'devastating surgical error'
News.content:
Woman given £12million payout after vital organ accidentally removed in 'devastating surgical error'

Emily Mitchell and her husband were awarded what is believed to be the largest sum from a medical malpractice lawsuit in Maine history after Ms Mitchell's bladder was removed

View 2 Images Surgeons accidentally removed a woman's entire bladder (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

A woman has been handed a massive £12million payout after surgeons erroneously removed her bladder during what her lawyers have said was "one of the most devastating surgical errors imaginable".

‌



Emily Mitchell, 41, was awarded the $17m (£12.79m) by Kennebec County Superior Court after the vital organ was removed by surgeons at Northern Light Inland Hospital in Waterville, Maine, in the US. She had undergone surgery to have an ovarian cyst removed at the hospital in March 2023, but was transferred to the Maine Medical Centre when her condition deteriorated.

‌



There, doctors discovered her bladder had been removed, a mistake that forced Emily to undergo months of corrective surgeries. Lawyers for Ms Mitchell from the firm Berman & Simmons said she had scheduled the surgery after imaging showed a benign ovarian cyst had significantly increased in size.

‌



Men accuse North Dakota hospital of robbing them of the lives after DNA proves they were switched at birth READ MORE :

View 2 Images Emily Mitchell has suffered for years due to the 'catastrophic' mistake (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

During the procedure, the lawyers said pathology confirmed that, instead of removing the cyst, surgeons removed "full-thickness bladder tissue". The firm said the doctors had extracted so much tissue that it would be impossible to "reconstruct or repair the organ".

Ms Mitchell spent the following eight months on bilateral nephrostomy tubes - surgically placed tubing inserted through her lower back and into both kidneys. They drained her urine directly from the kidneys and into external bags.

‌



The process left her with recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), kidney infections, and forced her to undergo multiple medical procedures that came with new complications. She was eventually sent to Massacheussetts, where surgeons fitted her with a neo bladder made from a section of her small intestine.

Nearly three years following the shock loss of her bladder, she "continues to live with the permanent effects of those injuries", her lawyers said.

Among the permanent effects, the lawyers said, is the requirement to insert a catheter multiple times a day so she can drain the neobladder, and ongoing medical treatment from specialists. Ms Mitchell won her lawsuit against Northern Light Inland Hospital and Northern Light Health last Thursday following a two-week medical malpractice trial.

‌



The massive award, believed to be the largest in Kennebec County history, composed of nearly $2m (£1.5m) for past and future medical expenses, $6m (£4.5m) for pain and suffering and $8 million (£6.01 million) for permanent injury. Ms Mitchell's husband, Joshua, received more than $1m (£752,000) for the loss of her care and companionship.

Attorney Susan A Faunce said in a statement following the payout that it was a multifaceted victory for Ms Mitchell, who was finally receiving closure she has "needed for a long time".

The lawyer said: "For our clients, this isn't just a legal victory—it's the closure they've needed for a long time. They can finally begin to move forward, knowing that what happened to them was seen, heard, and acknowledged. This verdict won't undo the pain our clients have endured, but it does offer something they haven't had in a long time: closure.

Article continues below

"They can finally put this chapter behind them." Ms Faunce added: “Although it doesn’t erase the pain and the loss that they’ve endured or that they continue to endure, the verdict recognizes the truth of what they’ve gone through and provides long overdue accountability. “

News.title: Trump live: Zelensky and Netanyahu court Donald with secretive closed-door meetings
News.content:
Donald Trump is holding crucial talks at the White House with Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu, who are both in Washington DC for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had a "good meeting" with Donald Trump after the two met in private to discuss air defences and Russian diplomacy during a face-to-face talk at the White House.

In a post on X following the meeting, Zelenskyy confirmed the pair had discussed the US president's recent pledge to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors as well as “several other ideas that could help” as the war with Russia enters its fifth year.

Trump also met Benjamin Netanyahu face-to-face for the first time since the start of the Iran war, with the Israeli president hailing the meeting as "one of the best conversations I’ve had with the President of the United States."

Speaking in another closed-door meeting with Trump's “entire senior team,” Netanyahu said the talks were “an opportunity to exchange ideas and to coordinate arrangements that are important for the security and future of the State of Israel.”

Following the discussions, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on X: “Both meetings were positive and productive!”

News.title: Japan earthquake live: Dozens still missing as search for survivors continues overnight
News.content:
Multiple people have died while more are missing after a shopping centre collapsed following a huge 7.1 magnitude earthquake on the Japanese island of Kyushu

Dozens of people are still reported missing following the horror collapse of a shopping mall in Japan that caused 'many fatalities' after being struck by a powerful earthquake.

Up to 30 others remain missing at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, while employees are also missing at the nearby Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant. Several people travelling in a high speed train were also injured after a chimney stack from the paper company fell on them during the quake, local media reports.

“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” a hospital employee told national broadcaster NHK.

“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures,” they added.

The massive quake measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan's own Shindo "scale of shaking" and has left tens of thousands without power. Kumamoto Airport has been closed indefinitely after the earthquake rocked its runway.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

News.content:
Will you be tonight's big EuroMillions winner?

News.title: 'Britain's Neets desperately need Andy Burnham to deliver — or they will lose hope'
News.content:
'Britain's Neets desperately need Andy Burnham to deliver — or they will lose hope'

Andy Burnham said reforms to education will help avert a new generation of "Neets" — the term used for people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are not in education, employment or training

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

More than a million young people are now outside education, employment or training. Behind that grim figure are wasted talents, damaged confidence and futures being allowed to slip away. Andy Burnham is right to reject the lazy claim that these youngsters simply do not want to work. Too many have been abandoned by a system that offers too little help, then punishes families when a teenager tries to take an apprenticeship. A household losing money because a child chooses training over benefits is plainly absurd. The new bursary of up to £4,500 a year will help remove that cruel trap and give more young people a proper route into skilled work. But this crisis has been years in the making and will demand far more than one payment. Colleges need investment, apprenticeships must lead to secure jobs, and young people need support before they lose hope. The Prime Minister says he is on a mission. Britain’s young people now need him to deliver.

‌



BBC refuses to be bullied

The BBC was wrong to broadcast a misleading edit of Donald Trump’s speech before the January 6 riots. It admitted the mistake and apologised. But that should never mean surrendering to a £7.5billion defamation demand. Unlike several American media giants that quickly paid Trump millions of dollars to make cases disappear, the BBC has chosen to fight. Now that courage has been rewarded. A judge has ruled that Trump cannot claim devastating damage to his businesses and brand while refusing to reveal the financial records that might prove whether any such harm exists. For years, Trump has guarded those records fiercely. Now his own lawsuit may force them into the open. The BBC has shown that accountability and capitulation are not the same thing. It made an error, owned up to it, and refused to be bullied.

It’s a Por show

Richard Hammond has been fined £1,771 after speeding in both a Porsche and a Bentley. Perhaps the former Top Gear presenter thought changing cars would confuse the cameras. Sadly, the law has excellent eyesight. Seven points later, he may finally have discovered a motoring challenge he cannot outrun.

News.title: 'Attention seeking' man jailed for arriving at school with hammer and kitchen knife
News.content:
'Attention seeking' man jailed for arriving at school with hammer and kitchen knife

Both Douk Deng, 21, was arrested after he went to Edgar Wood Academy in Heywood, Greater Manchester, armed with a hammer, a hatchet and a kitchen knife

View 3 Images Deng as he was wrestled to the ground (Image: Greater Manchester Police/PA Wire)

An "attention seeking" man who went to a school armed with a hammer, a hatchet and a kitchen knife has been jailed for two years.

‌



South Sudanese national Both Douk Deng, 21, was arrested after workmen confronted him on the premises of Edgar Wood Academy in Heywood, Greater Manchester, on August 6 last year.

‌



A member of the public earlier raised the alarm after he was observed “behaving oddly” in the street nearby en route to the secondary school holding a petrol can with a hammer tied to his belt.

‌



Deng was “mumbling” as he walked a “full circuit” around the school, which was closed to pupils for the summer, as he scanned the building and then approached it before builders working on site became concerned and called the police.

Donald Trump urged to help end one war and intensify another as he meets Zelensky and Netenyahu READ MORE :

The Buck Moon: Rare chance to catch glimpse of spectacular Full Moon this week READ MORE :

The defendant was walking away from the premises when he was detained, Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court heard.

‌



CCTV footage released by Greater Manchester Police showed Deng kicking over a traffic cone as he walked into the school’s premises and then stamping on another road sign aggressively.

He can also be seen appearing to wave, while carrying the green petrol can, at the workmen who approached him inside the school. A police car then pulled up near the school and bodycam footage showed Deng wailing as he was wrestled to the ground by a police officer.

Deng is told to “stop there” by the officer, who then tells him to “get on the ground now” as he attempts to run away. An officer can then be heard saying: “He does have a hammer with him as well. And a hatchet.” Footage then shows Deng being led away in handcuffs to a police van.

‌



The court heard that the defendant, an asylum seeker, had become “increasingly frustrated” that immigration authorities were not providing assistance in his bid to stay and work in the UK. Deng, who has applied for and been refused asylum on three occasions, wanted to “create a scene for attention” to aid his cause, the prosecution alleged.

View 3 Images Deng has been jailed (Image: Greater Manchester Police/PA Wire)

Along with the hammer and hatchet, he was found to be in possession of a seven-inch kitchen knife and a jerry can containing half a litre of petrol.

‌



A day earlier he was spotted “acting oddly” at another school, Holy Family RC and CE College in Rochdale, also closed to pupils, where he kicked and damaged its intercom.

Sara Haque, defending, said: “He maintains that his actions were not motivated by any desire to injury or harm any person. This was a bizarre and compulsive act lacking in any type of maturity at a time when he was in deep distress having left Sudan and his family in traumatic circumstances.

“He wanted attention and he was in crisis but he was not motivated by hostility towards children, teachers or the wider public. There is no evidence that he threatened any individual.”

‌



Deng, who has a wife and children, was placed in multiple accommodation housing (HMO) on his arrival in the UK, the court was told. Ms Haque said: “He found himself in a foreign country with very limited English and unable to work because of his immigration status. He believed and felt no-one was listening to him and no-one was helping him.

View 3 Images Deng seen as he walked around the grounds of Edgar Wood Academy in Heywood (Image: Greater Manchester Police/PA Wire)

“He felt he had reached the of his ability to cope within the HMO where others in similar circumstances to him had been assisted by the immigration authorities. He became increasingly frustrated that the same was not happening for him. His only wish is to work and find money to support his family.”

‌



Psychiatric reports on the defendant had not identified any major mental health issues, the court heard.

Deng, of Heywood, pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing to a range of offences including criminal damage and possessing weapons and a knife in a public place and on school premises. He has been jailed for two years and must serve up to half his sentence in custody and the remainder on licence.

Judge Bernadette Baxter told him: “I have no power to order the Home Office to do anything. But in my judgment, given your circumstances as a failed asylum seeker who has been in custody for the best part of a year, the Home Office should be doing something rather than nothing to deal with your status in this country.”

Article continues below

Detectives from Rochdale CID worked “thoroughly” to investigate Deng, including examining his mobile phone, but found no evidence of a particular motive or intent, said police.

Chief superintendent Helen Caldbeck, district commander for Rochdale, said: “I’m incredibly proud of the officers’ response to this incident. They were professional and brave in tackling a suspicious man armed with weapons and immediately confronted Deng to keep the public safe. Thankfully no one was close to coming to harm but this was nevertheless a disturbing incident.”

News.title: France wildfires live: 184 arsonists arrested as 'all regions' at risk of further fires
News.content:
Flames are nearing the French Atlantic Coast with raging wildfires now nine miles from Bordeaux as the city's mayor says he's prepared for 'all eventualities'

All regions of France are potentially at risk of wildfires tomorrow as the country grapples with what President Macron has claimed is the "most difficult situation" his country has dealt with since World War Two.

“We are facing two particularly critical days, with the heatwave and the very dry forest,” Gironde mayor Blandine Sarrazin. told local media. "This is the third fire to start here in the last two and a half days, it's really difficult," she added, telling residents it was not yet safe to return home.

Holidaymakers have been forced to leave campsites, tourist homes, holiday villages and leisure parks around Lacanau, which is around 40 miles from Bordeaux. The order comes as firefighters race against time to bring the fires under control before the country's south-west is blasted by a forecast 40C heatwave tomorrow (Wednesday).

Officials say the largest blaze has "stabilised" but have warned it could still burn out of control again as temperatures rise and humidity falls.

But a number of additional fires continue to burn with no end in sight, as local officials warn that the inferno could continue for months before it is fully contained.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez claimed wildfire season is "far from over," and said authorities have arrested 1 84 suspected arsonists since the start of the summer.

Meanwhile in Spain, 63,000 people have been evacuate from their homes near Madrid, with the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling it "the most painful expression of the climate emergency".

News.title: Some parents on benefits to get up to £4,500 for child starting apprenticeship
News.content:
Some parents on benefits will be given up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships, the government has said.

Under plans to encourage young people into work, families will be offered a bursary to replace Universal Credit payments lost by starting jobs.

The payment is expected to benefit an estimated few thousand households, who currently face losing between Â£17 and Â£330 a week if their children start apprenticeships.

The Conservatives welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's support for apprenticeships, but criticised his plans to fund the bursaries.

The bursary will be paid for from a Â£30m pot, funded through the growth and skills levy, a tax on employers with annual wage bills over Â£3m.

It followed the publication of a Social Security Advisory Committee report, external which warned of the "perverse effects" of the benefits system on young people's employment choices.

It said, for example, single parents with a disabled child could lose up to Â£340 per week in benefits if their child started an apprenticeship, exceeding the expected apprenticeship salary of Â£258 per week.

Because they are classed as paid employment, benefit payments are reduced to households where young people take on apprenticeships.

The committee said the system was hampering government efforts to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

In a recent report, former Health Secretary Alan Milburn warned that one in six young people could be Neet in the next five years unless urgent action is taken.

Official figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently Neet.

The government said its new bursary would remove a barrier to young people taking on apprenticeships, allowing them to "earn and learn".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "By providing bursaries to those who need them most and fully funding apprenticeship training, we are making sure cost is not the reason someone misses out."

It is part of a wider package of support for apprenticeships, including funding for apprenticeship training for under-25s and additional support for employers taking on apprentices.

Helen Whately, the Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, said: "I'm glad Burnham agrees: apprenticeships are a good thing, and we need more of them."

But she said the plan was "uncosted".

"It is spending money already committed elsewhere. So, either it is another unfunded announcement, or Andy Burnham is not being straight with us about his plans."

Burnham has said he is "on a mission" to reduce the number of Neets.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

As he continues a flurry of early policy announcements, Burnham on Tuesday set out plans to strike a balance in the education system between prioritising academic and technical skills.

News.title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' during MP's BBC interview
News.content:
A French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.

Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.

Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".

The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.

Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises.

"It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."

News.title: Grieving mum was told baby's ashes were animal remains
News.content:
Ness suffered a miscarriage just before she was due to have her 12-week scan on April 20 2021.

She told how she had treasured the ashes for three years.

"They had sat on my shelf next to my baby scan," said Ness.

In court, prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said "the ashes that Lucy was given could not have been those of her baby".

The barrister did not state that they were of animal origin.

Ness was clear to the BBC, however, that police had told her the ashes were animal remains.

Her disgust at Bush was clear.

She said: "How can somebody with a duty of care do this to my family?"

She and her partner, Callum Ellerby, were told their baby was cremated on 10 May 2021.

"We didn't know the gender," said Ness. "We were not going to know the gender."

The day after the cremation was meant to have taken place, Bush, from Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, rang her and asked her to collect the ashes, which she did.

They were contained in a white china urn with a teddy bear embossed on it, Ness recalled.

When Humberside Police announced they were investigating Legacy in March 2024, Ness rang the helpline set up for anyone concerned.

The force then contacted her to say the ashes she had in her home could not be that of her baby, she said.

Officers explained to Ness that they had checked records at the crematorium and found Bush collected the baby's ashes on 13 May - two days after he had presented Ness and Ellerby with the urn.

She said: "I have felt very up and down. This has definitely impacted on my mental health."

News.title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years
News.content:
Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about Â£360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

News.title: Powell says student loan system at top of in-tray
News.content:
Lucy Powell has said she wants to make sure the student loans system is "fair" and that the issue is at the top of her in-tray as the new education secretary.

Labour's deputy leader told the BBC she stood by comments she made in February that the interest rates graduates with Plan 2 loans were paying were "egregious".

She said she was committed to looking at the issue, although acknowledged she "can't make any promises" about changes.

Plan 2 loans were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.

In November last year, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the repayment threshold for students with Plan 2 loans would be frozen at Â£29,385 between 2027 and 2030, instead of rising with inflation.

The change would result in students starting to repay their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries leading to greater repayments.

Campaigners have called for that decision to be reversed.

Reeves later said the government's measures were "fair and proportionate" for getting "the balance right between tax and spending".

In April, the government said interest on some student loans in England - including Plan 2 - would be capped at 6%.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, Powell said she was "very familiar" with the issue as her eldest child has a Plan 2 loan.

She said: "I think it's not just about the threshold of when people start to pay it back, but also the interest rate which is RPI [retail prices index] plus 3%.

"I think I've called it in the past egregious and I'm not going to change my opinion on that just because I'm now the secretary of state.

"The government has committed to a review of that, it's very much at the top of my in-tray as the secretary of state, and I want to make sure we look at this so it's fair for students."

Powell described it as a "real cost-of-living issue" for young people, adding: "They're paying high repayments and never, ever paying off the capital of their student loan."

Pressed on whether it is something she will look at, Powell replied: "Yes. I can't make any promises, but it needs looking at."

MPs on the Treasury Committee this month said comparing student loan repayments to phone contracts or cinema tickets "amounted to mis-selling" by government.

It came after a BBC investigation found the government compared student loan repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts in promotional presentations to teenagers a decade ago.

Earlier this year, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would cut the rate of interest charged on Plan 2 loans, capping it at RPI only. The current RPI rate is 3%.

News.title: Richard Hammond fined £999 for  speeding offences
News.content:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has been fined Â£999 after being caught speeding twice in three weeks while driving luxury cars.

The 56-year-old was captured driving his Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo at 68mph in a 50mph limit on the A40 in Pencraig, Herefordshire on 2 December.

He was later clocked driving his Bentley Continental GT at 82mph in a 70mph limit on the M50 Rudhall Overbridge, also in Herefordshire, on 22 December.

Hammond pleaded guilty to two speeding charges through his solicitor. Two further charges that he had ignored the police letters and failed to identify himself as the guilty driver were withdrawn by police.

He was also given seven penalty points for his licence at the hearing last week.

Magistrate Ann Minton ordered him to pay a total of Â£1,771, comprising two fines of Â£333 and Â£666, Â£240 in costs and victim surcharges totalling Â£532.

News.title: Can Burnham's vision for Manchester's schools really work for the rest of England?
News.content:
Two years ago, I stood at the back of a conference room in Manchester Hall, sipping a coffee and watching Andy Burnham unveil his vision for transforming technical education in Greater Manchester.

He had announced plans for the Manchester Baccalaureate, or MBacc, the year before, and, armed with PowerPoint slides and guest speakers, was running through the ins and outs in front of a room full of education and business leaders.

Now, as prime minister, Burnham has announced plans to make that idea national, and overhaul the technical education system across the whole of England.

The details are still scarce at this stage. We know it will involve giving pupils the option to study more vocational courses and take up work experience from Year 10, but how it will work in practice is still up in the air.

One thing that is certain is that the thinking behind it, and the ambition, is the same as that which underpins the MBacc: a determination to give teenagers a clear, step-by-step route into more practical and technical jobs.

The trouble is, the MBacc itself can be quite a difficult concept to get your head around if you're not familiar with it.

Let's be clear from the start: it's not another type of qualification, like the T-levels and V-levels announced in England in recent years.

Instead, it's a framework that aims to give teenagers a "clear line of sight to good jobs" in vocational and technical areas.

The best way to think about it is a step-by-step route - picture a flow chart - that teenagers can follow from school into any given technical career.

It's set up in parallel to a more clearly defined academic route. During that conference event in July 2024, Burnham and other speakers made clear that those who want to go on to desk jobs can follow a well-trodden path of GCSEs, A-levels, and a university degree.

But for those who want more practical careers, the landscape is much more complicated.

The MBacc is best seen as an effort to simplify that landscape, spelling out for teenagers who want to go into more vocational or technical careers which courses they can study, and ensuring they have the opportunity to study them along with hands-on work experience.

It spells out routes to careers in seven different categories:

Construction and the green economy

Creative, culture and sport

Digital and technology

Education and early years

Financial, business and professional services

Health and social care

Manufacturing and engineering

Its success is difficult to measure, since the MBacc is still in its infancy.

It's not until 2030 that it seeks to achieve its mission of guaranteeing every young person a clear path to good jobs. By 2035, the aim is for every young person to have 45 days of work experience by the time they're 19.

According to the most recent data, the MBacc has been rolled out across 101 secondary schools and colleges in Greater Manchester - about 40% of the total.

The Greater Manchester Combined Authority says 1,405 young people accessed workplace experiences during its second year.

Time will tell, as those teenagers leave school and enter the world of work, how transformative it will be.

News.title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
News.content:
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.

This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.

News.title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral
News.content:
Dame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.

The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.

Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.

Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress".

"It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.

Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service.

"It caught her completely. She was very special."

News.title: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
News.content:
Police officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing.

Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.

As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery.

To mark the 40th anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.

In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".

News.title: Two-Michelin-star chef brings fine dining to town football club
News.content:
Football fans will have the chance to swap their traditional match day pint and pie for a pop-up dining experience created by a renowned two-Michelin-star chef.

Gareth Ward, the chef behind Ynyshir Restaurant and Rooms near Machynlleth, Powys - which has an almost Â£500 per head tasting menu - has partnered up with Aberystwyth Town Football Club, in Ceredigion.

The collaboration will bring supporters different match day dining experiences, hospitality packages and corporate events throughout the season.

Ward, who has featured as a guest judge on MasterChef: The Professionals, said he was "excited" for the new venture.

The chef-patron said football clubs should be at "the heart of their communities".

The club's team is in the Novira Cymru South division, the second tier of Welsh football.

He added: "I see a real opportunity to bring people together through food and unforgettable matchday experiences and corporate events."

News.title: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14 in England, Burnham says
News.content:
Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The government said the courses, which would be available from Year 10, would be linked to local industries and designed to give children a clearer pathway into work.

Data published this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, the highest level in more than 12 years.

Few details have been published about how the new vocational courses would work in practice and it is not clear how they would operate in areas with low industrial activity.

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

Later on Tuesday, the government also announced a new bursary of up to Â£4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary.

Speaking at a train manufacturing site in Derby, Burnham said: "We've had a system built for too long around the university route and it sends a message to some young people that they're some kind of second-class citizens, and it's just not right.

"They need an education system that works for them as well, that offers a path to all young people, that's balanced between academic and technical."

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet" - but declined to put a target date on his ambition.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

"It's hard to put a firm date on the moment when you can say there are fewer than now."

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said while there was a "broad consensus" on improving vocational education, it was "not a big bold announcement".

She told BBC Breakfast: "What's going on there is a drastic shortage of jobs because Labour's policies over the last couple of years have killed job opportunities for young people. This announcement will not solve that."

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

News.title: Man guilty of murdering two men found in woods
News.content:
Desborough stood to listen to the verdicts with his hands behind his back.

He was wearing a grey T-shirt and glasses, and maintained a neutral expression while listening.

He was told he should "be alive" to the prospect of a whole life sentence when he is sentenced by Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini on Wednesday.

Witness impact statements would also be read out at the hearing, the court was told.

After the verdict, Coleman's family said in a statement: "We as a family would like to thank the police, prosecution and everyone involved in getting justice for Dan.

"Dan was a loving, caring and compassionate man who will be forever loved and sadly missed."

Aquilino's family said: "We are completely and utterly mortified in the violent murder of Claudio and the manner in which his body was disposed.

"Claudio will always be in our thoughts and we now pray he is at peace."

They said they had faced a "profoundly sad ordeal".

Det Supt Rachael Bentley, of Devon and Cornwall Police's major crime investigation team, described the killings as "callous and cold-blooded", as "both men were vulnerable and trusted James Desborough as their friend" before he brutally murdered them and "savagely desecrated their bodies".

She paid tribute to the victims' families, saying they "conducted themselves with a quiet dignity throughout this investigation and who have had to listen to, and see, some harrowing evidence".

Desborough was previously found guilty of strangling his 65-year-old cellmate Steven Kempster in September 2025, while on remand awaiting trial over the deaths of Coleman and Aquilino.

That trial had heard Kempster's snoring had annoyed Desborough.

Bentley said Desborough's taking of Kempster's "in this way was cowardly".

Helen Phillips of the Crown Prosecution Service said after the hearing that it had been a "large and extremely complex case".

"We worked closely with police from the very start of their investigation in Paramoor Woods, and then later with a second police team on the investigation into the murder at HMP Exeter, which ran in parallel," she said.

"The families of Claudio and Daniel have been so dignified throughout the investigation and trial process, even when faced in court with awful descriptions of what happened to their loved ones, and Desborough's attempts to blame Daniel for somehow being involved in the disposal of Claudio's body.

"As Desborough faces justice for his actions, my thoughts remain with the families and friends of his three victims."

News.title: Chairman stole £22k from junior football club to fund cocaine habit
News.content:
A former junior football club chairman stole Â£22,491 from accounts and faked HMRC documents to feed his cocaine habit.

Karl Morecroft, 45, lied to club members at RTB Ebbw Vale while taking home the payments over the course of 15 months.

The club in Blaenau Gwent supported 330 children and relied on the goodwill of fundraisers, parents and volunteers to raise the money to keep going after the fraud.

Morecroft was given a 20-month jail term suspended for two years at Cardiff Crown Court on Monday, and must complete 180 hours of unpaid work and 50 rehabilitation days.

He was also ordered to pay Â£21,259 within three years and a default order of 12 months in prison if he failed to do so was imposed.

The U.S. Department of Education announced Tuesday that it is investigating allegations involving a Denver high school teacher who allegedly required same-sex students to kiss in front of their classmates, as well as a Washington state school district that displayed vials of testosterone in a Pride Month exhibit.

The investigations will examine whether Denver Public Schools and the Bethel School District, located about an hour south of Seattle, violated a federal law that allows parents to opt out of school surveys or evaluations involving topics such as sexual behavior or attitudes, according to the department.

“Parents must be the decision-makers in matters impacting the most intimate parts of their children’s lives,” Frank Miller, director of the Education Department’s Student Privacy Policy Office, said in a statement.

Denver Public Schools spokesman Scott Pribble said the district placed the teacher on administrative leave and conducted an investigation after students raised concerns in March 2025. He did not provide details about what prompted the students’ complaints.

The Trump administration has opened dozens of investigations into schools that make accommodations for transgender and LGBTQ+ students ( Roberto Schmidt / AFP via Getty Images )

The Board of Education fired the teacher in May, he said.

“The safety, emotional well-being, and dignity of our students are the absolute highest priorities of DPS,” the statement said. “Our actions to date have been wholly consistent with those priorities.”

Bethel School District said in a statement that the vials in a display at Graham-Kapowsin High School in June were not authorized by school administrators and were immediately removed and turned over to the Pierce County Sheriff's Office.

Testosterone is prescribed for gender-affirming care. The district added that it will cooperate fully with the Education Department's investigation.

The two districts are in states headed by Democrats. President Donald Trump is a Republican.

The Trump administration has opened dozens of investigations into schools that make accommodations for transgender and LGBTQ+ students, often taking aim at districts that allow students to use bathrooms or locker rooms that align with their gender identities. It accused Denver schools last year of violating Title IX protections against sex-based discrimination over such a bathroom policy.

Trump officials have also pushed against schools accused of keeping information about students’ gender identities confidential from their parents, which the department says is a violation of federal privacy laws.

The Education Department tied the new investigations to National Parents’ Day on Sunday. The agency said it will be announcing “significant actions” involving the enforcement of parental rights laws through the week.

The display at the high school in the Bethel district contained some vials with a “small amount of unknown liquid,” the district said in its statement.

Pierce County Sheriff's Deputy Carly Cappetto said school administrators identified the student who brought the vials to campus. The sheriff's office would test the liquid to determine whether it was testosterone — a controlled substance — if prosecutors made that request, she said.

An email to the Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney's Office was not immediately returned.

The district said in its statement it is reviewing its protocols for overseeing displays to “ensure all school materials strictly align with our educational standards and community expectations."

“Our primary focus remains on maintaining a safe, respectful, and focused learning environment for all of our students,” it added.

The Trump administration is poised to announce import bans on new Chinese robots and power inverters in a move that aims to shield the nation's artificial intelligence expansion from security threats and repatriate vital industries earmarked for significant growth.

The Federal Communications Commission is expected to announce the measures Tuesday afternoon. The restrictions will prohibit Chinese imports of new humanoid and quadruped robots, as well as connected power inverters, which are vital components enabling renewable energy sources and batteries to link with grids and data center infrastructure, sources indicated.

These impending restrictions, previously unreported, underscore the Trump administration's intent to fortify the U.S. artificial intelligence supply chain against potential Chinese disruptions, data theft, and cyberattacks. Concurrently, the policy aims to incentivize companies to shift manufacturing operations back to the United States.

An administration official, who requested anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the matter, stated, "The President has made clear that the United States must have independent and secure supply chains for critical and emerging technologies like robotic devices and power inverters."

The official added, "Economic security is national security, and the Trump administration continues to implement a nuanced and multi-faceted policy agenda to reindustrialize America." The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

open image in gallery The FCC plans to bar Chinese imports of new humanoid and quadruped robots, officials say ( AFP via Getty Images )

Analysts predict widespread adoption of humanoid robots, equipped with AI-powered "brains," across consumer and industrial sectors. Meanwhile, the explosive growth of data centers in the U.S. will heavily rely on dependable sources of inverters. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has previously warned that Chinese AI firms could face U.S. sanctions for intellectual property theft.

U.S. officials are also keen to prevent a repeat of the situation with rare earth minerals – essential inputs for tech manufacturing so dominated by China that Beijing has leveraged its control for significant international gains.

As part of the measures slated for Tuesday's announcement, the FCC will ban foreign imports of new models of the targeted technologies. It is then anticipated to exempt many non-Chinese suppliers from these restrictions, mirroring its approach with recent bans on foreign drones and routers, according to four additional sources.

These restrictions, effective upon publication, will apply exclusively to robot and inverter models not yet released, another U.S. official clarified. However, the FCC retains the authority to revoke authorizations for models already approved for purchase in the United States.

President Donald Trump is credited with elevating international awareness of the tech threat posed by China during his first term, vocalizing concerns about intellectual property theft by Chinese firms and the risk of state-sponsored espionage by telecom giants like Huawei. However, his second term has seen a more measured approach, particularly in response to Beijing's aggressive use of export controls on rare earth minerals last year.

open image in gallery The restrictions seek to curb national security risks and fuel onshoring ( AFP via Getty Images )

The robot ban is expected to significantly impact Unitree, a global leader in humanoid robots holding nearly a fifth of the world market share, according to Counterpoint Research. Unitree, one of three Chinese companies dominating this nascent industry, was recently added to the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, often a precursor to tougher U.S. action.

Unitree recently partnered with Nvidia to integrate the AI chip company's cutting-edge Blackwell chip into its robots. Nvidia has affirmed that data from these robots will remain in the U.S. and that Unitree's primary customers are U.S. academic and research institutions. China hawks, however, fear these robots could spy on critical U.S. industries, exfiltrating data to Beijing or disrupting essential functions.

China is the world's largest producer of inverters, with Sungrow Power Supply and Huawei leading the market. Huawei is already heavily sanctioned by the U.S. Beijing has been expanding its share in the Western inverter market by driving down prices. Reuters previously reported on the FCC's work towards a Chinese inverter ban, influenced by recent European actions and concerns over disruption and malware installation.

Authorities aim to avert another Chinese government-linked hacking campaign, such as the "Volt Typhoon" operation revealed in 2023, which sought to control privately owned routers to conceal subsequent attacks on American critical infrastructure. The U.S. Department of Defense is already prohibited from procuring solar photovoltaic cells, modules, or inverters manufactured by a foreign entity of concern, a category that includes Chinese companies.

Unitree, Sungrow, and Huawei did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Senator Lindsey Graham candidly warned that President Donald Trump was letting the war in Iran “slip away,” just weeks before the senator’s sudden death.

The South Carolina Republican, who died July 11, had been a vocal champion of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, which just hit its five-month-mark with no end in sight.

As part of filmmaker Alex Holder’s upcoming documentary, Lindsey’s Game, Graham divulged some of his honest thoughts about how Trump’s war has progressed during a June sit-down interview.

“Iran, he’s letting this thing slip away. We had them on the ropes, and his indecision is coming back to hurt us,” Graham said, according to a clip aired Monday on CNN. “I’ve got to go talk to him, you know?”

He continued: “Open up the straits, keep the pressure on, unleash Israel to hurt them, and maybe you’ll get a better deal. But the big deal — Saudi, Israel…that’s the big prize, and that can’t happen until Israel and Saudi believe Iran can’t be enough evil force — that they have been put in a box.”

open image in gallery Senator Lindsey Graham warned that President Donald Trump was letting the war in Iran ‘slip away’ just weeks before his death ( AFP/Getty )

Graham then noted that it was “good news” that the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “owe Trump a lot, they like Trump, but they’re afraid of Trump.”

“And Trump is the first president who doesn’t hold back when it comes to Israel. I mean, I think he’s going a bit too far, but he will dress Bibi down in a way that no other Republican president has ever done. That gives him some credibility in the Arab world,” Graham said of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is known as “Bibi.”

Graham, a foreign policy hawk who often advocated for greater U.S. intervention overseas, noted he was hoping to prove that “isolationism is an outlier” in the Republican Party.

“So this was a referendum on isolationism versus ‘Lindsey Graham MAGA Trump,” he said.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump eulogized the late senator Tuesday at Washington National Cathedral ( Getty )

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Several weeks after the interview, Graham died at his home in Washington, D.C., from an aortic rupture. He was 71.

The president eulogized Graham at Washington National Cathedral on Tuesday, calling the senator a “tough cookie” who “never saw a war he didn’t like.” Trump also recalled how, in 2015 while on the campaign trail, he publicly shared Graham’s personal cell phone number — and then proceeded to share it once again.

Graham’s younger sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term. She is now running for a full six-year term with Trump’s endorsement.
