Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Neither Anthony Joshua's chin nor his state of mind look capable of handling Tyson Fury in four months' time... but there is no way out, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
Neither Anthony Joshua's chin nor his state of mind look capable of handling Tyson Fury in four months' time... but there is no way out, writes JEFF POWELL MBE

Unlock more of the best of our boxing coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Catch-22 is the fabled paradox from which it is logically impossible to escape being exposed to mortal danger.

Good luck with that, AJ.

That catch phrase is the title of a 1961 novel by Joseph Heller in which World War II pilots had to prove they were insane to be excused missions of terrifying peril. But by making that claim of madness, they only proved to doctors that they were sane because they realised the jeopardy. So tallyho, carry on flying.

Catch-22 has gone into common usage to cover all manner of inescapable contradictions. For example, you cannot get a loan without having a bank account but you do not qualify for a bank account unless you have enough money.

Anthony Joshua is trapped in just such a parallel conundrum following his bizarre, down and up fight against the obscure Kristian Prenga in distant Saudi Arabia on Saturday night. Entwined as he is in two perverse conspiracy theories.

One, that his punch resistance has disappeared into the twilight of a career garlanded by Olympic gold and two world heavyweight championships.

Anthony Joshua is knocked down in the first round by Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia during his bizarre fight on Saturday night

Joshua clambers to his feet before going on to win the fight in the second round

Second, a public fixation that there was something fishy about how he could be dropped twice in the first round by an opponent who virtually stopped fighting in the second round until he was knocked out.

Either way, there is now no getting out of that far more hazardous fight against Tyson Fury for which the public have been baying for the best part of a decade. Not after the Gypsy King fulfilled his end of the bargain by beating up aged punch-bag Mariusz Wach the night before in Thailand.

There is a dispute over whether Joshua v Fury, The After-Thought, should take place in Wembley Stadium or New York’s Madison Square Garden. Wherever, Joshua has signed the contract in which too many hands are grubbing for so much money that he cannot afford to pull out.

Not even if that would be best for his future health, as many observers now believe. Not least some of those close to Joshua who are reporting that he looked oddly disconsolate and lonely in his dressing room before the fight. Lost, perhaps, in the memory of those two best friends who died in that car crash in Africa which he himself was lucky to survive.

Certainly, his mind was not on the job as he was dropped only 20 seconds after the first bell. Now, Prenga entered the ring with a record of 20 first and second round knockouts against only one defeat. Not that any of his victims would be recognised while standing upright in the street.

And yes, I wouldn’t have wanted to be on the receiving end of one of his punches. But neither the uppercut which dropped Joshua nor the combination which inflicted a second knockdown in round one looked perfectly timed or overly powerful by professional heavyweight standards.

And why did Prenga not press home his advantage in the second round? That question has been asked most insinuatingly by Simon Jordan, one-time football club owner turned talk radio star. What does he know? Probably no more than the rest of us. Which is that it was an odd, arguably manufactured weekend affair which ended with one referee not so much counting out Prenga when he went down but hovering over him in a manner which would have made it awkward for him to get up even if he wanted so to do.

Not that he showed any inclination to emulate Joshua’s courage in rising from the canvas. Not that he had the same incentive. His job was done. His reward banked. But Joshua had rescued the bigger and richer fight up the long road. Whether or not that is good for him.

Joshua puts Prenga through the ropes but the Albanian showed no inclination to rise from the canvas. Not that he had the same incentive. His job was done. His reward banked

Eddie Hearn pondered if he had let Joshua come back too soon after his bereavements. But not whether he will be ready for Tyson Fury in the autumn

Good old Eddie Hearn pondered if he had let AJ to come back too soon after his bereavements. But not whether he will be ready for Fury in the autumn.

Nor if it is his chin or his mental health which are party to the inevitable decline of a prize-fighter in his mid-30s. Or both. Fury will examine those possibilities more thoroughly than did Prenga.

If Joshua’s punch resistance was shattered permanently by the five knockdowns with which Daniel Dubois stopped him becoming a three-time world champion, the Gypsy King will find out. If his strength of will has been weakened, then beware Fury the master of mind games.

For AJ, there is no way out.

Not from Catch-22.

Sports.title: Former boxing world champion retires at 36: American superstar hangs up his gloves after latest brutal loss
Sports.content:
Former world champion Errol Spence Jr has officially announced his retirement from boxing at the age of 36 after suffering back-to-back career defeats.

The Long Island-born fighter confirmed his decision to hang up his gloves in his post-fight interview on Sunday, after falling to defeat against 31-year-old Tim Tszyu.

When asked if his career had come to an end following the unanimous decision loss in Australia, Spence said: 'I think, yeah. For sure.'

Expanding on his reasoning, the 36-year-old said: 'I've got my faculties intact. My money is good at working for itself. Everything's good, man.

'I've got a beautiful family and I thank God I'm grateful to leave this sport with my faculties intact and my family still by my side,' he added.

The abrupt announcement came after he suffered his second-ever career defeat, following a grueling 12-round bout against Tszyu in Sydney.

Former world champion Errol Spence Jr has officially announced his retirement from boxing

His decision to retire comes after his defeat to Australian boxer Tim Tszyu on Sunday

Judges officially scored the bout 118-110, 117-111 and 117-111 in favor of the Australian, who outlanded Spence 190 to 157 – despite the American attempting more punches.

Speaking after his victory, Tszyu hailed Spence as 'one of the greats' of his era.

'I had sleepless nights thinking about, 'What am I going to feel like facing a legend like that?' But it was one hell of a show and I understand why he's one of the greats.

'I'd love to fight for a title. That's what I'm aiming for. But I've got to say beating a great like Errol Spence tops a world title'.

Spence walks away from the sport with an impressive 28-2 professional record – including 22 victories by way of knockout. The Texas-raised star previously unified the WBC, WBA and IBF world titles at welterweight.

During his prime, Spence established himself as one of the pound-for-pound greats in the sport, defeating the likes of Kell Brook, Shawn Porter and Danny Garcia.

His trajectory shifted, however, following a terrifying car crash in Dallas in October 2019, where his Ferrari tumbled multiple times and he was thrown from the vehicle.

The Texas-raised star previously unified the WBC, WBA and IBF world titles at welterweight

Spence came up short in his highly-awaited bout against Terence Crawford back in 2023

Recently retired Crawford was in attendance in Australia to cheer on Spence on Sunday

According to Dallas Police, Spence's Ferrari 488 Spider had been travelling 'at a high rate of speed' before the crash. He made his return to the ring just 14 months later.

Eventually, his unbeaten run came to an end in July 2023, when he was stopped in nine rounds by Terence 'Bud' Crawford in a long-awaited welterweight clash.

The victory meant that Crawford, who was in attendance this weekend, became the first undisputed welterweight champion since 2006 and the first male boxer in the four-belt era to claim undisputed championship status in two weight divisions.

Following a three-year layoff prior to stepping into the ring with Tszyu, Spence's final bout marks the end of a decorated career for one of America's greatest ever boxers.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua fights back tears as he dedicates dramatic victory over Kristian Prenga to two best friends killed in car crash as he recovers from TWO knockdowns to win on return
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua fights back tears as he dedicates dramatic victory over Kristian Prenga to two best friends killed in car crash as he recovers from TWO knockdowns to win on return

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Anthony Joshua knows better than anyone how quickly heavyweight boxing can tear up the script. And for a moment on Saturday night in Jeddah, it looked as though another shock was unfolding as the British heavyweight was dropped twice and wrestled to the canvas in a chaotic opening round.

But Joshua dug deep, weathered the storm and, after finding another gear in the second, produced a devastating combination that flattened Albanian heavyweight Kristian Prenga, leaving the 35-year-old sprawled on his back and bringing a dramatic end to a fight that had threatened to derail his comeback before it had even begun.

Although, when AJ's hand was raised, the victory itself almost felt secondary.

For the first time since returning to the ring, the grief that he had worked so hard to suppress finally appeared.

The former two-time heavyweight world champion appeared, perhaps for the first time in public, to let the emotions he had buried since Latif 'Latz' Ayodele and Sina Ghami's tragic deaths in a car crash in Nigeria last December finally surface.

Joshua admitted before the fight that he had spent months suppressing the pain of losing the two men - Latz, his strength coach, and Sina, his personal trainer - insisting he did not want to make their deaths about himself while their families mourned.

Yet, after completing the hardest comeback of his career, both physically and mentally, the emotion could no longer be contained. Joshua broke down during his post-fight interview when crediting his friends for getting him through the first round before quietly saying: 'I don't want to talk about it anymore.'

Anthony Joshua gave an emotional interview after beating Kristian Prenga in Jeddah

When AJ's hand was raised, the victory itself almost felt secondary

Joshua was overcome with emotion after the fight, going from a euphoric high to an emotional low within minutes

For months after the crash, Joshua lived with constant pain. Simply getting out of bed became a struggle. He spent two months gently pedalling on a stationary bike before learning how to balance on a stability ball as he rebuilt his body from the ground up.

While the mental toll must have been every bit as demanding, if not more.

That said, Joshua and Eddie Hearn never liked calling this his 'comeback fight'. Seven months out of the ring is hardly unusual for a heavyweight. He had never truly been away from boxing.

But in every way that mattered, this was a comeback.

Because making it back into the ring after losing two of the people closest to him was perhaps Joshua’s greatest challenge of all.

There were moments when returning to the ring did not feel important, or even possible. But eventually, boxing became part of the healing process.

And so, under the bright lights of the Jeddah Superdome and with Latz and Sina embodied on the canvas, Joshua walked back into battle carrying far more than the pressure of victory on his shoulders.

Prenga was never supposed to be the final destination. The Albanian was always viewed as the bridge to something much bigger.

From the moment the fight was announced, it was understood that the real prize was Fury later this year.

This was the tune-up. The opportunity for Joshua to shake off the ring rust, rebuild momentum and remind the heavyweight division exactly who he is.

That is not to say there was no danger. There always is in the heavyweight division and Joshua was reminded of that the hard way.

Prenga entered the contest with 20 knockouts from 20 victories and just a single defeat. The power was genuine. In heavyweight boxing, one punch can change everything, and for a moment it looked as though it might.

The Albanian dominated a chaotic opening round, dropping Joshua twice and threatening to rip up the script.

Joshua was knocked down twice in the first round

But Joshua recovered in the second round, knocking Kristian Prenga out

It's anticipated that Joshua will finally fight Tyson Fury after both heavyweights won their fights this weekend

But there are levels in elite boxing. Prenga had never shared a ring with anyone approaching Joshua's pedigree or experience, and once the former two-time world champion returned to his corner and received a stern dressing down from his coaching team, he emerged with renewed purpose.

Still showing signs of the defensive vulnerabilities that have haunted him throughout his career, Joshua nevertheless displayed the resilience that has defined his comeback. He turned the tide in emphatic fashion, unleashing a devastating combination to stop Prenga 2:43 into the second round.

When Joshua's hand was raised, the emotion he had worked so hard to suppress could finally be contained no longer.

He had warned beforehand that he had kept so much inside. He did not want to centre himself in a story that belonged to grieving families. He wanted to honour his friends privately.

Instead, he pledged lifelong financial support to both families and vowed to continue pursuing the dreams they all shared together.

Yet as victory was confirmed in Jeddah, it was impossible not to think of everything he had endured to get there.

This was never just another win.

But there was one person missing: Tyson Fury.

Only 24 hours earlier, Fury had fought Mariusz Wach in Thailand, going seven rounds before the veteran Pole retired on his stool in a non-televised contest.

All week Fury had insisted he would not be travelling to Saudi Arabia for Joshua's fight and, despite widespread expectation that he would make a late appearance, the former world champion stayed away.

His absence did little to dampen the belief that British boxing's biggest fight is edging closer, but it denied fans the image they have waited years to see.

After so many failed negotiations, collapsed deals and false starts, supporters had hoped to see Joshua and Fury stand face-to-face in the ring for the first time with both men coming off victories.

But experience has taught Joshua not to assume anything in heavyweight boxing.

His long-awaited showdown with Deontay Wilder appeared all but set before Wilder suffered a shock defeat by Joseph Parker in December 2023 on the very same night Joshua won, sending months of planning into the bin.

The heavyweight division has a habit of snatching away the fights everyone wants to see.

Joshua wore a jacket featuring a medal bar with 'Sina' and 'Latz' pennants

Joshua honoured his friends, Latz and Sina, who were killed in a car crash in December

That is why there will remain a degree of caution until the AJ vs Fury fight is officially confirmed.

Joshua and Eddie Hearn have already revealed that the contract stipulates any showdown with Fury must take place in the United Kingdom because, in their eyes, the biggest fight in British boxing history belongs on British soil.

As things stand, however, Turki Alalshikh and Netflix are understood to favour Madison Square Garden in New York.

That means the contracts will need to be renegotiated.

The expectation is that discussions between all parties will take place over the coming days as they attempt to iron out the remaining details.

For now, Joshua's focus was not on what comes next, but on what he had already overcome.

The tears in Jeddah were not for Tyson Fury.

They were for Latz and Sina.

Sports.title: Simon Jordan airs Anthony Joshua conspiracy theory after boxer knocked out rival despite hitting the canvas TWICE to set up money-spinning Tyson Fury fight: 'Something not quite right'
Sports.content:
Simon Jordan airs Anthony Joshua conspiracy theory after boxer knocked out rival despite hitting the canvas TWICE to set up money-spinning Tyson Fury fight: 'Something not quite right'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Simon Jordan has questioned the nature of Anthony Joshua's victory over Kristian Prenga as he recovered from two knockdowns to set up a lucrative showdown with Tyson Fury.

Joshua, who had been returning to the ring after seven months of inactivity, appeared on the brink of defeat in the opening round against Prenga.

The Albanian heavyweight knocked Joshua down just 20 seconds into the contest with an uppercut.

Joshua then survived another knockdown later in the round, with fans fearing the long-awaited showdown with Fury was at risk.

The second round proved dramatically different as Joshua unleashed a series of heavy blows to force Prenga towards the ropes, before delivering a knockout blow.

Joshua's stunning turnaround, coupled with Fury's victory over Mariusz Wach just 24 hours earlier, cleared the path for the two British heavyweights to finally meet in one of the most lucrative fights in boxing.

Anthony Joshua survived two knock downs in the first round against Kristian Prenga

Joshua responded in the second by delivering a second round knockout of the Albanian

Simon Jordan questioned the nature of Joshua's victory given the difference between the two rounds

talkSPORT presenter Simon Jordan controversially questioned the dramatic difference in the rounds between Joshua and Prenga.

Jordan declared 'something not quite right' as he appeared to reference the sums on offer for Joshua's fight with Fury.

'Not having that… #anthonyjoshua fight,' Jordan posted.

'Dropped twice and sets the tempo, how's that ? … Prenga totally different in 2nd

'Something not quite right, all designed to rinse maximum amount of money…'

Punch stats for the fight revealed the stunning difference between the two rounds, with Joshua landing just five of his 22 attempted punches in the first, while Prenga connected with 15 of his 32.

The second round swung with Joshua landing with 13 of his 46 punches, as Prenga dramatically dropped off by landing three of 17 attempted.

Despite Jordan's comments on social media, Joshua insisted that 'champions rise' in a post-fight interview after coming through the test.

Prenga had stunned Joshua in the opening round and landed 13 of his 32 attempted punches

He landed just three of 17 punches in the second round as Joshua became the aggressor

Prenga was sent to the canvas by a brutal blow from Joshua, who later declared 'champions rise' when asked about the dramatic turnaround

'He [Prenga] gave me a good test but this is what champions do, we rise,' Joshua said.

'We get knocked down and stand up. That is life, that is life's motto.

'I want to give a massive thank you to Prenga and his team for putting up a good fight. It means a lot to them and it means a lot to me and that is why you see what you see in the ring.

'I want to give thanks to God. It was more than me in that situation, it can't just be me in them type of situations. There is a higher power that is calling.

'He's a strong guy and I think Eddie [Hearn] wants to sign him now! He is going to do well and he has a bright future.

'Maybe with a bit more experience, he [Prenga] will be up there with the rest of us. He is strong and durable.'

Looking ahead to the showdown with Fury, with contracts having already been signed, Joshua said in the ring: 'Have we got Tyson Fury in the room? Is he here or not?

'I am the meanest, most vicious champion. Nobody can stop me. He is no Oleksandr [Usyk].

'All jokes aside, there are two sides. One is the fighter and the other is respect. I respect everything he has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we're here now.

'I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat.'

Joshua had paid tribute to his two close friends, who were killed in a car crash in December.

Joshua will finally face Tyson Fury in a money-spinning contest with his rival having beaten Mariussz Wach a day earlier

Joshua paid tribute to his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, who died in a car crash in December

Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele died while the car they were travelling in struck a truck on a road near Lagos in December. The pair were on holiday with Joshua after he beat Jake Paul in Miami.

The heavyweight boxer, who was also in the vehicle, was taken to hospital before being discharged and flying home to the UK - where he attended the funerals of his strength and conditioning coach Ghami and Ayodele, one of his trainers.

Fighting in honour of Ghami and Ayodele, Joshua paid tribute to his friends by having their names printed on his military camouflage trunks.

He also walked to the ring wearing a military-style jacket to match his camo shorts. The jacket featured a medal bar displaying the IBF, IBO, WBA, and WBO titles - which he previously held - alongside pennants bearing Ghami and Ayodele's names.

Meanwhile, ‘Latz x Sina, My Brother's Keeper, MBK’ was printed on the canvas in his corner.

Asked about how he has been coping after beating Prenga, Joshua said: 'It's been tough,' before becoming emotional. 'That's my brothers. I don't want to talk about that.'

Speaking on DAZN, Matchroom Boxing chief Eddie Hearn admitted he feared the heavyweight had returned to the ring too soon after witnessing his struggles in the opening round.

'Nobody can imagine what he's been through in that last seven months. In that first round, I thought we'd come back too soon,' Hearn said.

'Boxing got him through. To even be in the ring tonight is astonishing. You don't know what he's been through. He had to go to the depths one more time to get up, like he has done the last seven months.'

In February, Joshua memorialised Ghami and Ayodele by having their names tattooed on his arm.
