World.title: Philips reclaims €186m after Supreme Court rules tariffs illegal
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Health technology firm Philips has received an €186 million windfall after the United States Supreme Court ordered Donald Trump’s administration to refund illegally imposed tariffs.

The figures were included in the Amsterdam-based company’s latest quarterly report, which was published this week.

Trump imposed import tariffs on products from dozens of countries, as well as the European Union, in April last year.

But in February the Supreme Court upheld a judgment by a lower court that the president had wrongly used emergency powers to introduce the tariffs.

The US government was also ordered to refund and compensate companies that had paid the tariffs or whose business had been damaged as a result.

CEO Roy Jakobs said: “We started a legal case as soon as we could, which is why we are one of the first to get our money back.” Most of the repayments have already been made.

The extra income helped Philips increase its turnover by 4% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. It recorded a profit of €386 million, but declining orders in both China and the US meant its share price dived by 10% on Tuesday.

Philips was founded in 1891 as a lightbulb manufacturer in Eindhoven and grew into one of the world’s largest producers of consumer electronics in the 20th century. Since 2010 it has focused on producing healthcare equipment.

World.title: Man arrested after disabled man found strangled in German hotel
World.content:
A man has been arrested in Almelo in connection with the death of a Dutch tourist who was found strangled in a hotel room in Germany, close to the border.

The 35-year-old victim was discovered by staff on Sunday at Hotel Rheinpark in Rees, a German town about 30km south of Doetinchem.

A postmortem examination confirmed that the man had been strangled. He checked in to the hotel with another man on Saturday evening, but only the victim’s details were recorded in the guest register.

RTV Oost reported that the victim, from Enschede, was disabled and used a wheelchair. He was found dead by hotel staff on Sunday morning an hour after he was supposed to have checked out of the room.

German media said the pair arrived on Saturday in a Dutch-registered car from the Enschede area. They are understood to have gone to see a firework show in the area earlier in the day.

The 42-year-old man was arrested at his home in De Burcht, near Almelo, while he was walking towards his car, local media reported. He is suspected of being involved in the violent death of his companion. The vehicle also been impounded.

World.title: Drought and low river levels threaten Rhine cruises
World.content:
Low water levels are putting river cruises on the Rhine in jeopardy, with excursions being cancelled or cut short because boats are unable to access sections of the river.

Cruise operators told NOS they are anxiously monitoring the water level on a daily basis to see whether their scheduled trips can go ahead.

Teun Sijbrands, of SijFa Cruises, said 140 passengers boarded the Otello this week for a trip to Strasbourg, but it was unlikely that the boat would be able to travel that far.

The Otello has a depth of 1.45m, which is currently too deep to go further than Koblenz. “To get to Strasbourg we need more rain, but there’s no sign of it coming. That’s a big problem for us.

“If people don’t get the trip that’s described in the brochure, they can claim their money back.”

A spokesman for De Zonnebloem, an Arnhem-based ship that hosts cruises for people with disabilities, said: “We can’t go to Germany for the time being. Our first trip that way is planned for September, but it’s uncertain whether it will go ahead.”

Summer droughts are expected to become more likely as a result of climate change, making it increasingly difficult for river traffic.

At Lobith in Gelderland, the point at which the Rhine enters the Netherlands, the flow of water was down to 745 m3 per second in mid-July, less than half the average for the time of year of 1,900 m3.

Highways and waterways agency Rijkswaterstaat, which is responsible for river traffic, said the river level is unusually low for so early in the year, causing problems for both leisure cruises and cargo barges.

The problems are caused by low rainfall not just in the Netherlands, but further upstream in the Alps, rivers specialist Daniël van Putten told NOS. “That water just isn’t reaching us,” he said.

World.title: Body parts found on Texel identified as Afghan refugees
World.content:
The police have identified the remains that washed on up a Texel beach in 2023 as two men from Afghanistan who are thought to have been trying to cross the North Sea to the United Kingdom.

A beachcomber made the gruesome discovery of legs and feet in October 2023.

Police could find no match to the DNA in missing persons databases, but aid organisations later notified Dutch authorities that two men from Afghanistan were missing. The Red Cross was able to collect samples from relatives and the police have now confirmed there was a match.

“With this DNA, it could be established that the body parts originated from two men aged 20 and 27 (in 2023), born in Afghanistan,” the police said in a statement.

No cause of death could be determined. The remains were buried in a city cemetery in Den Burg.

In 2014, the remains of a Syrian man, who was also thought to be trying to cross the Channel, washed up on Texel.

World.title: Dutch government is neglecting Bonaire climate change ruling
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The government is not taking measures to address its legal obligations to protect the former Dutch colony of Bonaire from the ravages of climate change, according to an investigation by NOS.

A court in The Hague ruled in January the government had acted in a discriminatory manner towards Bonaire by excluding the Caribbean island from its climate plans.

Although the cabinet has appealed, ministers are still obliged to comply with the terms of the judgment, including providing an assessment of how much greenhouse gas that the Netherlands believes it can still emit without exceeding the Paris climate goals.

That report was due today and, according to the NOS, the government has not submitted it.

“Failing to provide insight into that scope is simply negligent,” climate lawyer Laura Burgers of the University of Amsterdam told NOS.

In response to questions from the broadcaster, climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said that the cabinet will provide more information on Budget Day – 15 September – regarding how the Bonaire ruling will be implemented.

Eight people from the Caribbean island of Bonaire joined forces with environmental organisation Greenpeace to sue the Dutch government for failing to protect them against climate change.

World.title: Vandals attack homes as row over asylum seekers turns violent
World.content:
A bitter war has broken out in two Brabant villages over plans to accommodate 50 refugees in the area, with supporters having their homes vandalised by anti-immigration campaigners.

Slogans using words such as teef (bitch) and hoer (whore) were scrawled on the walls and windows of homes in Bokhoven and Engelen, near Den Bosch, where the council’s plans have been the focus of heated protests and riots.

One couple, who gave their names as Rob and Ingrid, told Omroep Brabant they were not outright supporters of the plan, but had called for an open debate about the implications.

“We understand that people in De Vutter [the location of the proposed shelter] have real concerns,” Rob said.

He accused opponents of the scheme of trying to shut down the discussion through intimidation and violence. “A few months ago Ingrid called in our village newspaper for us to stand together as a village and organise things properly,” he said.

“That open approach has meant that the media and others have put us on the side of the actual supporters and our name has been circulated by extreme opponents.”

Spreading law

The municipality announced in April it wanted to house 50 boys and girls aged between 15 and 18 on an industrial site in the area, to meet its obligations under the so-called “spreading law” that requires councils to share the responsibility for accommodating asylum seekers.

Demonstrations that were held outside community meetings turned to riots as stones were thrown and fireworks were let off.

Police in riot gear with dogs cleared away a group of 100 protesters, some of whom tried to block the A59 motorway, and arrested two people during two nights of violence.

In May the council announced it was postponing the decision so it could hold more community information sessions. Two days later an explosion damaged the building where the refugees were due to be held.

Rob said it was clear from camera footage that the attacks on his home had been carried out by a group of youths.

“Once the police have caught the youths, we would like to have a conversation with them,” he said. “They probably have no idea how it affects you emotionally when you go through this.”

Syrians attacked

In a separate incident, police in Geesteren said a family of asylum seekers from Syria had been targeted several times by vandals and had their car set on fire after moving in to the village earlier this year.

The family, whose children are aged six, three and one, were allocated the house after being granted settled status, four years after they first arrived in the Netherlands.

Windows in the property have been smashed three times since March and on Sunday night their car was set ablaze. Police are treating the incident as arson, but say locals are too anxious to come forward with information.

Community silence

“The anxiety means people don’t dare to talk to us,” local police spokeswoman Chantal Westerhoff told NOS. “What I mean by that is that we have no tips at present or indications of who caused this.”

The mayor of Tubbergen, Anko Postma, whose municipality includes Geesteren, said extra protection was being arranged for the family.

“This must have a big impact on a family just as they are trying to build a new life here,” he said. “We are in contact with them and are looking at what support they need.”

The father, Al Arab, told NOS he was considering leaving the village because he was worried his family were becoming a burden. “Maybe it’s better if we go. Our dear neighbours are getting scared,” he said.

World.title: Four Dutch tourists found after speedboat goes missing in Malawi
World.content:
Four Dutch tourists who were reported missing when a speedboat failed to return from a trip on Lake Malawi have been found safe.

Malawian authorities put out an alert after the Tanzanian-registered boat failed to arrive at the expected time at Nkhata Bay on Sunday.

Three crew members, two from Malawi and one from Tanzania, were also on board, but there had been no contact from the vessel since it left Mbamba Bay, on the Tanzanian side of the lake, between 10am and 11am.

The Dutch foreign affairs ministry said the visitors were safely on land and had been given medical assistance, but did not give any further details of their condition, citing privacy concerns.

“Thanks to the search operation by the local authorities, in co-operation with the embassy, this worrying situation has thankfully been concluded.”

The speedboat belonged to a Tanzanian businessman, who alerted the authorities when he was unable to contact the crew and visitors on board, local news site the Nyasa Times reported.

Boats crossing the lake are required to register their arrival time with the port master 24 hours in advance, but this protocol was not followed. Local fishermen, boat operators and lakeshore communities were all urged to look out for the missing vessel during the search operation.

World.title: Prince Bernhard cashes out of real estate to go into AI
World.content:

Prince Bernhard has sold his entire business portfolio, including his stake in the Zandvoort motor racing circuit, and will now focus on AI.

The first cousin of king Willem-Alexander told Dutch press agency ANP that he was selling his interest in Media Park in Hilversum, IT company Levi9, and his extensive real estate portfolio to his business partners.

“The world is changing faster than ever. New technologies, artificial intelligence, and major societal changes are creating opportunities that we could hardly have imagined ten years ago,” he said.

The 56-year-old did not disclose the amount of the sale, but business magazine Quote has estimated his net worth at around €160 million.

Bernhard’s large real estate holdings – 98 buildings according to Quote – have earned him the nickname pandjesprins, or the property prince.

In 2017, an investigation by Amsterdam newspaper Het Parool found that Bernhard’s companies engaged in practices that violated Amsterdam’s housing regulations.

Earlier this year, Bernhard announced he and his wife, Princess Annette, were separating after 25 years of marriage.

The prince bought the Zandvoort circuit 10 years ago with the aim of bringing Formula 1 back to the Netherlands. F1 racing returned to Zandvoort in 2021 after a 36-year absence, after the scheduled 2020 race was cancelled because of the coronavirus pandemic.

The final edition of the Dutch Grand Prix will be held later this year. Organisers announced in 2024 that they wouldn’t continue beyond the current contract because the costs were too high.

World.title: Polish court finds regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage registration unconstitutional
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. Nielegalny Trybunał Konstytucyjny po raz kolejny próbuje zatrzymać państwo, które wykonuje obowiązujące prawo i wyroki europejskich sądów. Transkrypcja zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych jest i będzie legalna. Rozporządzenie, które przyjęliśmy porządkuje dokumenty i… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. World.title: Residents oppose move to add Polish village to list of protected monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. It will help write letters, analyse inquiries from residents, and summarise long documents https://t.co/SLrmVg9VBz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 Earlier this month, Poland’s government approved a resolution enabling the country to participate in the European AI Gigafactory programme, committing more than 400 million zloty towards what the government says would be the largest computing centre in the country’s history. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”. World.title: UNESCO adds Poland’s modernist port city of Gdynia to World Heritage List
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. UNESCO has added the modernist city centre of the Polish port city of Gdynia to its World Heritage List, recognising its interwar urban planning and architecture. The designation, approved during the World Heritage Committee’s 48th session in Busan, South Korea, is Poland’s 18th World Heritage site and comes as Gdynia marks the centenary of gaining city rights. In its justification, UNESCO referred to “an urban organism that harnesses a building-block-based planning approach to develop a characteristic, compact complex of modernist architecture, with robust individual architectural expressions”. Gdynia’s city centre “illustrates a critical break with historicism in the progression of turning the village of Gdynia into a new major sea gateway of the first Polish Republic between the First and Second World Wars”, it added. Granted city status in 1926, Gdynia was rapidly developed by the newly independent Polish state from a small fishing village into a major Baltic seaport, growing to more than 100,000 residents in under 20 years and providing Poland with a modern maritime gateway. It is now Poland’s 13th largest city by population, with just under 210,000 residents, and the third largest by area when including its maritime territory. Nowy tydzień zaczynamy od dobrych wieści! Komitet Światowego Dziedzictwa UNESCO oficjalnie uznał modernistyczne centrum Gdyni za dobro o wyjątkowym znaczeniu dla całego świata. Nie ma lepszego momentu niż 100-lecie Gdyni na to wyjątkowe wyróżnienie!https://t.co/L3WZZCJCAz — Gdynia (@MiastoGdynia) July 27, 2026 Oktawia Gorzeńska, Gdynia’s deputy mayor, who represented the city in Busan, celebrated the decision of the committee as “a wonderful gift for our anniversary and a tribute to the vision and determination of the people who created one of Europe’s great modernist cities”. The city’s mayor, Aleksandra Kosiorek, added that the decision “confirms that the vision which launched the history of modern Gdynia over a century ago has retained its power and universal significance.” Gdynia’s central district of Śródmieście was built largely between 1926 and 1939. Its rapid development at the time drew international attention, with a National Geographic reporter writing that “Poland dreams of building her New York”. Unlike Warsaw and nearby Gdańsk, it escaped extensive destruction during World War Two, preserving much of its original street layout and interwar architecture. According to the city authorities, UNESCO experts have recognised the Gdynia’s centre as one of the world’s most outstanding examples of early modernism in urban planning. The nomination also highlighted Gdynia’s distinctive model of modernist urban planning, setting it apart from contemporaneous developments such as Germany’s Bauhaus, Berlin’s housing estates, Kaunas in Lithuania and Tel Aviv. Gdynia’s modernist architecture is characterised by white façades and maritime-inspired details, including round windows and building forms resembling ship hulls. Gdańsk in Poland has been named a global City of Literature by @UNESCO. It is now one of only 63 such cities in the world, and the third in Poland to obtain the distinction https://t.co/QdMxlT65V4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2025 Notable examples include the so-called “bank building”, a modernist tenement block, and the Museum of Emigration, housed in the former Maritime Station, which from the 1930s until 1979 was a transit building from which thousands of Polish emigrants left for their new homelands. According to the city, the road to recognition took over 20 years, beginning in 2007, when the historic urban layout was entered into the regional register of monuments. It was designated a Monument of History in 2015, and Poland submitted the site to UNESCO’s Tentative List in 2019. Two sites in Poland were included in the inaugural World Heritage List in 1978: the Historic Centre of Kraków and the nearby Wieliczka and Bochnia Royal Salt Mines. Gdynia’s inscription is the 18th for Poland overall and the first for a Polish modernist urban complex. The most recent Polish additions before Gdynia were the Krzemionki Prehistoric Striped Flint Mining Region in 2019 and, in 2021, the beech forests in the Bieszczady Mountains. World.title: Polish president obstructs windfall tax on fuel firms’ excess profits, prompting government criticism
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s “shocking decision” not to sign into law the government’s planned windfall tax on excess profits by fuel companies amid a sharp surge in fuel prices caused by the war in Iran. While Nawrocki did not veto the bill, he exercised his right to refuse to sign it and instead send it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment, a process that can take years. The president argued that the retroactive nature of the tax “raises serious constitutional concerns”. Nowy podatek nie obniża cen paliwa. Ma przede wszystkim dostarczyć pieniędzy do budżetu. Nie mogę zaakceptować sytuacji, w której próbę łatania finansów państwa przedstawia się obywatelom jako ochronę ich interesów, podczas gdy skutkiem będzie kolejna fala podwyżek – Prezydent… pic.twitter.com/LqI7Cojdrr — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 In mid-June, the government approved a 60% tax on excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€927 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among others, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. The bill was approved by parliament on 3 July. It received support from Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, but was opposed by the right-wing and far-right opposition. According to a regulatory impact assessment, state energy giant Orlen is expected to account for about 60% of the tax base for the windfall tax, with the remaining 40% generated by other market participants. Poland’s government has approved a windfall tax on fuel companies' excess profits after the surge in energy prices due to the war in Iran. It expects the measure, which still requires parliamentary and presidential approval, to raise 4bn zloty (€940m) https://t.co/DpXa8VJDjf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 The legislation then passed to Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year. However, this time he instead exercised his right to refer the bill to the TK without either signing or vetoing it. In a speech announcing his decision on Friday, Nawrocki said that the proposed measures “raise serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that tax would be retroactive: it would go into force in August but would apply to revenue earned from the beginning of March. “In a democratic state governed by the rule of law, citizens and businesses must know what regulations apply at the time decisions are made,” said Nawrocki. “The state cannot change the rules a few months later and send a bill for actions taken in accordance with applicable law.” The president also argued that, ultimately, the costs of the tax would be passed on to consumers, who have already been paying much higher fuel costs since the government’s protective measures expired at the end of June. “Unfortunately, it appears that the government first lowered fuel prices for propaganda purposes, and now has decided to impose a hefty bill on Poles,” declared Nawrocki. Once a bill is sent to the TK for assessment, there is generally no time limit on how long the tribunal can take to consider it. In practice, this means that some cases can can remain unresolved for years. If the TK does find a bill to be constitutional, the president must sign it into law. Currently, a majority of judges on the TK, including its chief justice, were appointed by and are regarded as aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland until 2023 and which supported Nawrocki’s presidential candidacy last year. The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision not to approve the windfall tax was condemned by government figures, including finance minister Andrzej Domański, who accused the president of “once again striking against Poland’s public finances”. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increased tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. “Instead of standing on the side of Poles, he sided with fuel corporations reaping huge profits from the current situation on the fuel market,” wrote Domański on social media. Tusk, meanwhile, wrote that the president had “blocked a bill that would have allowed taxing the gigantic profits of fuel conglomerates, making it possible to fund cheaper fuel at our stations”. He told consumers to “remember this [when you are] at the fuel pumps”. In response, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, called Tusk an “economic dilettante” for thinking that imposing a tax would somehow lower costs rather than cause prices to rise. He instead called on the government to again lower VAT and excise duty on fuels. Od dawna wiadomo, że obecny premier jest gospodarczym dyletantem. Teraz próbuje przekonać Polaków, że nałożenie nowego podatku na paliwa sprawi, iż ceny na stacjach spadną. Zamiast nakładać kolejne podatki, proszę obniżyć VAT i akcyzę, tak jak robił to rząd Prawa i… https://t.co/3xvav6Dieu — Paweł Szefernaker 🇵🇱 (@szefernaker) July 25, 2026 The dispute over the tax comes as Poland faces an increasingly difficult fiscal situation. It had the second-largest budget deficit in the European Union last year, at 7.3% of GDP. That was far higher than the 5.5% the Polish government had pledged in 2024 when it was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Data released last week by Eurostat showed that, in the first quarter of 2026, Poland had the EU’s third-largest annual increase in debt-to-GDP ratio, at 4.5 percentage points. In March, credit rating agency Fitch, which last year switched Poland’s credit outlook to negative, warned that the “political gridlock” between the president and the government will continue to hinder policymaking, including tackling “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. World.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz (pictured above on the right), a prominent figure in the underground resistance that fought against the Soviet-installed communist authorities in the years after World War Two. Dziemieszkiewicz, who was killed by the communist security services in 1951 and dumped in an unmarked mass grave, was identified through a combination of historical detective work and genetic testing, including exhuming the remains of his deceased mother and sister to obtain DNA samples. “Once again, we can say that the communist authorities did not win. Heroes prevail,” declared Krzysztof Szwagrzyk, deputy head of the IPN. “Even in the most difficult situations, we must seek the truth, find those of whom no trace was supposed to remain, and restore their names.” While World War Two officially came to an end in 1945, tens of thousands of Poles, known as the “cursed soldiers” (żolnierze wyklęci), continued to fight against the Soviets and the communist regime they installed in Poland. While most had laid down arms by 1947, some continued fighting well beyond then, including Dziemieszkiewicz, who operated under the nom de guerre “Rój” (meaning “swarm”). Dziemieszkiewicz, who was 20 years old when the war ended, came from a family that had been part of Poland’s wartime resistance. His anti-communist views were hardened when his elder brother, Roman, was killed by Red Army soldiers in 1945. After being conscripted that year into the Soviet-backed Polish People’s Army, Dziemieszkiewicz defected and joined the underground resistance forces, where he rose to command a unit tasked with eliminating regime officials and members of the communist Polish Workers Party (PPR). Dziemieszkiewicz’s group killed around two dozen members of the communist security services and more than 20 informants, according to the IPN. In 1950, the communist authorities intensified efforts to dismantle Dziemieszkiewicz’s unit, using threats and blackmail to recruit hundreds of agents and informants in an effort to locate the resistance fighters. Eventually, one such informant gave up Dziemieszkiewicz’s location in exchange for a promise to release her parents from captivity. Dziemieszkiewicz found himself surrounded by several hundred soldiers and was killed while trying to escape. After his body had been identified by his family, Dziemieszkiewicz was buried in a section of Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw where the remains of those killed by the communist security services were placed en masse in unmarked graves. Exhumations by the IPN, which was established after the fall of communism to investigate communist and Nazi crimes in Poland, have located over 200 complete bodies at that site as well as several thousand bone fragments. During that work, one set of remains was found buried with an eagle symbol and remnants of a black cloth. IPN researchers realised that the item was similar to a beret that appeared in posthumous photographs of Dziemieszkiewicz’s body taken by the communist security services. That prompted them to carry out genetic testing on the remains and compare them to samples taken from Dziemieszkiewicz’s mother and sister, who were buried in a cemetery in the town of Maków Mazowiecki. “We have found ‘Rój’, commander of one of the longest-fighting units of the independence underground,” declared the IPN on Friday, announcing the confirmation of his identity. They described Dziemieszkiewicz as “legend in life and a symbol of the fight against communist oppression”. The identification was announced today during a press conference at @PrzystanekH. The identification is the result of many years of work carried out by the IPN. It was preceded by extensive archival and investigative research, the analysis of forensic evidence, archaeological… https://t.co/Rcf4wemJFc pic.twitter.com/XgMUAgSQc6 — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) July 24, 2026 At a conference announcing the findings, the IPN noted that Dziemieszkiewicz’s remains had been located right next to those of another prominent anti-communist resistance fighter, Zygmunt Szendzielarz, who fought under the nom de guerre “Łupaszko”. “It is an incredible situation that two great and distinguished soldiers of the Polish underground lie next to each other in this part of the Powązki Cemetery,” said Szwagrzyk. However, Szendzielarz, who was executed by the communist authorities in 1951, has a contested legacy, given evidence that his unit was involved in the massacre of dozens of Lithuanian civilians. Some other “cursed soldiers” have faced similar accusations of war crimes. While it was often IPN historians who uncovered evidence of such actions, the institution has more recently begun to honour those figures, particularly under the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice government between 2015 and 2023. Opposition MPs walked out of parliament yesterday as the chamber commemorated an underground officer who fought against Nazi-German occupation and the imposition of communism in Poland, but has also been accused of a war crime against civilians https://t.co/MIY7krOxTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 9, 2022 Dziemieszkiewicz himself, however, like most of the cursed soldiers, has not faced such accusations. In 2007, President Lech Kaczyński posthumously awarded Dziemieszkiewicz the Commander’s Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta, one of Poland’s highest honours. In 2020, his image was featured on a commemorative silver coin issued by the National Bank of Poland. Through a combination of brutal repression and offering amnesties, the communist authorities managed to end most resistance efforts by 1947. However, the last “cursed soldier” to die in combat, Józef Franczak, was killed in 1963, 18 years after the end of the war. World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Inside IAM Prague: How a Travelling Exhibition Laid the Foundation for One of the City’s Top-Rated Museums
World.content:
Just off Old Town Square, past the cafes and the crowds waiting for the Astronomical Clock, sits a museum that started almost by accident.

Today, IAM Prague has welcomed well over 1 million visitors from around the world and has held TripAdvisor’s Travelers’ Choice Award for five straight years.

From Shopping Malls to Old Town Square

The museum wasn’t originally supposed to be a… museum. Co-founder Jakub Bechyně and his partner Patrik Proško had been running a traveling illusion exhibit that moved between shopping malls, renting space for a month at a time before packing up and relocating. It worked, but it wasn’t permanent.

Then, in 2017, the owner of a building on Old Town Square approached them with an idea: turn part of it into a museum. The catch was the timeline. They wanted it open in two months.

Rather than build something from scratch, the team pulled from what they already had on the shelf, opening with one floor and sixteen exhibits in 2018. The collection has grown to more than 60 pieces since.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Illusion Art Museum Prague (@iamprague)

The museum moved to its current location in 2022 after the original building was sold. The new space, ideally located between Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, needed walls removed and floors rebuilt to accommodate the art. The costs were substantial, but it turned out to be a good problem to have as the location dramatically increased the exhibition’s visibility to passersby on one of Prague’s busiest tourist thoroughfares.

Choosing Technique Over Fame

IAM Prague doesn’t chase famous names. It chases techniques. The team looks for a specific kind of illusion craft, one with real artistic quality, a genuine optical trick, and ideally a story behind it worth telling.

That approach led them to reverse-perspective specialist Patrick Hughes, and to artists whose work they discovered secondhand and eventually acquired outright rather than simply displaying on loan. In several cases, the museum ended up owning the pieces after renting them for years and deciding they belonged permanently in the collection.

About 80 percent of the exhibition has changed since opening. Early pieces built quickly to fill the space have gradually been replaced as the museum brought in stronger, more polished work from local and international artists.

The exhibition’s evolution continues, with four new pieces from international artists like Jonty Hurwitz and Andrej Boleslavsky, ranging from traditional mirror anamorphoses to digital art, recently unveiled in June.

History Hidden in Plain Sight

Much of what makes IAM Prague distinct is how it uses illusion as a delivery method for history. A glass-art piece featuring four endangered animals turns out to double as an environmental message.

A defenestration scene lets visitors reenact one of Prague’s most repeated historical events, tied to the 1618 uprising that helped trigger the Thirty Years’ War. Even the museum’s own opening date, a century after Czechoslovak independence in 1918, was picked on purpose.

One exhibit nods to Karel Čapek, the Czech writer who coined the word “robot,” a term that entered global use even though it comes from a Slavic word for forced labor.

Another traces the story of Tomáš Baťa, the industrialist who pioneered mass shoe manufacturing and built factories across multiple continents, including a Pakistani city that still carries his name today.

AI’s Impact on Art & Travel

Though much has been made on artificial intelligence’s impact on the world of art, the team’s biggest current concern isn’t AI-generated art replacing the exhibition’s themselves. It’s the shift in how travelers plan their trips.

For years, visibility depended on traditional guidebooks, online travel agencies, physical advertising, and street presence. Increasingly, travelers are relying on AI chat tools to create itineraries, shifting the importance of more “traditional” visibility mechanisms, which is forcing venues like Illusion Art Museum Prague to adapt.

Despite the changing landscape, the plan going forward leans further into digital and kinetic art, including new motion-based installations recently brought in from Berlin by artists like Florian Goerlitz.

For a museum that started as a temporary mall exhibit, the goal has stayed consistent since day one: make people stop, look twice, and leave with a story they didn’t expect to learn.

World.title: Nearly One in Five Prague Farmers’ Market Vendors Fail Veterinary Inspections
World.content:
Nearly one in five vendors inspected at Prague’s farmers’ markets during the first half of 2026 were found to have breached food safety or labeling regulations, according to the State Veterinary Administration (SVS).

Between January and June, veterinary inspectors checked 53 vendors across Prague and identified violations in 10 cases, representing almost 19 percent of all inspections.

Nationwide, inspectors carried out 165 inspections, with irregularities detected in 27 cases, or roughly 16 percent.

Officials said the most common problems in Prague involved improper storage temperatures for food of animal origin, incorrect or incomplete product labeling, and inadequate protection of food from contamination during sale.

Inspectors also highlighted several cases they considered particularly serious. In one instance, a vendor was found producing meat products without the legally required authorization while packaging them with the identification mark of a production facility that no longer exists. Authorities said such practices can mislead consumers about where products originate.



The SVS warned that food safety risks increase during the summer months, especially at outdoor markets where high temperatures make it more difficult to maintain proper cooling conditions.

Across the Czech Republic, labeling violations were the most frequently recorded offense this year, accounting for 26 cases. Problems related to hygiene and production practices—including incorrect storage temperatures and insufficient protection against contamination—followed with 22 cases.

Inspectors also documented 18 violations involving improper handling of food products and 12 cases where the origin of goods was unclear or could not be verified.

The SVS noted that a single inspection may uncover multiple breaches. While inspectors found violations in 27 inspections nationwide, the total number of individual offenses reached 82.

Inspection results remained largely unchanged compared with the same period last year. During the first six months of 2025, inspectors also carried out 165 inspections, finding violations in 16 percent of them. The main difference was that hygiene-related shortcomings topped the list last year, while labeling issues have become the most common problem in 2026.

Looking at the full year, the SVS carried out 380 market inspections across the Czech Republic in 2025, compared with 372 inspections in 2024. The proportion of inspections uncovering violations rose slightly from 17 percent to 18 percent.

World.title: Not an Official Visit: Petr Pavel Attends Hungarian GP as F1 Photographer
World.content:
The president of the Czech Republic, Petr Pavel, has made his way to the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday – but was not an official visit.

Ever wondered what world leaders do in their free time? For Czech Republic president Petr Pavel, the answer is sports photography – and he’s particularly passionate about motorsport.

This weekend, he was attending the Hungarian GP with a full photography kit – and an official FIA accreditation. He arrived at the Hungaroring for Saturday’s sessions and was already taking pictures, accompanied by Czech F1 photographer Jiri Krenek.



This wasn’t the first time he was seen at a major motorsport event as a hobby photographer. Most recently, Pavel travelled to France in June to attend the Le Mans 24 Hours, once again equipped with full camera gear.

In fact, the former NATO Military Chairman has attended several races on both two and four wheels over the years.

Within the Czech Republic, Pavel covered the MotoGP and World Superbike events at Brno, while he has travelled as far as the US and Saudi Arabia to photograph NASCAR and the Dakar Rally respectively.

Last year, he also raised nearly 30,000 euros for a charity dedicated to children, single parents and the elderly by auctioning a photo album.

While it is unusual for politicians to attend races purely for leisure, several leaders regularly appear at major motorsport events in their own countries.

Last year, then British Prime Minister Keir Starmer hosted F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, drivers and senior team figures at a reception in 10 Downing Street ahead of the British GP.

World.title: Best Petting Zoos in Prague for Families with Kids (2026 Guide)
World.content:
Prague Zoo gets all the attention — and fair enough, it’s consistently ranked among the top zoos in the world — but the city is also full of smaller, low-key spots where kids can get hands-on with animals.

These mini farms and forest parks are perfect for a relaxed weekend outing, most are free or nearly free, and several are just a short metro ride from the centre.

Here’s our pick of the best small zoos and petting farms around Prague.

1. Milíčovský dvůr – Prague 11

Right on the edge of Milíčov forest, this outdoor farm is home to a horse, an ostrich, a fox, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits and more. Feed dispensers let kids feed the animals directly, and there’s a sandpit, a wooden playground and a small snack stand on site. Entry costs just 20 CZK. Closed Mondays.

📍 K Milíčovu 100/8, Prague 11 — nearest metro: Háje



2. Chuchle Grove Mini Zoo – Prague 5

Set on a hillside inside the Chuchle Grove nature park, this zoo run by Prague’s city forestry service cares for injured and orphaned wildlife. Expect to see mouflons, deer, wild boar, owls, lynxes and more — though petting isn’t allowed here, since the focus is conservation and education. Free entry, open 24/7, with a playground and refreshment kiosk nearby

📍 V Lázních 8, Prague 5

3. Station of Young Biologists – Prague 5

A mix of indoor and outdoor spaces near Anděl, with a tropical terrarium (crocodiles, monkeys, boas), an aviary, and outdoor pens with kangaroos, llamas, ponies and goats. Regular workshops and interactive shows run alongside the animal exhibits. General entry is free; the terrarium and greenhouses cost a small fee (20–40 CZK).

📍 Drtinova 1A, Prague 5 — near Anděl metro

4. Toulcův dvůr – Prague 10

An 8.5-hectare environmental education centre in Hostivař with cows, horses, chickens, pigs, sheep and goats, plus a cherry orchard, wetlands and a farm-to-table restaurant. Petting and feeding aren’t permitted, but it’s a beautifully kept site for a nature walk.

📍 Kubátova 1/32, Prague 10

Honourable mentions

If you’re just after a nice walk with a chance of spotting animals, these free spots are worth a detour:

Wild Garden Hostivař (Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk.

(Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk. Kunratice Forest (Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails.

(Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails. Kamýk Forest (Prague 12) — a small goat enclosure and pheasant aviary tucked next to the gamekeeper’s lodge, surrounded by walking and cycling trails.

World.title: Stromovka: A Green Paradise in the Heart of Prague
World.content:
Stromovka is one of the largest and most popular parks in Prague, drawing visitors with its beautiful nature, rich history, and numerous activities.

Let’s explore what Stromovka offers and how to get there.

Why Visit Stromovka?

Looking for a break from the city’s hustle and bustle or the perfect spot for a picnic with friends? Stromovka is your ideal choice. This vast park features green meadows, shady alleys, and ample opportunities for sports and cultural events.

What is Stromovka?

Stromovka, officially known as Královská obora, spans more than 95 hectares, making it one of Prague’s largest green spaces. Located in Prague 7, the park is a favorite among joggers, cyclists, families, and anyone looking to escape into nature without leaving the city.

It’s perfect for walks, picnics, sports, or simply relaxing on the grass.



A Brief History

Stromovka’s history dates back to the 13th century when it was established as a royal hunting ground. Over time, it evolved and expanded, becoming a public park in the 19th century. The park is home to the original Vltava Creek and several ponds, which host various water birds.

Throughout its history, Stromovka has undergone many changes, shaping it into the popular relaxation spot it is today.

Activities in Stromovka

Stromovka offers a wide range of activities for all ages. Here are some ideas:

Walking and Running: Enjoy the scenic trails.

Cycling: Explore the park on two wheels.

Picnics: Large meadows and shady spots are perfect for a picnic.

Sports: Play football, volleyball, and other sports.

Cultural Events: Attend various events hosted in the park.

How to Get to Stromovka

By Metro: The nearest metro station is Nádraží Holešovice (line C). From there, it’s just a few minutes’ walk to Stromovka.

By Tram: Trams also reach the park. The nearest stops are Výstaviště Holešovice (lines 6, 12, 17) and Planetarium Prague (line 6).

By Bike: Cycling enthusiasts can easily access Stromovka by bike. Bike-sharing stations like Rekola and Nextbike are available around the park, allowing you to ride directly into this natural haven.

World.title: August 12-31: Prague to Host Festival of New Circus Letní Letná
World.content:
The international festival of new circus and theatre, Letní Letná 2026, will take place in Prague on August 12-31.

The festival will feature over 200 performances, workshops, concerts, and various acts by circus artists from 14 countries, including a special program for children.

This year marks the 23rd edition of the festival. Letenské sady park will once again be the main venue, with tents set up to create a mini-town complete with a coffee shop and an evening bar.



Many performances will be free of charge. Additionally, the festival will offer a rich and varied daily program: children’s shows, circus, juggling and acrobat workshops, music concerts, exhibitions, lectures, creative workshops, and more.

One of this year’s highlights is Wolf by Australia’s renowned Circa ensemble. The international lineup also includes Switzerland’s Accademia Teatro Dimitri, presenting its graduate production La Grinta, and Seismic, a collaboration between French choreographer Marie Gourdain and German artist Felix Baumann, featuring Czech performers.

The Czech program includes the premiere of Vertige by AirGym Art Company, Enola by Eliška Brtnická, new productions from Losers Cirque Company, and Hey, Earth! by Cirque La Putyka.

Emerging talent will also take center stage, with performances by CZirkidz Dance Company, Teens Cirkabaret, and recent graduates of international circus schools.

Audiences will have the chance to experience works in progress, including K voknu by Michaela Stará and Filip Zahradnický, followed by discussions with the artists.

For adults, Světla a stíny by Silk&Steel explores the darker sides of human experience through aerial and ground acrobatics, while family-friendly performances include the popular (Not Only) Juggling Galashow and Orbiting Zero by Czech juggler Aleš Hrdlička.

Beyond the performances, visitors can enjoy free workshops, children’s activities, concerts, open-air events, food stalls, bars, and relaxation areas throughout the festival grounds. Babysitting is available during selected performances, and the venue is fully accessible, making Letní Letná a festival for all ages.

World.title: New Railway Tunnel to Cut Prague to Pilsen Journey to 45 Minutes
World.content:
The Czech government has approved the next phase of one of its largest railway infrastructure projects: a new tunnel connecting Prague and Beroun.

Construction is expected to begin in 2032, with completion scheduled for 2044.

The 24.7-kilometre double-track tunnel will significantly shorten travel times on one of the country’s busiest rail corridors.

Once completed, trains will travel between Prague-Smíchov station and Beroun in around 13 minutes, reducing the current journey time by more than 30 minutes.

The project will also improve connections towards western Czechia and neighbouring Germany. The journey from Prague to Pilsen is expected to take approximately 45 minutes, while international rail services to Munich and Nuremberg will become faster and more reliable.



New railway line designed for speeds of up to 200 km/h

The planned railway route will include a new high-speed section designed for trains travelling at up to 200 km/h. The tunnel will begin near Prague-Smíchov station, pass beneath the Barrandov area, and emerge near Beroun.

A separate connection on the Prague side is also planned, linking the new line with Braník Bridge and Prague-Krč. The additional infrastructure will improve connections within the capital while increasing capacity on the wider railway network.

Construction preparation underway

Preparatory work for the tunnel is already in progress. Geological surveys and technical documentation are currently being completed, with the application for a construction permit expected to be submitted between 2028 and 2029.

After the approval process, Správa železnic will launch a tender to select the construction company responsible for building the tunnel.

The Czech Railway Administration estimates the total cost of the project will continue to rise due to inflation and increasing construction expenses. However, its director general Tomáš Tóth said the estimated cost of around CZK 3 billion per kilometre remains comparable with similar railway tunnel projects abroad.

The project is expected to increase railway capacity towards western Czechia, improve timetable reliability, and strengthen connections between Prague, Pilsen, and major German cities.

World.title: Up to 160 new, eco-friendly low-floor trolleybuses could come to Budapest
World.content:
The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has paved the way for the city’s fleet to be expanded by as many as 160 new, eco-friendly, low-floor trolleybuses, should the necessary funding become available, the company said on Tuesday.

In a statement to MTI, BKK said it had signed the framework agreement for the vehicle procurement with Electrobus Europe Zrt. and Yutong, the companies that won the public tender, meaning that once the money is in place, the modernisation of Budapest’s vehicle fleet can continue, further improving the standard of public transport in the capital, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

To bring the framework agreement into force, funding for the purchase of the 40 vehicles covered by the commitment — 16 single-unit trolleybuses and 24 articulated trolleybuses — must be secured within six months of the contract being signed.

The transport organiser said it still aims to deliver the project with the help of European Union funding.
