“How can a writer be liked by everyone? Is there a single writer who is universally admired? How can anyone even make such a claim? Or say that a public figure must be liked by everyone? Only a dictator wants that. He wants everyone to like him. And anyone who does not must be neutralised, driven out, persecuted and beaten. That is why he creates groups like these.

“These restrictions are designed to instil a climate of irrational fear, discouraging people from thinking independently, protesting and speaking out. The current situation is exactly the one Bidzina Ivanishvili wants most, and he is using every mechanism at his disposal to maintain it. The only force capable of dismantling these mechanisms is society itself — a society with a firm stance. I do not believe society is silent. I am convinced that our society will resist.”

Civil confrontation in Georgia

World.title: Opinion: ‘Energy assets must be bought back at any cost’
World.content:
Erekle Pirveli, a professor at the Caucasus University and director of the Erekle Pirveli Research Centre, says the European Union’s 21st sanctions package, which targets the Russian state-owned company Inter RAO, has a direct impact on Georgia‘s energy system. The expert argues that the situation presents an opportunity for Georgia to regain control of its strategic energy assets.

The European Union has imposed sanctions on the Russian state-owned energy company Inter RAO. Through its subsidiaries, the company is the indirect owner of Telasi, Telmiko, and the Khrami I and Khrami II hydropower plants in Georgia.

Erekle Pirveli: “as a country, we need to make a strategic choice and strive to become more self-sufficient. This is far from a minor issue—we are talking about a strategic sector, and we need to reduce our dependence on a neighbouring state.

“Even if the value of these assets on the company’s books differs from their actual market value, the overall cost is ultimately not so great or burdensome for Georgia that it should entrust such vital strategic assets to others and remain dependent on someone else’s goodwill. This is something that clearly deserves a strategic reassessment and decisive action. Yet years have passed, and we have still not seen any meaningful steps in that direction.”

He added that “this must be done at any cost. We have estimated the company’s capital, and if the goal is to reduce its stake by 25%, its value based on the capital would be around 125 million lari (about $46.3m). The actual figure may differ, but we should be working step by step to reduce the foreign stake and increase our own.

“The Russian state-owned company effectively holds a monopoly in Georgia, as it controls electricity generation, distribution and supply. This is not just a business issue—it also concerns political and strategic interests. When a neighbouring and unpredictable state owns your strategic assets, it creates long-term macroeconomic risks.

“At the same time, these companies generate relatively modest annual profits compared with their capital—around 3%—which suggests that, for Russia, these assets are more a tool of political influence than a source of economic gain.”

Inter RAO and Georgia’s Energy Sector

World.title: US Embassy expresses concern over creation of Georgia’s hate speech unit
World.content:
The US Embassy in Georgia says it is concerned by the creation of a new hate speech unit, according to a written response to a request from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

The unit was established under the Ministry of Internal Affairs and began operating on 1 June 2026. According to the official description, it is responsible for “monitoring and taking legal action in response to hate speech, abusive campaigns and aggressive communication in the public sphere.”

The embassy stressed that the administration of President Donald Trump and the United States regard freedom of speech as a fundamental pillar of a functioning society and strongly oppose censorship.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty sent its request to the US Embassy on 22 July, after journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days in administrative detention over a Facebook post insulting members of the ruling Georgian Dream party — Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vlado Bozhadze.

What the embassy said

“The Donald Trump administration has made it clear that the United States views freedom of speech as a fundamental pillar of a functioning society, and we strongly oppose censorship and restrictive laws used to silence people whose views are deemed undesirable.

As we have shared with our Georgian partners, stability requires a political opposition that engages with state institutions on behalf of the citizens who elected it. Political stability, underpinned by broad representation of different views, is among the factors that make Georgia a reliable partner for US investment, security cooperation and a long-term strategic partnership.

We are concerned by the Georgian government’s creation of a hate speech unit. The best response to falsehoods and misguided views is more free speech, not enforced silence.”

Georgia’s hate speech unit

World.title: Abkhazia to buy Russian electricity ‘just in case’ from August to November
World.content:
The state-owned energy company Chernomorenergo plans to import electricity from Russia into Abkhazia between August and November to preserve water levels in the Jvar reservoir, which supplies the Ingur hydropower plant.

Until now, electricity imports took place only during the winter months, when water levels at the plant dropped. However, as electricity prices are significantly higher during that period, the Abkhaz authorities have decided to stock up on electricity while it is cheaper.

The 40% share of electricity generated by the Inguri hydropower plant allocated to Abkhazia under an informal agreement reached after the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war has, over the past decade, proved insufficient to meet the republic’s electricity needs.

According to Chernomorenergo Director General Timur Dzhindzholia, the annual shortfall amounts to around 500–650 million kWh. While Abkhazia’s budget now includes funding for electricity imports, it is not enough to fully cover the deficit. As a result, the government has opted to purchase Russian electricity during the months when prices are at their lowest.

As recently as two years ago, largely because of uncontrolled cryptocurrency mining, electricity consumption in Abkhazia reached 3 billion kWh a year. During the autumn and winter months, the republic experienced rolling blackouts.

A series of measures to optimise electricity consumption has significantly reduced the deficit. In 2025, around 320 million kWh was covered by humanitarian electricity supplies from Russia, while the remaining shortfall had to be met through commercial imports.

Timur Dzhindzholia said that eliminating the deficit entirely would require the construction of new power generation facilities.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Electricity imports from Russia to Abkhazia

World.title: Study finds women in Armenia work more hours than men because of unpaid household work
World.content:
Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

Women in Armenia work roughly four to five times more than men on unpaid household and care responsibilities, according to a study conducted by Ameria for the Armenian office of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). The study found that women spend an average of 15.3 hours a week on household chores, including cooking, cleaning and laundry. They also devote another 8.6 hours to childcare, caring for elderly family members and other family responsibilities.

According to economist Tigran Jrbashyan, head of management consulting at Ameria, women aged 30 to 35 carry the heaviest workload. They spend between 44 and 49 hours a week on these responsibilities.

“This is unpaid labour. No one pays for it. Yet by doing this work, women create value. That is extremely important and deserves recognition,” Jrbashyan said.

By comparison, men spend an average of less than four hours (3.6) a week on household chores. They devote just over two hours (2.2) to caring for family members. Men aged 30 to 40 record the highest figures, spending between eight and 11 hours a week.

Women receive no pay for 78% of the work they do

The researchers found that women in Armenia spend more time on various activities than men. Much of that time goes to household responsibilities, placing a heavier physical burden on them. Yet no one pays them for caring for their families.

According to Tigran Jrbashyan, women receive no pay for 78% of the work they do, as household responsibilities account for that share of their overall workload.

“In effect, women receive pay for only 22% of the work they do. For men, unpaid work accounts for around 11%, while paid work makes up the remaining 89%.”

‘It is important to make workplaces more family-friendly’

Lusine Sargsyan, head of the Yerevan office of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), says that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on unpaid household work often forces women to make a choice: whether to enter the workforce, whether to prioritise their careers or focus on starting a family and having children.

“We need to create conditions where women no longer have to choose one or the other. They should be able to have both. It is important that women can pursue formal employment while also having time for their families. Otherwise, the country will face demographic challenges,” she said.

When Sargsyan talks about creating better conditions for working women, she refers in particular to expanding access to nurseries and kindergartens, as well as developing childcare centres for young children.

Remote work is already available in Armenia, and working mothers can take advantage of it with their employer’s consent. The government has also recently introduced a “parental hour” policy. Under the new rules, working parents with children under the age of 12 can either arrive at work later or leave earlier. Parents with one or two children can reduce their working day by 30 minutes. Those with three or more children can shorten it by one hour. However, experts say these measures do not go far enough to create a truly family-friendly working environment.

Lusine Sargsyan stresses that spending 44 to 49 hours a week on household responsibilities means some women effectively work two full-time jobs. In addition to unpaid domestic work, they spend another 40 hours a week working for an employer.

She argues that this is problematic both economically and from a human rights perspective because women are left with little or no time for themselves. She also says excessive workloads reduce productivity at work and affect the quality of care they can provide for their children at home.

Sargsyan emphasises that workplaces need to become more family-friendly. That would allow women to fulfil their potential while also spending meaningful time with their families.

“Employers need to recognise that their employees have families. It is extremely important that women do not live with a constant sense of guilt. They should not feel guilty about spending too little time with their families. Nor should they worry at home about work they did not finish,” she explained.

Both Sargsyan and Jrbashyan stressed that many women are highly productive and, in many cases, better educated than men.

They argue that the country needs to create better conditions for women to work. Otherwise, the economy risks missing out on the higher value they could generate.

At the same time, both experts stressed that they are not arguing every woman should have formal employment or receive pay for household work. Instead, they say women should have the freedom to decide how they want to organise their lives. They believe giving women that choice would benefit the country’s economy, improve business performance and create a healthier family environment.

Women in Armenia work more than men, study finds

World.title: GYLA: ‘Georgia has effectively created an informal ‘morality police’, which could become a new form of violence’
World.content:
GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) has responded to reports about the creation of a movement to protect traditional values, warning that alongside existing legal restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and civic participation, the initiative could introduce new mechanisms of violence in the country.

The movement was announced on 26 July by MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili and several supporters. At a press briefing, he said the organisation would “respond immediately” to issues involving the country’s ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. Kartvelishvili said the movement would be “highly active, respectable and constructive”, adding that any “patriotic Georgian” would be welcome to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

GYLA described the initiative as the creation of an informal “morality police”, warning that it poses a threat to freedom of expression in Georgia.

According to the organisation, “everything suggests that the group’s aim may be to informally monitor, intimidate or pressure people who are critical of the authorities.”

GYLA’s lawyers added that “attempts to establish vigilante groups in the country are particularly alarming” given the rise in violence and intimidation targeting government critics in recent years.

GYLA said members of the new group are using defamatory and disinformation-laden language that closely mirrors narratives promoted by the authorities and pro-government media.

In particular, the group says it is launching a campaign “against people and organisations funded from abroad, enslaved to foreign interests and driven by a perverse ideology.”

According to GYLA, the group’s statements contain signs of incitement to violence. The lawyers pointed in particular to its declaration that “if circumstances leave no alternative, members of the group will not be afraid of going to prison.”

GYLA said the group has already demanded an apology from stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, who was recently severely beaten in the street after making a joke referring to Georgian literary classic Nodar Dumbadze.

The group has also asked prosecutors not to seek a prison sentence for the person accused of attacking Okriashvili. Otherwise, its representatives warned, there could be reprisals, according to GYLA.

“We will hold people accountable for every action and comment that insults the dignity of the Georgian people,” the group said in a statement cited by GYLA.

GYLA said such statements echo remarks made by senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party which, in the organisation’s view, call for greater control over freedom of expression.

The organisation also noted that attacks by third parties targeting people critical of the government were widely documented during the 2024 protests and in the months that followed.

According to GYLA, such incidents were often accompanied by statements from state officials appearing to support the attackers or by an inadequate response from law enforcement.

“Against this background, it is clear that the creation of a vigilante group and its declared intention to police citizens’ freedom of expression are closely linked to the state’s ongoing normalisation of violence,” GYLA said.

The organisation noted that Georgian criminal law prohibits the creation, leadership or membership of illegal armed or violent groups. It also bans the establishment of associations, or participation in them, if their activities involve violence against individuals.

GYLA said law enforcement authorities must take all measures provided for by law to prevent violence or intimidation against people exercising their fundamental rights.

According to the organisation, “pro-government media are actively contributing to the demonisation and targeting of individuals, which may amount to incitement to violence and complicity in it. The inaction or delayed response of state institutions creates an environment that enables violence to spread.”

GYLA warns violence could escalate in Georgia

World.title: Georgian banks to continue servicing local subsidiaries of sanctioned Russian energy giant Inter RAO
World.content:
Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

The National Bank of Georgia has announced that the country’s commercial banks will continue providing services in the national currency to Telasi, despite the company being owned by Russian energy giant Inter RAO, which was included in the European Union’s latest, 21st package of sanctions against Russia. The central bank confirmed the decision to BM.GE.

At the end of July, the European Union imposed sanctions on the Russian state-controlled energy company Inter RAO. Through its subsidiaries, the company is the indirect owner of Georgia’s electricity distribution companies Telasi and Telmiko, as well as the Khramhesi-1 and Khramhesi-2 hydropower plants.

The National Bank said that Telasi itself is not included on any sanctions list and that its uninterrupted operation is essential for the country’s population and economy. According to the central bank, while compliance with international sanctions is important, it is equally crucial to ensure the uninterrupted provision of essential services to the public.

The National Bank said that each sanctions-related case would be assessed on its individual merits. As a result, banks will continue providing services to Telasi “in compliance with the applicable sanctions regime, as well as in accordance with their own internal policies and risk assessment procedures.”

Georgian banks to continue servicing Telasi

World.title: Nine teenagers charged over alleged Melbourne carjackings
World.content:
Police have charged nine teenagers over several alleged carjackings in Melbourne's north this month.

Victoria Police said officers executed search warrants between July 22 and 28, arresting nine boys aged between 15 and 17.

Officers found an allegedly stolen vehicle as well as drugs, tasers, an incorrectly stored firearm, peptides and steroids during the raids.

The teenagers have been charged with a total of 61 offences, including aggravated carjacking, carjacking, discharging a firearm, affray and intentionally causing injury.

The charges follow a series of 18 alleged carjackings across Melbourne's northern suburbs, including Coburg, Fawkner, Hadfield, Campbellfield, Mickleham and Wallan between July 1 and 10.

The teenagers were all remanded and will face a children's court at a later date.

World.title: 'Very bad look': Brisbane defender given three-game ban
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop has been suspended for three games for a serious misconduct act he admits is a "very bad look".

Gallop pleaded guilty at the AFL Tribunal on Tuesday night for what he described as retaliation on Mitch Georgiades after the Port Adelaide forward grabbed his broken thumb.

The 20-year-old had tackled Georgiades to the ground during Sunday's clash in Brisbane and, after the ball left the area, shoved the Port attacker face-first into the turf.

Gallop played the match with strapping on a broken right thumb.

"Mitch has grabbed my thumb as I have gone to stand up," Gallop said, adding Georgiades' action was intentional.

But Gallop expressed remorse for retaliating, saying he had phoned Georgiades to apologise.

"Looking back now and watching the footage, I understand that the retaliation to what happened wasn't fair," he said.

"I have gone out of my way to push him down, which I am sorry for and I do regret. I'd like to have that time over again.

"It's a very bad look and there's no room for it in footy."

Gallop said his retaliation was an "immediate reaction".

"I have grabbed the back of his jersey and pushed him back into the ground," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I think I play a hard brand of footy but I play a very fair brand of footy as well … it was purely out of retaliation."

Under questioning from the AFL's counsel Nick Pane, Gallop agreed his act was totally unreasonable and unacceptable.

Pane asked the tribunal for a three-game suspension.

"Georgiades' head made forceful contact with the ground," Pane said. "The action had significant potential to cause serious injury."

The Port spearhead wasn't hurt in the incident.

Gallop's counsel Adrian Anderson said the 23-gamer had "lashed out" but argued for a two-match ban.

"There is a context here," Anderson said.

"It's different where someone has a broken thumb and it's grabbed and they react in the heat of the moment."

After hearing just over one hour of evidence, tribunal chairman Jeff Gleeson KC and members Darren Gaspar and Scott Stevens returned a verdict some 50 minutes later.

AFL Saturday live North Melbourne survives a nervy finish to break a decade-long drought against Essendon as star ruckman Tristan Xerri rubs blood on Andrew McGrath's face in a heated exchange.

Gleeson said the tribunal gave no weight in its deliberations to Gallop's thumb being grabbed before his misconduct.

"The vision of the serious misconduct is startling in the degree to which it is unsportsmanlike," he said.

Gallop is the sixth AFL player suspended on a serious misconduct charge and the second this season, following North Melbourne ruckman Tristan Xerri's three-game ban for wiping blood onto the face of Essendon captain Andrew McGrath in a match in March.

Gallop will now miss Brisbane's games against Carlton, Hawthorn and Gold Coast, and will not be available until the round 24 games against Collingwood at the MCG.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Hundreds of Queensland social housing tenants evicted after review
World.content:
Dozens of households have been kicked out of social housing in Queensland after being found to own property or earn more than $80,000 a year.

A state government review of 46,210 households in public housing over the last financial year has led to 359 leaving.

Of those, 76 owned property or had a high income — less than 1 per cent of those reviewed.

Another 143 public housing tenants are being examined further after being identified as potentially owning property.

Meanwhile, 3,709 households have had their rent reduced because it was found they were paying more than a quarter of their income.

For households found to be paying less than 25 per cent of their income as required, rent rises are capped at $15 a week each year.

Public housing evictions triple in a year Under the new policy, tenants who receive three warnings for serious behaviour, including aggressive language, harassment and deliberate damage, in a year are evicted.

Last year the government announced it would review tenants' eligibility and rents for social housing annually.

Public housing tenants are not allowed to own or part-own property in Australia or overseas, including vacant land.

A household's income must not exceed $80,000, and tenants must provide information to confirm their ongoing eligibility when requested.

In the 2025-26 financial year, 211 households were moved on after failing to provide information within 28 days, 38 left while under review, and three vacated after a tribunal process.

Housing Minister Sam O'Connor said the figures showed the importance of undertaking reviews.

Sam O'Connor says thousands of the state's most vulnerable had been paying too much in rent. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

"We're restoring fairness and making sure as many taxpayer-funded homes as possible are for the Queenslanders who most need a place to call home," he said.

In the last financial year, another 267 households chose to downsize, which the Department of Housing says freed up 401 bedrooms for families in need of larger homes.

Change to income limits not on the table

In Queensland, the income limit for a single person with no children applying for social housing is $609 per week, and $755 for a couple.

The opposition has called on the government to review income thresholds for public housing eligibility in case it is excluding people who need help.

Asked by Labor in budget estimates last week, Department of Housing and Public Works Director-General Mark Cridland said there would be no change to eligibility income limits while more than 20,000 approved households were on the register.

Department of Housing and Public Works Director-General Mark Cridland faced budget estimate hearings last week.

It was also revealed in budget estimates that the average wait time for a household on the social housing register had increased by 10 months in a year, from 21.2 months last year to 31.7 months as of June.

Mr Cridland said the department currently had an "incredibly low" vacancy rate because very few people were leaving public housing.

Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

World.title: Trump airs frustration with Netanyahu before Oval Office meeting
World.content:
Donald Trump has used a TV interview to publicly express his frustration with Benjamin Netanyahu's apparent efforts to pressure him to keep attacking Iran.

In the latest sign of shaky relations between the war-entangled leaders, Mr Trump voiced his annoyance just before a meeting with Mr Netanyahu, who was in Washington for a memorial service for senator Lindsey Graham.

The New York Post had earlier reported that Mr Netanyahu was planning to use the meeting to present evidence that Iran was building up its Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facilities.

Asked about this on Fox News, Mr Trump said:

" I don't need Bibi [Netanyahu] to tell me that. Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved. "

Mr Trump said Mr Netanyahu had "announced" the information about Pickaxe Mountain, though it was not clear what he meant. The New York Post report had cited an unnamed source in Jerusalem.

"I heard Bibi announced that. I said, 'Why didn't you just tell it to me? Why do you have to announce it to the world?'

"I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem. We took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take Pickaxe if we don't make a deal."

His comments were later clipped up and shared online by the White House's "Rapid Response" X account.

Public support for Israel has been in steep decline in the US. In recent AP-NORC polling, only 20 per cent of respondents said they had a favourable view of Mr Netanyahu, compared to 38 per cent with an unfavourable view and 41 per cent who did not express a view either way.

'A little difference'

In the five months since the start of the war with Iran, Mr Trump's strained patience with Mr Netanyahu has been increasingly on display.

Israel's ongoing attacks on Lebanon, undermining an early ceasefire deal, prompted Mr Trump to tell Mr Netanyahu he was "f***ing crazy", according to reports.

He later said publicly that Mr Netanyahu must be "more responsible with respect to Lebanon".

A preliminary ceasefire deal, signed by Mr Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian less than two weeks ago, angered many members of Mr Netanyahu's government.

The deal was quickly undermined by Iranian hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and US strikes on Iran. Since then, Mr Trump has repeatedly threatened to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure if a peace deal is not reached.

But in his Fox News interview, Mr Trump acknowledged such actions would hurt civilians.

"In less than, I would say, two hours, most of the bridges, the major bridges will all be gone. And the power plants in one day," he said.

"And then there's always the desalination plants. And who am I hurting then? I'm hurting the people. So I'm not looking to do that."

Mr Trump ordered a pause on attacks at the weekend.

On Monday, local time, he said the US and Iran had resumed "good talks". When asked if he and Mr Netanyahu were still aligned on the war on Iran, he said: "We have a little difference, but pretty close."

The Trump-Netanyahu meeting was the eighth between the pair since the start of their war with Iran.

Mr Trump also held Oval Office talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was also in Washington for Senator Graham's funeral.

The meetings were closed to the media. White House spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt said both meetings were "positive and productive".

World.title: Ben Carroll begins first full day as Victorian premier
World.content:
Ben Carroll is beginning his first full day as Victorian premier, just four months out from the state election.

Mr Carroll emerged from a chaotic caucus meeting yesterday as the third Labor leader this term.

The 51-year-old has already promised significant reform, but questions remain as to how this will be achieved with so little time until the state poll in November.

Ben Carroll has four months to win over voters Victoria's new premier Ben Carroll has only four months to convince voters he could be the man for the top job after the toppling of Jacinta Allan.

After the vote yesterday, Mr Carroll staked his leadership on launching a royal commission into alleged corruption on the taxpayer-funded Big Build.

"Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews. I am not Jacinta Allan," Mr Carroll declared at a press conference shortly after he was sworn in at Government House.

While he is yet to detail the terms of reference for the royal commission, Mr Carroll said it would be expansive and established as soon as possible.

Ben Carroll and Gabrielle Williams address the media at their first press conference as Premier and Deputy Premier. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Reform to the state's anti-corruption watchdog IBAC will be introduced this term, Mr Carroll said.

The new premier also pledged yet-to-be detailed law-and-order changes, as well as a shift in focus towards businesses.

"I will do things differently, because different times require a new approach," Mr Carroll said.

"In my government, integrity will not be optional."

In the meantime, Mr Carroll will need to rejig his frontbench.

His own education portfolio will be up for grabs, and he will need to pick a replacement for his predecessor Jacinta Allan.

Several sources told the ABC that Mordialloc MP Tim Richardson would enter cabinet, but other changes to the previous Allan ministry are yet to be revealed.

Yelling from the party room a soundtrack to chaotic caucus meeting

Yesterday's leadership battle unfolded behind closed doors after a rollercoaster period for Labor, that began with Ms Allan vowing to contest a party ballot on Monday, and ended with Mr Carroll elected unopposed by lunchtime on Tuesday.

Ms Allan had on Monday vowed to fight on.

But on the same day, Mr Carroll, then her deputy, stated his intention to challenge for the leadership.

By Tuesday morning, Ms Allan realised she had lost the support of her caucus.

She resigned as premier at 9:30am, despite claiming she would win a ballot of the entire Victorian Labor membership.

As she announced her departure from the state's top job, Ms Allan — who was the youngest ever woman MP elected in Victoria and just the second woman premier — put her support behind whoever was victorious in her place.

It seemed like the stage was set for Mr Carroll's ascent.

But once the 10am caucus meeting was underway, Ms Allan's key ally Attorney-General and Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny made her own play for the leadership.

Outgoing premier Jacinta Allan walks into Labor caucus meeting flanked by a loyal Sonya Kilkenny, who would make a brief bid for leadership. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The caucus meeting spanned almost two hours, and yelling could be heard from the halls of parliament.

At one point, Ms Allan could be heard saying loudly: "hang on, hang on, one at a time."

When Ms Kilkenny withdrew her candidacy, it was in exchange for securing an agreement — this included that she would keep her own roles in cabinet, that Mr Richardson would enter cabinet, that there would be no bloodletting, and that all MPs would sign Mr Carroll's nomination form.

Ultimately, Mr Carroll walked out as the Labor leader alongside his new deputy Gabrielle Williams.

Ms Allan is yet to declare whether she will remain in parliament, though she's expected to retire ahead of the state election in November.

The former premier said she would address her supporters in Bendigo, where she has held the seat of Bendigo East since the 1999 state election.

Shorten backs switch to Carroll

On Tuesday night, former federal Labor leader Bill Shorten said the ALP's Victorian wing would have faced "extinction level results" if Ms Allan had remained premier.

"I think, as much as people don't want to hear this in Labor, I think they were facing extinction-level results worse than 1992 when Jeff Kennett wiped out Labor," Mr Shorten told 7.30.

"I understand why people acted."

Former federal opposition leader Bill Shorten told 7.30 that the switch from Jacinta Allan to Ben Carroll made political sense for Victorian Labor. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

As to whether Mr Carroll could do enough to keep Labor in power, Mr Shorten said he felt he would make them competitive at the November state election.

"I think he can move them from the low 20s, to at least the mid-30s [per cent of the vote]," he said.

"[Mr Carroll is] doing this to make sure the can try to win and make Labor competitive. I think he will give them a bump.

"Changes sometimes work, sometimes they don't. But I can think of plenty of examples where they have worked."

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson will now face Premier Ben Carroll in the 2026 Victorian election campaign, with the state heading to the polls in November. (ABC News)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson faced Mr Carroll in question time on Tuesday, taking aim at the new premier whose leadership bid came after recent declarations of support for Ms Allan.

"Only last month, [Ben Carroll] said: 'I've got a young daughter at home and I couldn't be more proud to make sure she grows up knowing I supported Jacinta Allan.'" Ms Wilson said.

"How can Victorians possibly believe this premier can act with integrity when governing Victoria, when he can't even be honest with his own daughter?"

Victoria's election will be held on November 28.

World.title: Underbelly of Victoria's Big Build to be exposed by royal commission
World.content:
A new leader's first press conference is usually a chance for them to introduce themselves to the wider public.

But after toppling his boss yesterday, new Victorian Premier Ben Carroll took a different approach, opting to tell voters who he is not.

"I am not Daniel Andrews, I am not Jacinta Allan," he said.

In his first speech, Ben Carroll has promised integrity. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

In the end — a lacklustre response to reports of widespread union-led corruption on the sites of Victoria's major infrastructure projects sunk Jacinta Allan.

She resisted calling a royal commission into the state's construction sector until the end.

It was the first announcement Mr Carroll made as premier, saying in his government "integrity will not be optional".

What is the Big Build?

Big Build construction sites have been plagued by violence and intimidation, courtesy of the Victorian branch of the CFMEU. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The Victorian government's so-called "Big Build" is a multi-decade, $100 billion construction project comprising new roads, railway stations and tunnels.

It has delivered several impressive new pieces of public infrastructure but, according to corruption-busting barrister Geoffrey Watson SC, has also been plagued by violence and intimidation, courtesy of the Victorian branch of the CFMEU.

Nine Newspapers first aired allegations of stand-over tactics and criminal infiltration of parts of the union.

The reporting saw the federal government place parts of the union into administration.

The CFMEU under John Setka was investigated. (AAP: Stefan Postles)

Following this, the union's administrators tasked Mr Watson to report on the way the CFMEU was operating under former union boss John Setka.

The report, titled Rotting From The Top; The CFMEU in Victoria During the Setka Era, found the union in Victoria had "collapsed into a squalid mess".

He found the Victorian construction division of the CFMEU began controlling which subcontractors and labour hire companies were allowed on major construction sites.

In Victoria, he found widespread corruption "of a very organised kind, which involved not only financial crimes against the people of Victoria in terms of what was going on there, but also sites being used as drug dealing points".

Mr Watson also found bikies and organised criminals working in conjunction with the CFMEU, and suggested Victorian taxpayers had lost as much as $15 billion to organised crime on Big Build projects.

The Victorian government has disputed that figure, but Mr Watson has told the ABC he stands by it.

"Because it includes a whole lot of things," he said.

"It includes bloated contract prices, delays, all of the matters which went to rewarding criminals at the expense of genuine contractors and rewarding criminals at the expense of genuine workers."

Death threats

Mr Watson's report also found the $100 billion Big Build hosted and enabled systemic corruption, sexual exploitation, and drug trafficking.

He also found that after the union was placed in administration in August 2024, threats were made against the life of administrator Mark Irving.

Geoffrey Watson's report found the $100 billion Big Build hosted and enabled systemic corruption, sexual exploitation, and drug trafficking.

He said threats were also made against ACTU secretary Sally McManus and the then federal Minister for Workplace Relations Murray Watt, requiring both to employ personal security, as did The Age's investigative journalist Nick McKenzie.

Mr Watson's report sought a response from Mr Setka and received an expletive-laden reply, including: "leave me alone, you f****n' fat ugly c***."

Mr Watson has since warned other states about the dangers of Victorian-style corruption infiltrating construction sectors.

Allan resisted royal commission

Ms Allan had faced growing pressure over her handling of the alleged criminal infiltration of the Big Build before she was told she had lost the support of caucus earlier this week.

As well as immediately reversing that decision and announcing a royal commission, Mr Carroll also announced the establishment of a special prosecutor to work alongside it.

He has also vowed to bring forward greater powers for the state's anti-corruption watchdog.

Mr Carroll hasn't announced when the royal commission commences, who will lead it, or what its terms of reference will be.

But Labor strategist-turned-professional pollster Kos Samaras says the announcement sends a strong signal.

"That he is not an extension of the Andrews administration," he said.

"And this is one of the strategic challenges that Jacinta Allan faced in trying to project to the Victorian public that she was a different government. And to a certain extent, she was not successful in doing that."

So why did Ms Allan resist calling a royal commission, even up until the very end of her reign?

Jacinta Allan refused to call a royal commission. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr Samaras reckons "the resistance is probably institutional".

"The Labor Party does have some pretty strong connections with the union movement.

"There would be people within the union movement that are probably suffering a bit of PTSD from the last time there was a royal commission into unions.

"So I think it's largely more institutional rather than actually of any legal concern."

What will a royal commission do?

Former IBAC commissioner Robert Redlich KC says while it is "encouraging" a royal commission into the state's construction sector has been called, a lot will depend on the terms of reference the government's prepared to give it.

"Because there have been occasions when governments have called royal commissions, but given the royal commission very, very limited jurisdiction to investigate," Mr Redlich said.

Mr Watson SC believes a royal commission is warranted

"They can compel people to come and give evidence. They can get access to financial records and do a lot of things which the police can't do.

"This has been a very bad problem for Victoria, and it's time that the people knew that the government was going to do something, get to the bottom of it and prevent it from occurring again, as well as exposing those who were engaged in it along the way."

Ben Carroll will replace Jacinta Allan. (AAP:James Ross)

Victorians head to the polls in November, meaning the new premier has just four months to win back the trust of Victorian voters.

CFMEU inquiry names people behind corruption Members of bikie gangs, convicted murderers and violent criminals are among more than 25 people who allegedly benefited from or are linked to corrupt behaviour at the CFMEU, according to a report.

Mr Watson will be watching to see how that goes.

"This is a great first step toward trying to restore public confidence in the building industry and in the way in which government oversees its responsibility in spending public money on major infrastructure projects," he said.

"Let's see what happens."

Meanwhile, he's calling for a public acknowledgement of the journalism he sees as responsible for much of the information about the Big Build coming to light.

"This wouldn't have come about; this expose would never have started without the amazing work of the great journalist Nick McKenzie," he said.

"They should put a statue in Victoria. They should build a statue for that fellow."

World.title: Brothers who bashed teen in shipping container slammed by judge
World.content:
A Tasmanian man who helped his brother assault a teenage boy before tying him up and locking him in a shipping container has avoided a jail term.

Brady John Ludbey, 26, appeared in the Supreme Court in Burnie on Tuesday, having pleaded guilty to two counts of assault committed against a 17-year-old at Strahan on Tasmania's west coast three years ago.

In sentencing, Justice Tamara Jago was scathing of Brady Ludbey's behaviour but noted his crimes were less serious than those committed by his brother, Wayne Ludbey, who has also pleaded guilty to two counts of assault.

"Your behaviour was… very concerning. The complainant was only 17 years of age," Justice Jago told Brady Ludbey.

" He was a child. "

Assault began after belief teen had stolen

Justice Jago told the court Wayne Ludbey, 29 at the time, believed the victim had been stealing from him and confronted him on the main street of Strahan on September 12, 2023.

In the initial altercation, the elder brother assaulted the teenager — who cannot be named — and attempted to force him into the front passenger seat of his car, the court was told.

Brady Ludbey, 23 at the time, then arrived on the scene and helped restrain the boy with the seatbelt held against his neck while Wayne Ludbey returned to the driver's seat.

"By holding him in the front passenger seat you deprived him of his liberty," the judge said.

The court heard that the teenage victim was terrified during the protracted assault. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham )

Justice Jago said the boy and Brady initially believed Wayne was going to drive him to the police station, but instead drove to his own home, where the shipping container was located.

"The complainant was scared and unsure what fate awaited him," Justice Jago said.

" You must've appreciated your brother was not simply trying to passively resolve the alleged theft. "

The court was told the two men then bound the teenager with straps and zip ties around his hands and ankles and continued to assault him.

During the ordeal, the teenager was tripped when he tried to stand and struck multiple times to the head and body with a piece of wood, and sprayed with water from a hose.

At one point, the judge said, Wayne Ludbey stood in the door of the shipping container with a running chainsaw, which he then turned off and held against the boy's neck.

They then closed the shipping container and locked it with a chain and padlock, leaving the boy tied up inside "scared, cold and trapped".

Judge lashes man for failure to intervene

"At no point did you seek to intervene," Justice Jago told Brady Ludbey.

"Your failure to do anything while your brother continued to assault the complainant and then trapped him inside … speaks in clear terms to your moral culpability.

" You were willing to, at the very least, turn a blind eye. "

The judge said the ordeal ended when Brady Ludbey cut the container open with an angle grinder, unbound the boy, returned his mobile phone and told him to go home.

The boy was taken to the North West Regional Hospital where he was treated for cuts and bruises.

Justice Jago said she had received a victim impact statement from the boy, which indicated he suffered psychological harm and continues to be affected by the ordeal.

"No doubt he was terrified," the judge said.

" You chose to become involved with a very serious act of violence… for entirely unjustifiable reasons. "

Judge considers crimes an 'aberration'

In sentencing, Justice Jago considered a lack of prior convictions before or since the attack on the teenager, and several character references that had been provided.

She said she found it "difficult to reconcile" the character references given the seriousness of the violence, but said they were consistent with the absence of a criminal history.

" [This suggests] your behaviour this day was something of an aberration. "

Brady Ludbey was sentenced to an eight-month suspended jail term, and ordered to complete 98 hours of community service.

Wayne Ludbey will be sentenced on August 14.

World.title: Warning social media giants might wear fines to help sink the age ban
World.content:
Companies who sell age-checking software want Australia to grant the eSafety Commissioner investigative powers to "test" if social media companies are using their technology properly.

The Age Verification Providers Association (AVPA) has backed Labor's bill to strengthen Australia's social media age laws and called on the federal government to go further with a mandatory audit of every platform captured by the under-16s ban.

The group warned social media giants could opt to wear fines, no matter how large, if it helped to sink the age laws.

Age assurance companies, which often sign confidentiality agreements with social media platforms, also asked for legal protections for providing information "in good faith" to an eSafety investigation.

Australia flags strengthen social media ban Australia will strengthen its social media ban for young people as a priority amid concerns the powers behind the world-first laws are not strong enough.

Support was mixed in submissions to a Senate inquiry into Labor's proposal to double the maximum penalty to $99 million for tech companies that fail to take "reasonable steps" to enforce the age limit.

The bill would also allow eSafety to compel documents from social media platforms and third parties when investigating suspected systemic failures to uphold the ban.

Legal experts recommended Labor narrow the scope of these investigative powers to explicitly protect children and parents, while the tech sector opposed the larger fines.

Social media companies accused of wanting ban to fail

In a damning submission, the AVPA, which represents third-party age technology companies, warned big fines could still be seen as a "small price to pay" if it allowed Australia's ban to "wrongly" be portrayed as a failure.

Early research into the efficacy of the ban in preventing Australians aged under 16 from accessing the likes of TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram has found the majority of young people were still able to log in to at least one platform.

Loading...

AVPA said expanding the eSafety Commissioner's power so it could compel documents from tech companies was "necessary to test whether social media platforms have effectively configured the age assurance systems they claim to have implemented".

The group recommended Australia go further by having a "mandatory independent audit and certification requirement" for every social media platform captured by the ban.

"The expanded power will also reach our members … which are typically bound contractually by confidentiality obligations," the submission said.

"Most such agreements already permit disclosure that is required by law, so compliance with a valid notice should not expose suppliers to significant contractual risk."

Call to protect kids and parents in beefed-up law

The Law Council of Australia has made a submission flagging concerns the scope of the proposed section on information-gathering extended "beyond its intended operation".

"As drafted, the provision appears capable of applying to any person, including end-users who are children and their parents or guardians, where they possess relevant information or documents," the submission said.

The council recommended the bill be amended to ensure it "better reflects" the government's policy intentions and provides "certainty" that children were not "inadvertently" captured by the expanded information-gathering power.

"If the power is not intended to apply to children and their parents or guardians, its scope should be revised to ensure that it is appropriately targeted," it said.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said eSafety would not compel documents from children and parents because "everyday Australians" did not have evidence of "systemic non-compliance with the law by billion-dollar tech companies".

Anika Wells reassures parents that the strengthened powers are intended to target third-party companies, such as age assurance technology providers. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

"Instead, these strengthened powers are intended to target third-party companies, such as age assurance technology providers and app-stores, where the eSafety Commissioner suspects they may hold evidence of systemic non-compliance," she said.

"We know social media companies are doing the bare minimum to comply with our social media minimum age law; that's why we are strengthening eSafety's powers and doubling fines for non-compliance."

Tech companies oppose tougher fines

Digital Industry Group Inc (DIGI), an industry group that advocates on behalf of the sector in Australia, has criticised the proposed bill, arguing the government had not tested if gaps in enforcement could be addressed in other ways.

It also opposed the doubling of the maximum penalty because, with no fines yet issued, it was not clear if there was a "link" between the dollar figure and the effectiveness of the age ban.

DIGI said the eSafety Commissioner already had an "extensive suite of investigative and enforcement powers" related to the social media age restrictions and argued the government should be clear about any "deficiency" the new bill was trying to remedy.

The group raised concerns about the new information and document-gathering powers being "very broad" noting they were not limited to app stores and age assurance providers.

"Australians should not have to rely on a regulator exercising restraint as the sole safeguard against the misuse of broad-ranging powers against individual citizens," the submission said.

DIGI said any increased powers should be accompanied by greater transparency about how they were used.

"Powers of this breadth should be matched by clear public reporting on the types of services and individuals to whom notices are issued, and the basis on which the Commissioner decides to open an inquiry into a service or person," the submission said.

eSafety can't reach 'onus of proof' without documents

The eSafety Commissioner has backed the expanded powers as currently any investigation into tech giants suspected of failing to take "reasonable steps" to block under-16s from their social media platforms relies on "representations" from those same companies.

"Without access to primary documents relevant to compliance with the [social media minimum age] obligation, the Commissioner would likely be unable to discharge the onus of proof required in any civil penalty proceeding brought to the courts against a provider of a [platform]," eSafety said.

The commission said information and documents from third parties, such as age assurance providers, would be "instrumental" in determining whether the tech giants had taken sufficient steps to comply with Australia's laws.

In its submission, eSafety also argued the "full suite" of investigative powers available to it elsewhere in the Online Safety Act, such as the ability to "compel witnesses to give evidence on oath or affirmation", should apply uniformly.

World.title: ASX set to rise, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company Stan Choe Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most of Wall Street rose, even as stocks of computer chipmakers continued to tumble worldwide. Oil prices, meanwhile, eased further from the two-month high they hit last week. The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent, but the modest move masked big swings underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537 points, or 1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after briefly dropping 9.3 per cent below its record set last month. The slump in Wall Street’s AI stocks picked up pace on Tuesday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.14am AEST pointing to a jump of 76 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.6 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.77¢. On Wall Street, Apple became just the second company ever to achieve a $US5 trillion ($7.2 trillion) market valuation.



Related Article Opinion

Property market Real estate agent’s viral posts show our property market angst Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The iPhone maker’s shares rose as much as 1.8 per cent to $US342.89 early in the session, pushing the company’s market capitalisation to above $US5 trillion for the first time before falling back below the mark as shares eased before closing at $US340.80. Nvidia closed at a record $US5.7 trillion on May 14, but it has since lost roughly $US1 trillion in valuation. Apple is now the biggest company in the S&P 500 Index. The majority of the US market rose after more companies delivered stronger profits for the spring than analysts expected. Coca-Cola climbed 5 per cent after its revenue rose 7 per cent despite what CEO Henrique Braun called “a dynamic consumer landscape.” Sherwin-Williams rallied 8.3 per cent, and Illinois Tool Works rose 3.6 per cent after both likewise reported stronger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Stock prices generally follow the trend of corporate profits over the long term, and expectations are high for this most recent round of reports with the US stock market still near its all-time high. Such expectations are weighing particularly heavily on stocks of chipmakers and other companies that have been huge winners from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology.



Micron Technology’s stock came into the day having more than tripled for the year following gangbuster growth, for example. During the three months through May 28, its revenue more than quadrupled from a year earlier. But worries are rising about whether such growth is sustainable. Big spenders on computer memory could pull back on investments if AI does not produce as much profit or productivity as promised. Lower-cost AI models from China could also mean less demand for memory and computing power than earlier expected. Micron dropped 8.9 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. Others also helping to keep the market in check were Advanced Micro Devices, down 8.1 per cent, and Applied Materials, down 7.8 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 rose 15.60 points to 7,428.78. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537.24 to 52,747.32, and the Nasdaq composite fell 55.17 to 24,876.91. The losses for chip stocks were even worse earlier in the day in other markets worldwide.



Sharp drops for SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dragged South Korea’s Kospi index down 10.8 per cent. The market’s losses were so big that trading was temporarily halted at times in Seoul. “We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chipmaking equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chipmaking and chip equipment leaders,” said equity analyst Jing Jie Yu of Morningstar. “That said, we believe the sell-off today is largely a knee-jerk reaction and overdone,” he said. The dominant position of global chipmaking leaders is unlikely to be threatened meaningfully, he said. Several huge spenders on AI chips and data centres are scheduled to report their latest quarterly results this week, which could offer updates on how much they’re planning to invest. Meta Platforms and Microsoft are reporting on Thursday (AEST), while Amazon is due the following day. Because AI superstar stocks have grown so big, their movements carry more weight on the S&P 500 and other indexes than many other companies. But the broad US market could hold up despite their swings if other, less-loved areas are able to keep rising. It’s a rotation that some strategists have suggested could be healthy for the overall stock market.



In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in October fell 4.4 per cent to settle at $US82.08. It’s been falling since late last week, when the price for a barrel to be delivered in September briefly shot as high as $US102. Related Article Opinion

Global economy We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Pushing up on prices have been worries that worsening fighting in the Middle East could slow the global flow of oil. On the other side, though, are hopes that the United States and Iran could still negotiate something to allow oil tankers to use the Strait of Hormuz to move crude. Lower oil prices helped to ease Treasury yields in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.60 per cent from 4.65 per cent.



A weaker-than-expected reading on confidence among US consumers also weighed on yields. Fewer consumers are saying they feel good about current business conditions, according to the latest survey released by the Conference Board. The drop in oil prices helped push traders to trim their bets that the Federal Reserve could announce a hike to interest rates following its latest meeting on Wednesday. They’re forecasting a 31.5 per cent probability, down from more than 36 per cent a day before, according to data from CME Group. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow. Long-term mortgage rates have already hit their highest level in nearly a year, chilling the housing industry. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran Michael Koziol Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:26am ,first published 3:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump publicly rebuked Benjamin Netanyahu over plans for escalating the war in Iran as the two men met at the White House for the first time since the conflict commenced five months ago. The meeting came as the Israeli leader – and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky – visited Washington for the funeral of Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a staunch advocate for military aid to both countries. President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other dignitaries at the funeral of Lindsey Graham on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin At the White House, Netanyahu made an understated arrival using the West Wing’s side entrance, and his meeting with the US president and senior administration figures was closed to the media. But only a few hours earlier, Trump expressed frustration about reports that Netanyahu intended to present Israeli intelligence that Iran was fortifying Pickaxe Mountain – an underground nuclear site near its Natanz uranium enrichment facility.



“I don’t need Bibi to tell me that,” Trump told Fox News, using an affectionate term for the Israeli PM. “Bibi’s telling me that because he wants me to stay involved … We have the greatest cameras in the world focused on [Pickaxe Mountain], we know exactly what’s going on.” The New York Post reported on Tuesday (US time) that Netanyahu would use the visit to present evidence of ongoing Iranian nuclear activity and demonstrate that Tehran was not negotiating in good faith, citing a source in Jerusalem. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the funeral for Republican senator Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Netanyahu did not publicly declare what he intended to tell Trump, but the US president appeared to interpret the reporting as a statement from Netanyahu. “I heard Bibi announce that,” Trump told Fox News. “I said, ‘Why don’t you just tell it to me, why do you have to announce it to the world?’ I know exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe, it’s not a big problem.”



Trump repeated his threat to destroy the facility if a deal with the Iranians was not forthcoming. He also spoke about “competing factions” within the Republican Party, some of whom wanted him to escalate strikes and others who preferred a diplomatic solution. It was not clear whether Netanyahu actually presented Trump with intelligence about Pickaxe Mountain or any other Iranian nuclear site. The meeting lasted just over an hour. The meeting was closed to the media but the Israeli government distributed photos of the two leaders. Credit: Maayan Toaf / Israel Government Press Office Photographs from the meeting by the Israeli government showed Trump beaming, and there is no suggestion of a blow-up between the two leaders. But the president’s willingness to publicly push back on Netanyahu is indicative of a relationship that is more strained than before the war. Trump’s observation that Netanyahu “wants me to stay involved” – or seeks to prolong the war – is also a candid admission of the prevailing dynamic between the two leaders.



The Israeli prime minister is primarily in Washington for the funeral of Graham, who died suddenly this month at 71 from what medical reports said was an aortic tear. The long-serving senator was a close friend of Israel and Ukraine, and a cheerleader for US military intervention in Iran and elsewhere. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also travelled to Washington for the funeral, and held a similarly private White House meeting with Trump just an hour before Netanyahu. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky meets with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. @ZelenskyyUa Zelenksy said it was a good meeting that included discussion about US plans to allow Ukraine to licence production of Patriot missile interceptors, “and several other ideas that could help” in the war against Russia. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said both meetings were “positive and productive”.



On Monday night, after arriving from Israel, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, attended a private memorial dinner with Graham’s family, friends and several Trump administration officials at the Four Seasons Hotel in Washington. “America has lost a great patriot. Israel has lost one of its greatest friends and supporters. And I have lost a dear friend,” Netanyahu told the gathering, according to his office. Benjamin Netanyahu with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the funeral for Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Graham’s flag-draped casket is carried down the steps of the US Capitol. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib US news site Axios reported the dinner was hosted by Lebanese banker and film producer Antoun Sehnaoui and Trump’s former deputy Middle East envoy Morgan Ortagus.



Other attendees included Meta president Dina Powell McCormick, Trump aide Stephen Miller and his wife Katie, and a slew of Republican and Democratic senators – among them Darline Graham, who has taken her late brother’s Senate seat. Dozens of high-ranking dignitaries attended Tuesday’s funeral service at the Washington National Cathedral, including cabinet secretaries, top White House aides and members of Congress. President Donald Trump delivering a eulogy for Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly this month. Alex Brandon/AP Pool via AP News Corp and Fox chairman Lachlan Murdoch attended, as did former vice president Mike Pence and Fox News host Sean Hannity, who, like Trump, delivered a eulogy. The program featured contrasting messages about Graham, a well-known foreign policy hawk who urged Trump to attack Iran. “He was extremely hawkish,” the president told mourners. “He never saw a war that he didn’t like.”



Earlier, Trump told Fox News: “Lindsey liked war. I said, ’You’re a nice guy, how come you like war so much? He was a guy that liked war.” Related Article Analysis

US politics Lindsey Graham, the ‘Three Amigos’ and the shifting politics of Israel But Hannity said the common portrayal of Graham as a warmonger was wrong. “The truth is the opposite,” he said. “Lindsey desperately wanted – and talked to the president about – lasting peace in the Middle East. He wanted every country in the region on that path to peace. That was Lindsey’s dream. “[But] Lindsey had moral clarity. He knew – as President Trump knows, as Israel knows, as I know – there can be no path to peace until evil is defeated.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’
World.content:
SportBoxingCommonwealth Games Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’ Hannah Kennelly July 29, 2026 — 5:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The boxer grandson of Idi Amin has vowed to become the “king of Scotland” by winning gold for Uganda at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Aziz Abdul, a heavyweight boxer for Uganda, will take on Englishman Damar Thomas on Thursday morning (AEST). Former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin, who died in 2003, and his grandson Abdul Aziz, who is competing in Glasgow. AP/Instagram But he has grabbed attention before even stepping in the ring with his comments to media over the last couple of days. “My idol is Mike Tyson, the baddest man on the planet,” Abdul told media earlier this week. “If I win the gold medal, I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow and the new king of Scotland.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games First shoes, now speed suits: Australia joins arms race to get an edge in athletics Abdul’s reference hearkens back to his late grandfather Amin, who was married six times and fathered around 60 children. Amin was nicknamed “the Butcher of Uganda” – but also proclaimed himself the king of Scotland in 1976. He had a fixation for the country, sparked by his time as a soldier in the British colonial army, and often wore kilts and played the bagpipes. Also a one-time heavyweight boxing champion, Amin seized power on January 25, 1971, overthrowing president Milton Obote while Obote was abroad. Human rights groups say as many as 500,000 people were killed during Amin’s eight-year rule over Uganda until he was forced out of the country in 1979. He was never tried for his crimes in an international court and died in Saudi Arabia in 2003. “My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” said Abdul, whose nickname is Ringo. “He was a heavyweight boxer like me, and I am so proud of him. Now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.



“I believe in myself and I mean what I say. When I say I will do it, I will do it. Let them not doubt me. I am aiming for the gold medal.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Australia won 15 medals in the pool, but this Scottish swimmer with terminal cancer stole the show In a later interview with BBC Scotland, Adbul would not respond when asked if he was proud to be the grandson of the dictator, who also forced the expulsion of Uganda’s entire Asian minority, and whose rule led to total economic collapse. But Abdul did address how it feels to be linked to someone with such a sinister reputation. “Sometimes people say positive about him, but others say negative about him,” Abdul said. “That’s why I don’t want to talk more about him. “It’s not good to say something negative about someone who is not there, and it’s not good to say something about someone negative who was not there by the time when the incident happened, if it happened.”



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games LIVE: Australian sprinters blitz 100m semis at the track; Medals roll in for swimmers including Southam gold Abdul is 25, and according to the BBC Scotland report never met his grandfather. In the ring, he said, his big weapon is the “Ringo punch”. “I am not going to tell you about it – I will show you on the day if the right time comes,” he said. “You will see what the Ringo punch looks like. The big boys are here now. “Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”

World.title: Five fees, one room: How aged care costs are actually calculated
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion Five fees, one room: How aged care costs are actually calculated Rachel Lane Money contributor July 29, 2026 — 5:01am

July 29, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When people start looking at residential aged care, the first number they find is the Refundable Accommodation Deposit (RAD). It’s the figure advertised on aged care websites, listed in brochures and often used to compare one home with another. While the RAD is an important number, normally $750,000 or more, it’s only one piece of the puzzle. There are actually five different fees; understanding all of them is the only way to calculate what aged care will cost you. Here’s what to look for. Understanding these five costs is the first step in answering the critical question of ‘how much will my aged care cost?’ Dominic Lorrimer 1. The accommodation cost. This is the price of your room. There are three ways you can pay. First is the lump sum Refundable Accommodation Deposit (RAD), which is refunded when you leave (less 2 per cent per annum, up to 10 per cent). Alternatively, you can pay a Daily Accommodation Payment (DAP), calculated using the government set interest rate, currently 8.43 per cent per annum on any unpaid RAD. The third way is by combination, which can include deducting your daily payment from your lump sum.



Choosing how to pay isn’t simply a cash-flow decision. It can also affect your age pension, your means-tested fees and the amount of capital available for future needs. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care How the ‘cheapest’ retirement village could leave you paying more Rachel Lane Money contributor 2. The Basic Daily Fee. Every resident pays the Basic Daily Fee. Set at 85 per cent of the single basic age pension, currently $67 per day, it contributes towards everyday living expenses such as meals, cleaning, laundry and utilities. 3. The Hotelling contribution. The Hotelling contribution is a means-tested contribution towards everyday services such as meals, cleaning and laundry. It is capped at $22 per day. 4. The Non-Clinical Care Contribution. The Non-Clinical Care Contribution is a means-tested contribution towards your personal support, like assistance with showering and dressing.



Like the Hotelling Fee, the amount you pay depends on your assets and income. This fee is capped at $107 per day. There is also a time cap of four years or when you reach the lifetime cap of $137,917 (which includes any prior home care contributions). 5. The Higher Everyday Living Fee. Many aged care homes offer extras such as wine with meals, newspapers, beauty services and entertainment programs. These services are paid for on a user-pays basis through a Higher Everyday Living Fee. Understanding these five costs is the first step in answering the critical question of ‘how much will it cost?’ But remember, this is the cost of care, not your cost of living. You’ll still need to budget for personal expenses such as clothing, toiletries, hairdressing, medications and other day-to-day spending. Finally, it’s not just what you pay that matters but how you pay. Whether you keep or sell the family home, use savings or investments, or pay a RAD as a lump sum or daily payment can affect your pension, cash flow, aged care fees and your estate planning. It’s worth seeking advice to understand your options and avoid costly mistakes.



Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing.
