World.title: Should the family home be included in the age pension calculation?
World.content:
July 29, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I recently read a report by the Policy Institute Australia titled Home Truths: Rebalancing to Better Means Testing. One of its recommendations is to include at least part of the family home in the assets test for the age pension. It made me wonder: if the family home is no longer sacrosanct for the pension, could capital gains tax on the family home be next? I suspect I’m not alone in finding this deeply unsettling. Many Australians have worked hard, paid tax all their lives, and sacrificed to own their home outright, believing it would provide security in retirement. Now it seems even that security is being questioned. The report argues this is about “intergenerational equity”, but many older Australians will see it differently. They will feel that the goalposts are once again being shifted after decades of playing by the rules. Is this something retirees should genuinely be worried about, or is it simply another policy idea that is unlikely ever to become law? Adding the family home to the age pension asset test would be unpopular politically, and could put many pensioner’s income in peril. Simon Letch This is a proposal that surfaces occasionally, but politics is the art of the possible. While think tanks are free to recommend bold reforms, governments have to persuade voters. I struggle to see any government winning support for including the family home in the age pension assets test. The report proposes exempting the first $500,000 of the family home’s value and counting the balance under the assets test. On paper that may sound reasonable, but the practical consequences would be enormous.



The age pension cuts out completely for a homeowner couple with assessable assets of around $1.1 million. With Sydney’s median house price now around $1.75 million, hundreds of thousands of retirees could lose their pension despite having no greater spending power than people living in much cheaper parts of Australia. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Should I get my super as a $1.7m lump sum, or a yearly pension? Paul Benson Money contributor The same problem applies to suggestions of imposing capital gains tax on the family home. Property values vary dramatically across the country, making a single national rule difficult to apply fairly. A more realistic way for governments to reduce pension costs would be to tighten the assets test by lowering the thresholds or changing the taper rate. Even that would be politically contentious because it would directly affect retirees who have arranged their affairs under the existing rules. For now, I think the proposal is best regarded as part of the policy debate rather than something likely to become law in the foreseeable future.



I bought shares for $1 each on January 1, 2024. By June 30, 2027 if they hypothetically were worth $2, I would have an unrealised capital gain of $1. My understanding is that this gain would still qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount. If I then sold the shares on August 1, 2027 for $1.50, the shares would have fallen 50¢ from their June 30 value. Does that mean the 50-cent loss cancels the earlier discounted 50-cent gain so that I pay no tax? Julia Hartman says that assuming you have no other capital gains or capital losses, the legislation requires the 50¢ loss after June 30, 2027 to be deducted from the $1 pre-June 30 capital gain before the 50 per cent discount is applied. That leaves a net pre-2027 gain of 50¢, and after the 50 per cent discount you would be taxed on a capital gain of 25¢. One important point is still uncertain. The legislation also provides an alternative method that allows the capital gain to be calculated over the entire period of ownership. That approach may produce a better result in some situations, but the detailed rules have not yet been released, so we do not yet know exactly how that calculation will work in practice. I am nearly 80 and my partner is 13 years younger. She has no superannuation and her only income is the age pension. She is both the executor of my will and the nominated beneficiary of my superannuation. She also knows how to access my super account online, and any lump sum withdrawals are normally paid into our joint bank account. With all the recent publicity about delays in paying superannuation death benefits, I am concerned she could be left short of money after I die. If, immediately after my death, but before the fund has been notified, she logged into my account and withdrew money to cover her living expenses until the death benefit was paid, would there be any legal or tax consequences? I suspect we may be on thin legal ice and would appreciate your guidance.



I think there could be a problem if you try to withdraw money from the account of a deceased person. To me, a better option is for you to simply withdraw some money from your superannuation and open a new superannuation account for her. That keeps things legal and transparent while giving her the liquidity she needs. You recently mentioned investment bonds as a good way to invest for grandchildren. Your article renewed my interest because our daughter and son have each given us grandchildren, with another on the way. Editor's pick Opinion

Hip pocket The best way to spend your tax refund, no matter the amount Dominic Powell Money Editor One example in your article involved grandparents investing for a grandchild, but having the investment bond owned by the child’s parent. Does that mean we should establish one bond in our daughter’s name for her children and another in our son’s name for his children? What are the advantages of doing that instead of owning the bonds ourselves? Also, going back to my original question, how safe are investment bonds? There is no single right way to do it. The best ownership structure depends on what you are trying to achieve. If the bond is owned by your daughter or son, they have legal control of the investment and can use it for their children.



If you own the bond yourself, you keep control and can nominate who will receive the proceeds when you die. The better option depends on your family circumstances and estate planning goals. Investment bonds are issued by life insurance companies regulated by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), so the providers operate under strict financial rules. However, the value of the bond depends on the investments you choose. If you invest in shares, the value will rise and fall with the sharemarket, while more conservative investments are likely to fluctuate less. Like any investment, there are no guaranteed returns, which is why investment bonds are generally best suited to long-term investing. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. World.title: Cruising the Greek Islands never appealed to me. This trip changed my mind
World.content:
InspirationCruises Cruising the Greek Islands never appealed to me. This trip changed my mind Brian Johnston July 29, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Istanbul cruise terminal knocks Istanbul airport for six. Sleek as a contemporary art museum, it looks over the hum and chug of one of the world’s most historic harbours. It’s an anteroom to the Mediterranean. Plaka on the island of Milos. iStock The first thrill – technically, not quite the Mediterranean – is sailing out of Istanbul as an orange sun collapses onto the turrets of Topkapi palace. Next morning my ship, Explora II, squeezes through the Dardanelles and into the Aegean. How can you not be delighted to be on a luxury ship in a place so rich in maritime lore? Greece was the first place I visited as an independent adult. I’d just turned 18 and rumbled about the mainland in buses, hitchhiked when I needed to and racketed around the Greek islands on ferries that stank of oil and rust. I never thought I’d be cruising the Greek islands. I’m not sure I knew cruise ships existed because I grew up far from the coast. Eventually when I did know, I thought they’d never be for me.



Things have moved on, not least my open mindedness, greater need for comfort and lowered patience for travel’s irritations. While I’d never travel exclusively by cruise ship, they’re an enjoyable respite from do-it-yourself galumphing. 



You can be off the ship all day and slurp up all the local experiences you want. In Milos I’m off on the public bus to hilltop Plaka for a gloriously scenic walk that I share with only two other tourists. Then I walk down to Klima through dilapidated fields that smell of rosemary and goat, and don’t meet a single person. The fishing village of Klima on Milos. iStock The experiences you have wherever you go, whether by cruise ship or otherwise, is the result of your choices. A cruise ship is merely the facilitator. Besides, it presents you with a maritime perspective you won’t otherwise get. You never see the bad side of Greek islands from a cruise ship. All you get is blue sea, rusty rock, golden cliffs, hot skies. Over the centuries, islanders have added blue-domed chapels and whitewashed windmills, castles and fishing ports. You won’t see an airport terminal or a carpark. Almost every view is worthy of being featured on a postcard or printed calendar, if such things still exist. The ship is well-matched to the Greek islands. It is light-filled, breezy, unfussy and serene. Its subdued decor doesn’t try to compete with the explosion of colour outside.



The ship has no formal dress code, hardly any tablecloths, and little fuss despite the luxury levels. Who would want to sail here and squeeze into a dinner jacket? Comfort and ease aren’t the only reasons that cruising is the way to go in Greece. Most islands can be appreciated in a single day, and you get an overview of several in a short time. They’re often further from the crowds than you might think. You aren’t going to escape the tourist hordes in Greece all of the time, and that time is Rhodes on my cruise. But choose an itinerary that takes in less well-known islands, too, and you’ll be richly rewarded. Samos is one of the Greek Islands that hasn’t yet been overwhelmed by tourists. iStock Milos, Samos and Paros haven’t as yet been carbuncled with luxury resorts and nightclubs. Life here hasn’t been overwhelmed by the jetsetters and Instagrammers who play and party on Santorini and Mykonos.



You can head into the interior and hike amid landscapes that would make a petulant Greek god smile. Hills are stitched together by dry stone walls. Windmills are white, church domes blue, the window frames of houses green and red. Chapel interiors glimmer gold. In the village of Podromos on Paros I eat in a cafe surrounded by retirees swinging worry beads. As the ship sails away, I can enjoy a sunset without being jostled, as the blue-and-white colours of the Cyclades morph into orange and red. As evening falls, there are no thumping nightclubs and raucous stag parties, just a twinkle of stars, the muted burble of a fishing boat’s engines, the black outline of islands and a good dinner. One of Explora II’s four pools. Explora II has numerous restaurants, and no complaints about that. I can hop from Japan to France to the American West for an aged black Angus steak from a fine beast that might have been lassoed by a cowboy. But I keep wandering back to Med Yacht Club. For a start, I like its jaunty nautical theme: model ships, porthole-shaped windows only far larger, contemporary contours.



I like its cuisine, too. The menu rambles gently across the Mediterranean, sometimes unexpectedly, such as in tomato and strawberry salad with burrata. I can have a Greek meal here: shrimp saganaki, grilled octopus, some fine fish with a splash of lemon and herb salad. No baklava for dessert, but I’m not grumbling about the hazelnut semifreddo. Related Article Greece Beyond the islands, this peninsula is an underrated gem of Greece Nothing about the ship will irritate anyone, not even the princess with her pea. But I have to admit that one annoying thing is the bed because I seldom want to get out of it. I dare say it’s the best bed at sea. But still, it can’t compete with the Greek islands. I wrestle with my urge to snuggle down and amp up early, ready for the next arrival. I never thought I’d cruise the Greek islands, but never say never is a good philosophy to travel by. THE DETAILS



Cruise

Explora Journeys offers various cruises in the Greek islands on regular departures until mid-November 2026 and resumes from March 2027. None match the itinerary described here but each is similar in spirit. A seven-day “Journey Through Mythical Isles” cruise between Piraeus (Athens) and Istanbul visits Nafplio, Paros, Skiathos, Volos and Kusadasi. World.title: Do the friends we make at 15 stay with us for life?
World.content:
The last time I saw Elsa, we were teenage girls in Melbourne, crying over a goodbye. Now, standing in a bustling square in France with my four daughters, I scan the crowd for a face I hope I will still recognise. What will it feel like to see each other again after all this time? More importantly, will our friendship still be there?

Then I spot her, making her way through the crowd. Time has changed us both, but her smile is unmistakable. She laughs, and I am transported back to the French village where we spent three months together, 35 years ago. Within seconds, we are in each other’s arms, talking over one another. There is an instant ease that feels both surprising and deeply familiar.

Elsa (left) and the author, Michaela, reuniting in eastern France in April, having met 35 years before.

I was 15 when I went to France as an exchange student. I’d lobbied for the United States, but my Francophile parents were convinced France would be better for me. I, however, was terrified. My anxiety eased when I learnt my host family had a daughter my age. Coming from a family of five girls, I liked the idea of a ready-made sister. I collected brochures from a travel agency, imagining life in a French city … but they didn’t live in a city. After arriving in Paris, I took a train alone to a station in eastern France, where Elsa and her mother picked me up and took me to their tiny village. It was a shock. Rolling green hills and ancient stone houses in every direction. Elsa’s home was surrounded by dense pine forest and farms – a world away from the eastern suburbs of Melbourne.

The first few weeks were miserable. I was homesick, overwhelmed by a language I barely understood. Many nights I cried into my pillow. Starting school was particularly tough. One lunchtime, some boys in the cafeteria began teasing me. I couldn’t understand the words, but I recognised the tone. I just sat there, embarrassed, willing myself not to cry. Elsa quietly picked up my tray and moved us to another table.

The two of us bonded over music, chocolate, teenage crushes and badly dubbed episodes of the 1980s American TV soap series Santa Barbara. We laughed our way through conversations in a muddled mix of French and English. Elsa’s humour was wickedly dry. When I was served venison for Christmas lunch, she looked at my plate and said, completely deadpan, “Bambi’s father”. I was horrified. She dissolved into laughter.

World.title: ASX set to rise, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company Stan Choe Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most of Wall Street rose, even as stocks of computer chipmakers continued to tumble worldwide. Oil prices, meanwhile, eased further from the two-month high they hit last week. The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent, but the modest move masked big swings underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537 points, or 1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after briefly dropping 9.3 per cent below its record set last month. The slump in Wall Street’s AI stocks picked up pace on Tuesday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.14am AEST pointing to a jump of 76 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.6 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.77¢. On Wall Street, Apple became just the second company ever to achieve a $US5 trillion ($7.2 trillion) market valuation.



Related Article Opinion

Property market Real estate agent’s viral posts show our property market angst Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The iPhone maker’s shares rose as much as 1.8 per cent to $US342.89 early in the session, pushing the company’s market capitalisation to above $US5 trillion for the first time before falling back below the mark as shares eased before closing at $US340.80. Nvidia closed at a record $US5.7 trillion on May 14, but it has since lost roughly $US1 trillion in valuation. Apple is now the biggest company in the S&P 500 Index. The majority of the US market rose after more companies delivered stronger profits for the spring than analysts expected. Coca-Cola climbed 5 per cent after its revenue rose 7 per cent despite what CEO Henrique Braun called “a dynamic consumer landscape.” Sherwin-Williams rallied 8.3 per cent, and Illinois Tool Works rose 3.6 per cent after both likewise reported stronger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Stock prices generally follow the trend of corporate profits over the long term, and expectations are high for this most recent round of reports with the US stock market still near its all-time high. Such expectations are weighing particularly heavily on stocks of chipmakers and other companies that have been huge winners from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology.



Micron Technology’s stock came into the day having more than tripled for the year following gangbuster growth, for example. During the three months through May 28, its revenue more than quadrupled from a year earlier. But worries are rising about whether such growth is sustainable. Big spenders on computer memory could pull back on investments if AI does not produce as much profit or productivity as promised. Lower-cost AI models from China could also mean less demand for memory and computing power than earlier expected. Micron dropped 8.9 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. Others also helping to keep the market in check were Advanced Micro Devices, down 8.1 per cent, and Applied Materials, down 7.8 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 rose 15.60 points to 7,428.78. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537.24 to 52,747.32, and the Nasdaq composite fell 55.17 to 24,876.91. The losses for chip stocks were even worse earlier in the day in other markets worldwide.



Sharp drops for SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dragged South Korea’s Kospi index down 10.8 per cent. The market’s losses were so big that trading was temporarily halted at times in Seoul. “We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chipmaking equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chipmaking and chip equipment leaders,” said equity analyst Jing Jie Yu of Morningstar. “That said, we believe the sell-off today is largely a knee-jerk reaction and overdone,” he said. The dominant position of global chipmaking leaders is unlikely to be threatened meaningfully, he said. Several huge spenders on AI chips and data centres are scheduled to report their latest quarterly results this week, which could offer updates on how much they’re planning to invest. Meta Platforms and Microsoft are reporting on Thursday (AEST), while Amazon is due the following day. Because AI superstar stocks have grown so big, their movements carry more weight on the S&P 500 and other indexes than many other companies. But the broad US market could hold up despite their swings if other, less-loved areas are able to keep rising. It’s a rotation that some strategists have suggested could be healthy for the overall stock market.



In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in October fell 4.4 per cent to settle at $US82.08. It’s been falling since late last week, when the price for a barrel to be delivered in September briefly shot as high as $US102. Related Article Opinion

Global economy We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Pushing up on prices have been worries that worsening fighting in the Middle East could slow the global flow of oil. On the other side, though, are hopes that the United States and Iran could still negotiate something to allow oil tankers to use the Strait of Hormuz to move crude. Lower oil prices helped to ease Treasury yields in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.60 per cent from 4.65 per cent.



A weaker-than-expected reading on confidence among US consumers also weighed on yields. Fewer consumers are saying they feel good about current business conditions, according to the latest survey released by the Conference Board. The drop in oil prices helped push traders to trim their bets that the Federal Reserve could announce a hike to interest rates following its latest meeting on Wednesday. They’re forecasting a 31.5 per cent probability, down from more than 36 per cent a day before, according to data from CME Group. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow. Long-term mortgage rates have already hit their highest level in nearly a year, chilling the housing industry. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran Michael Koziol Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:26am ,first published 3:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump publicly rebuked Benjamin Netanyahu over plans for escalating the war in Iran as the two men met at the White House for the first time since the conflict commenced five months ago. The meeting came as the Israeli leader – and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky – visited Washington for the funeral of Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a staunch advocate for military aid to both countries. President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other dignitaries at the funeral of Lindsey Graham on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin At the White House, Netanyahu made an understated arrival using the West Wing’s side entrance, and his meeting with the US president and senior administration figures was closed to the media. But only a few hours earlier, Trump expressed frustration about reports that Netanyahu intended to present Israeli intelligence that Iran was fortifying Pickaxe Mountain – an underground nuclear site near its Natanz uranium enrichment facility.



“I don’t need Bibi to tell me that,” Trump told Fox News, using an affectionate term for the Israeli PM. “Bibi’s telling me that because he wants me to stay involved … We have the greatest cameras in the world focused on [Pickaxe Mountain], we know exactly what’s going on.” The New York Post reported on Tuesday (US time) that Netanyahu would use the visit to present evidence of ongoing Iranian nuclear activity and demonstrate that Tehran was not negotiating in good faith, citing a source in Jerusalem. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the funeral for Republican senator Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Netanyahu did not publicly declare what he intended to tell Trump, but the US president appeared to interpret the reporting as a statement from Netanyahu. “I heard Bibi announce that,” Trump told Fox News. “I said, ‘Why don’t you just tell it to me, why do you have to announce it to the world?’ I know exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe, it’s not a big problem.”



Trump repeated his threat to destroy the facility if a deal with the Iranians was not forthcoming. He also spoke about “competing factions” within the Republican Party, some of whom wanted him to escalate strikes and others who preferred a diplomatic solution. It was not clear whether Netanyahu actually presented Trump with intelligence about Pickaxe Mountain or any other Iranian nuclear site. The meeting lasted just over an hour. The meeting was closed to the media but the Israeli government distributed photos of the two leaders. Credit: Maayan Toaf / Israel Government Press Office Photographs from the meeting by the Israeli government showed Trump beaming, and there is no suggestion of a blow-up between the two leaders. But the president’s willingness to publicly push back on Netanyahu is indicative of a relationship that is more strained than before the war. Trump’s observation that Netanyahu “wants me to stay involved” – or seeks to prolong the war – is also a candid admission of the prevailing dynamic between the two leaders.



The Israeli prime minister is primarily in Washington for the funeral of Graham, who died suddenly this month at 71 from what medical reports said was an aortic tear. The long-serving senator was a close friend of Israel and Ukraine, and a cheerleader for US military intervention in Iran and elsewhere. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also travelled to Washington for the funeral, and held a similarly private White House meeting with Trump just an hour before Netanyahu. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky meets with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. @ZelenskyyUa Zelenksy said it was a good meeting that included discussion about US plans to allow Ukraine to licence production of Patriot missile interceptors, “and several other ideas that could help” in the war against Russia. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said both meetings were “positive and productive”.



On Monday night, after arriving from Israel, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, attended a private memorial dinner with Graham’s family, friends and several Trump administration officials at the Four Seasons Hotel in Washington. “America has lost a great patriot. Israel has lost one of its greatest friends and supporters. And I have lost a dear friend,” Netanyahu told the gathering, according to his office. Benjamin Netanyahu with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the funeral for Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Graham’s flag-draped casket is carried down the steps of the US Capitol. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib US news site Axios reported the dinner was hosted by Lebanese banker and film producer Antoun Sehnaoui and Trump’s former deputy Middle East envoy Morgan Ortagus.



Other attendees included Meta president Dina Powell McCormick, Trump aide Stephen Miller and his wife Katie, and a slew of Republican and Democratic senators – among them Darline Graham, who has taken her late brother’s Senate seat. Dozens of high-ranking dignitaries attended Tuesday’s funeral service at the Washington National Cathedral, including cabinet secretaries, top White House aides and members of Congress. President Donald Trump delivering a eulogy for Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly this month. Alex Brandon/AP Pool via AP News Corp and Fox chairman Lachlan Murdoch attended, as did former vice president Mike Pence and Fox News host Sean Hannity, who, like Trump, delivered a eulogy. The program featured contrasting messages about Graham, a well-known foreign policy hawk who urged Trump to attack Iran. “He was extremely hawkish,” the president told mourners. “He never saw a war that he didn’t like.”



Earlier, Trump told Fox News: “Lindsey liked war. I said, ’You’re a nice guy, how come you like war so much? He was a guy that liked war.” Related Article Analysis

US politics Lindsey Graham, the ‘Three Amigos’ and the shifting politics of Israel But Hannity said the common portrayal of Graham as a warmonger was wrong. “The truth is the opposite,” he said. “Lindsey desperately wanted – and talked to the president about – lasting peace in the Middle East. He wanted every country in the region on that path to peace. That was Lindsey’s dream. “[But] Lindsey had moral clarity. He knew – as President Trump knows, as Israel knows, as I know – there can be no path to peace until evil is defeated.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’
World.content:
SportBoxingCommonwealth Games Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’ Hannah Kennelly July 29, 2026 — 5:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The boxer grandson of Idi Amin has vowed to become the “king of Scotland” by winning gold for Uganda at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Aziz Abdul, a heavyweight boxer for Uganda, will take on Englishman Damar Thomas on Thursday morning (AEST). Former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin, who died in 2003, and his grandson Abdul Aziz, who is competing in Glasgow. AP/Instagram But he has grabbed attention before even stepping in the ring with his comments to media over the last couple of days. “My idol is Mike Tyson, the baddest man on the planet,” Abdul told media earlier this week. “If I win the gold medal, I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow and the new king of Scotland.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games First shoes, now speed suits: Australia joins arms race to get an edge in athletics Abdul’s reference hearkens back to his late grandfather Amin, who was married six times and fathered around 60 children. Amin was nicknamed “the Butcher of Uganda” – but also proclaimed himself the king of Scotland in 1976. He had a fixation for the country, sparked by his time as a soldier in the British colonial army, and often wore kilts and played the bagpipes. Also a one-time heavyweight boxing champion, Amin seized power on January 25, 1971, overthrowing president Milton Obote while Obote was abroad. Human rights groups say as many as 500,000 people were killed during Amin’s eight-year rule over Uganda until he was forced out of the country in 1979. He was never tried for his crimes in an international court and died in Saudi Arabia in 2003. “My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” said Abdul, whose nickname is Ringo. “He was a heavyweight boxer like me, and I am so proud of him. Now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.



“I believe in myself and I mean what I say. When I say I will do it, I will do it. Let them not doubt me. I am aiming for the gold medal.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Australia won 15 medals in the pool, but this Scottish swimmer with terminal cancer stole the show In a later interview with BBC Scotland, Adbul would not respond when asked if he was proud to be the grandson of the dictator, who also forced the expulsion of Uganda’s entire Asian minority, and whose rule led to total economic collapse. But Abdul did address how it feels to be linked to someone with such a sinister reputation. “Sometimes people say positive about him, but others say negative about him,” Abdul said. “That’s why I don’t want to talk more about him. “It’s not good to say something negative about someone who is not there, and it’s not good to say something about someone negative who was not there by the time when the incident happened, if it happened.”



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games LIVE: Australian sprinters blitz 100m semis at the track; Medals roll in for swimmers including Southam gold Abdul is 25, and according to the BBC Scotland report never met his grandfather. In the ring, he said, his big weapon is the “Ringo punch”. “I am not going to tell you about it – I will show you on the day if the right time comes,” he said. “You will see what the Ringo punch looks like. The big boys are here now. “Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”

World.title: Five fees, one room: How aged care costs are actually calculated
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion Five fees, one room: How aged care costs are actually calculated Rachel Lane Money contributor July 29, 2026 — 5:01am

July 29, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When people start looking at residential aged care, the first number they find is the Refundable Accommodation Deposit (RAD). It’s the figure advertised on aged care websites, listed in brochures and often used to compare one home with another. While the RAD is an important number, normally $750,000 or more, it’s only one piece of the puzzle. There are actually five different fees; understanding all of them is the only way to calculate what aged care will cost you. Here’s what to look for. Understanding these five costs is the first step in answering the critical question of ‘how much will my aged care cost?’ Dominic Lorrimer 1. The accommodation cost. This is the price of your room. There are three ways you can pay. First is the lump sum Refundable Accommodation Deposit (RAD), which is refunded when you leave (less 2 per cent per annum, up to 10 per cent). Alternatively, you can pay a Daily Accommodation Payment (DAP), calculated using the government set interest rate, currently 8.43 per cent per annum on any unpaid RAD. The third way is by combination, which can include deducting your daily payment from your lump sum.



Choosing how to pay isn’t simply a cash-flow decision. It can also affect your age pension, your means-tested fees and the amount of capital available for future needs. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care How the ‘cheapest’ retirement village could leave you paying more Rachel Lane Money contributor 2. The Basic Daily Fee. Every resident pays the Basic Daily Fee. Set at 85 per cent of the single basic age pension, currently $67 per day, it contributes towards everyday living expenses such as meals, cleaning, laundry and utilities. 3. The Hotelling contribution. The Hotelling contribution is a means-tested contribution towards everyday services such as meals, cleaning and laundry. It is capped at $22 per day. 4. The Non-Clinical Care Contribution. The Non-Clinical Care Contribution is a means-tested contribution towards your personal support, like assistance with showering and dressing.



Like the Hotelling Fee, the amount you pay depends on your assets and income. This fee is capped at $107 per day. There is also a time cap of four years or when you reach the lifetime cap of $137,917 (which includes any prior home care contributions). 5. The Higher Everyday Living Fee. Many aged care homes offer extras such as wine with meals, newspapers, beauty services and entertainment programs. These services are paid for on a user-pays basis through a Higher Everyday Living Fee. Understanding these five costs is the first step in answering the critical question of ‘how much will it cost?’ But remember, this is the cost of care, not your cost of living. You’ll still need to budget for personal expenses such as clothing, toiletries, hairdressing, medications and other day-to-day spending. Finally, it’s not just what you pay that matters but how you pay. Whether you keep or sell the family home, use savings or investments, or pay a RAD as a lump sum or daily payment can affect your pension, cash flow, aged care fees and your estate planning. It’s worth seeking advice to understand your options and avoid costly mistakes.

World.title: Should the family home be included in the age pension calculation?
World.content:
July 29, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I recently read a report by the Policy Institute Australia titled Home Truths: Rebalancing to Better Means Testing. One of its recommendations is to include at least part of the family home in the assets test for the age pension. It made me wonder: if the family home is no longer sacrosanct for the pension, could capital gains tax on the family home be next? I suspect I’m not alone in finding this deeply unsettling. Many Australians have worked hard, paid tax all their lives, and sacrificed to own their home outright, believing it would provide security in retirement. Now it seems even that security is being questioned. The report argues this is about “intergenerational equity”, but many older Australians will see it differently. They will feel that the goalposts are once again being shifted after decades of playing by the rules. Is this something retirees should genuinely be worried about, or is it simply another policy idea that is unlikely ever to become law? Adding the family home to the age pension asset test would be unpopular politically, and could put many pensioner’s income in peril. Simon Letch This is a proposal that surfaces occasionally, but politics is the art of the possible. While think tanks are free to recommend bold reforms, governments have to persuade voters. I struggle to see any government winning support for including the family home in the age pension assets test. The report proposes exempting the first $500,000 of the family home’s value and counting the balance under the assets test. On paper that may sound reasonable, but the practical consequences would be enormous.



The age pension cuts out completely for a homeowner couple with assessable assets of around $1.1 million. With Sydney’s median house price now around $1.75 million, hundreds of thousands of retirees could lose their pension despite having no greater spending power than people living in much cheaper parts of Australia. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert Should I get my super as a $1.7m lump sum, or a yearly pension? Paul Benson Money contributor The same problem applies to suggestions of imposing capital gains tax on the family home. Property values vary dramatically across the country, making a single national rule difficult to apply fairly. A more realistic way for governments to reduce pension costs would be to tighten the assets test by lowering the thresholds or changing the taper rate. Even that would be politically contentious because it would directly affect retirees who have arranged their affairs under the existing rules. For now, I think the proposal is best regarded as part of the policy debate rather than something likely to become law in the foreseeable future.



I bought shares for $1 each on January 1, 2024. By June 30, 2027 if they hypothetically were worth $2, I would have an unrealised capital gain of $1. My understanding is that this gain would still qualify for the 50 per cent CGT discount. If I then sold the shares on August 1, 2027 for $1.50, the shares would have fallen 50¢ from their June 30 value. Does that mean the 50-cent loss cancels the earlier discounted 50-cent gain so that I pay no tax? Julia Hartman says that assuming you have no other capital gains or capital losses, the legislation requires the 50¢ loss after June 30, 2027 to be deducted from the $1 pre-June 30 capital gain before the 50 per cent discount is applied. That leaves a net pre-2027 gain of 50¢, and after the 50 per cent discount you would be taxed on a capital gain of 25¢. One important point is still uncertain. The legislation also provides an alternative method that allows the capital gain to be calculated over the entire period of ownership. That approach may produce a better result in some situations, but the detailed rules have not yet been released, so we do not yet know exactly how that calculation will work in practice. I am nearly 80 and my partner is 13 years younger. She has no superannuation and her only income is the age pension. She is both the executor of my will and the nominated beneficiary of my superannuation. She also knows how to access my super account online, and any lump sum withdrawals are normally paid into our joint bank account. With all the recent publicity about delays in paying superannuation death benefits, I am concerned she could be left short of money after I die. If, immediately after my death, but before the fund has been notified, she logged into my account and withdrew money to cover her living expenses until the death benefit was paid, would there be any legal or tax consequences? I suspect we may be on thin legal ice and would appreciate your guidance.



I think there could be a problem if you try to withdraw money from the account of a deceased person. To me, a better option is for you to simply withdraw some money from your superannuation and open a new superannuation account for her. That keeps things legal and transparent while giving her the liquidity she needs. You recently mentioned investment bonds as a good way to invest for grandchildren. Your article renewed my interest because our daughter and son have each given us grandchildren, with another on the way. Editor's pick Opinion

Hip pocket The best way to spend your tax refund, no matter the amount Dominic Powell Money Editor One example in your article involved grandparents investing for a grandchild, but having the investment bond owned by the child’s parent. Does that mean we should establish one bond in our daughter’s name for her children and another in our son’s name for his children? What are the advantages of doing that instead of owning the bonds ourselves? Also, going back to my original question, how safe are investment bonds? There is no single right way to do it. The best ownership structure depends on what you are trying to achieve. If the bond is owned by your daughter or son, they have legal control of the investment and can use it for their children.



If you own the bond yourself, you keep control and can nominate who will receive the proceeds when you die. The better option depends on your family circumstances and estate planning goals. Investment bonds are issued by life insurance companies regulated by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), so the providers operate under strict financial rules. However, the value of the bond depends on the investments you choose. If you invest in shares, the value will rise and fall with the sharemarket, while more conservative investments are likely to fluctuate less. Like any investment, there are no guaranteed returns, which is why investment bonds are generally best suited to long-term investing. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. World.title: Cruising the Greek Islands never appealed to me. This trip changed my mind
World.content:
InspirationCruises Cruising the Greek Islands never appealed to me. This trip changed my mind Brian Johnston July 29, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Istanbul cruise terminal knocks Istanbul airport for six. Sleek as a contemporary art museum, it looks over the hum and chug of one of the world’s most historic harbours. It’s an anteroom to the Mediterranean. Plaka on the island of Milos. iStock The first thrill – technically, not quite the Mediterranean – is sailing out of Istanbul as an orange sun collapses onto the turrets of Topkapi palace. Next morning my ship, Explora II, squeezes through the Dardanelles and into the Aegean. How can you not be delighted to be on a luxury ship in a place so rich in maritime lore? Greece was the first place I visited as an independent adult. I’d just turned 18 and rumbled about the mainland in buses, hitchhiked when I needed to and racketed around the Greek islands on ferries that stank of oil and rust. I never thought I’d be cruising the Greek islands. I’m not sure I knew cruise ships existed because I grew up far from the coast. Eventually when I did know, I thought they’d never be for me.



Things have moved on, not least my open mindedness, greater need for comfort and lowered patience for travel’s irritations. While I’d never travel exclusively by cruise ship, they’re an enjoyable respite from do-it-yourself galumphing. 



You can be off the ship all day and slurp up all the local experiences you want. In Milos I’m off on the public bus to hilltop Plaka for a gloriously scenic walk that I share with only two other tourists. Then I walk down to Klima through dilapidated fields that smell of rosemary and goat, and don’t meet a single person. The fishing village of Klima on Milos. iStock The experiences you have wherever you go, whether by cruise ship or otherwise, is the result of your choices. A cruise ship is merely the facilitator. Besides, it presents you with a maritime perspective you won’t otherwise get. You never see the bad side of Greek islands from a cruise ship. All you get is blue sea, rusty rock, golden cliffs, hot skies. Over the centuries, islanders have added blue-domed chapels and whitewashed windmills, castles and fishing ports. You won’t see an airport terminal or a carpark. Almost every view is worthy of being featured on a postcard or printed calendar, if such things still exist. The ship is well-matched to the Greek islands. It is light-filled, breezy, unfussy and serene. Its subdued decor doesn’t try to compete with the explosion of colour outside.



The ship has no formal dress code, hardly any tablecloths, and little fuss despite the luxury levels. Who would want to sail here and squeeze into a dinner jacket? Comfort and ease aren’t the only reasons that cruising is the way to go in Greece. Most islands can be appreciated in a single day, and you get an overview of several in a short time. They’re often further from the crowds than you might think. You aren’t going to escape the tourist hordes in Greece all of the time, and that time is Rhodes on my cruise. But choose an itinerary that takes in less well-known islands, too, and you’ll be richly rewarded. Samos is one of the Greek Islands that hasn’t yet been overwhelmed by tourists. iStock Milos, Samos and Paros haven’t as yet been carbuncled with luxury resorts and nightclubs. Life here hasn’t been overwhelmed by the jetsetters and Instagrammers who play and party on Santorini and Mykonos.



You can head into the interior and hike amid landscapes that would make a petulant Greek god smile. Hills are stitched together by dry stone walls. Windmills are white, church domes blue, the window frames of houses green and red. Chapel interiors glimmer gold. In the village of Podromos on Paros I eat in a cafe surrounded by retirees swinging worry beads. As the ship sails away, I can enjoy a sunset without being jostled, as the blue-and-white colours of the Cyclades morph into orange and red. As evening falls, there are no thumping nightclubs and raucous stag parties, just a twinkle of stars, the muted burble of a fishing boat’s engines, the black outline of islands and a good dinner. One of Explora II’s four pools. Explora II has numerous restaurants, and no complaints about that. I can hop from Japan to France to the American West for an aged black Angus steak from a fine beast that might have been lassoed by a cowboy. But I keep wandering back to Med Yacht Club. For a start, I like its jaunty nautical theme: model ships, porthole-shaped windows only far larger, contemporary contours.



I like its cuisine, too. The menu rambles gently across the Mediterranean, sometimes unexpectedly, such as in tomato and strawberry salad with burrata. I can have a Greek meal here: shrimp saganaki, grilled octopus, some fine fish with a splash of lemon and herb salad. No baklava for dessert, but I’m not grumbling about the hazelnut semifreddo. Related Article Greece Beyond the islands, this peninsula is an underrated gem of Greece Nothing about the ship will irritate anyone, not even the princess with her pea. But I have to admit that one annoying thing is the bed because I seldom want to get out of it. I dare say it’s the best bed at sea. But still, it can’t compete with the Greek islands. I wrestle with my urge to snuggle down and amp up early, ready for the next arrival. I never thought I’d cruise the Greek islands, but never say never is a good philosophy to travel by. THE DETAILS



Cruise

World.title: Do the friends we make at 15 stay with us for life?
World.content:
The last time I saw Elsa, we were teenage girls in Melbourne, crying over a goodbye. Now, standing in a bustling square in France with my four daughters, I scan the crowd for a face I hope I will still recognise. What will it feel like to see each other again after all this time? More importantly, will our friendship still be there?

Then I spot her, making her way through the crowd. Time has changed us both, but her smile is unmistakable. She laughs, and I am transported back to the French village where we spent three months together, 35 years ago. Within seconds, we are in each other’s arms, talking over one another. There is an instant ease that feels both surprising and deeply familiar.

Elsa (left) and the author, Michaela, reuniting in eastern France in April, having met 35 years before.

I was 15 when I went to France as an exchange student. I’d lobbied for the United States, but my Francophile parents were convinced France would be better for me. I, however, was terrified. My anxiety eased when I learnt my host family had a daughter my age. Coming from a family of five girls, I liked the idea of a ready-made sister. I collected brochures from a travel agency, imagining life in a French city … but they didn’t live in a city. After arriving in Paris, I took a train alone to a station in eastern France, where Elsa and her mother picked me up and took me to their tiny village. It was a shock. Rolling green hills and ancient stone houses in every direction. Elsa’s home was surrounded by dense pine forest and farms – a world away from the eastern suburbs of Melbourne.

The first few weeks were miserable. I was homesick, overwhelmed by a language I barely understood. Many nights I cried into my pillow. Starting school was particularly tough. One lunchtime, some boys in the cafeteria began teasing me. I couldn’t understand the words, but I recognised the tone. I just sat there, embarrassed, willing myself not to cry. Elsa quietly picked up my tray and moved us to another table.

The two of us bonded over music, chocolate, teenage crushes and badly dubbed episodes of the 1980s American TV soap series Santa Barbara. We laughed our way through conversations in a muddled mix of French and English. Elsa’s humour was wickedly dry. When I was served venison for Christmas lunch, she looked at my plate and said, completely deadpan, “Bambi’s father”. I was horrified. She dissolved into laughter.

World.title: University procedures for harassment not good enough, students and staff say
World.content:
This story discusses sexual harassment.

The university community is calling institutions to do better at preventing and responding to bullying, harassment, and sexual violence on campuses.

Student representatives and staff told RNZ that the current procedures are simply not good enough.

'Listen to your students'

Thiyona Singh, co-president of the University of Auckland branch of Thursdays in Black, said while some progress had been made over the years, basics were still lagging.

"I think at times you feel some progress is being made, we're heading in the right direction and then another story comes out and you just think, oh, well, are we really moving forward? Are we taking a couple of steps back?"

Thiyona Singh is the co-president of University of Auckland's branch of Thursdays in Black. Thiyona Singh

The group is part of a student-led campaign working towards eliminating rape and sexual violence from tertiary spaces.

In 2017, the national group surveyed students and launched its first report, exposing widespread prevalence of sexual violence on Aotearoa's campuses.

Last year, the University of Auckland branch surveyed students again and concluded: "The core issues remain unresolved."

One hundred and twenty responses were collected from students across tertiary institutions in Auckland, and Singh said among them were stories about improper consent education, confusing reporting process, complaints swept under the rug, and the lack of accountability within institutions.

She said students deserved to feel safe and listened to by their universities.

"If we truly want to fight against sexual violence and we truly want to achieve a world where we don't have to beg for things like consent education or just for people to believe us when we share our stories, everyone needs to get involved. Everyone is accountable for it."

The report concluded by urging changes through better consent education, more visible reporting process, and stronger accountability within institutions. Singh said it was asking for the basics.

"Universities are such highly regarded institutions. And as students, we pay a lot of fees towards being able to go to these universities and to have these opportunities. To me, it is the bare minimum for these big institutions to have these policies in place."

She said polices about victim survivor welfare were often made without their presence, and she wanted leaderships to reconsider how they made decisions.

"Listen to your students. Listen to what they are calling for and do something about it ... The way things are is not working. "

Another group has made similar demands.

In 2020, Stop Sexual Harm on Campus (SSHOC) wrote an open letter to Universities New Zealand - the vice chancellor's committee and statutory body responsible for quality assurance in the university sector.

The letter called for a list of actions, including reviewing the use of non-disclosure agreements, considering independent investigation of sexual harassment complaints, and supporting members of universities to commit to prevention efforts.

Nicola Gaston, a professor in physics and author of Why Science is Sexist, was part of the group.

Gaston said not much had changed since then.

"If anything, I think the environment has gotten more difficult for survivors of harassment to speak out."

Nicola Gaston at the MacDiarmid Institute Annual Symposium held at the University of Auckland on 27 November 2025. Dean Carruthers / MacDiarmid Institute for Advanced Materials and Nanotechnology

She said the problem was not constrained to Aotearoa.

With the political climate and attacks on universities across the globe, it was now harder to have conversations about sexism and racism on campuses, she said.

Universities New Zealand has not responded to RNZ's inquiry by the publication of this story.

'Not a standard HR environment'

Gaston says universities were "not a standard HR environment" and existing policies were often not fit for purpose.

"My personal feeling is that universities lean too much into treating these issues as employment matters rather than as health and safety matters, which is what they really are when looked at from the point of view of a victim or a survivor."

She said often perpetrators were repeat offenders, and not handling a complaint correctly risked the welfare of other staff and students.

Richard Easther, a physics professor at University of Auckland, said power imbalances and the nicheness of research made academia a particularly challenging environment for victim survivors.

"It's not like they can simply move to another place in the way that a young lawyer, say, who's finding that a senior partner is being difficult, that's still going to be traumatic, but there will be other places where that person can seek employment. But in the case of many academic fields, you might even be looking to move to another country."

Richard Easther is a professor of physics at University of Auckland. Supplied

In 2017, the American Geophysical Union redefined "scientific misconduct" to include harassment, bullying, and discrimination, recognising the harm these behaviours could cause to science.

Easther said sexual harassment had significant impact on victims, and needed to be taken more seriously in academia.

"Anything that happens in the career of a young scientist that might derail them or slow them, that is like a young sports person having an injury at a crucial stage in their career. And this is a headwind that will blow very much in the faces of women who are trying to participate in the field, but not so much in men. And so if we're concerned about participation in science, and particularly in physical sciences, then this is something we have to take very seriously."

And after over two decades spent in the field, he'd like to see more academics speak up for their community.

"I think it's easier than people think. Obviously, I try to be measured about what I say in public. But I think once you do realise that you're established, then I think it's absolutely incumbent on you to make it easier for everybody and you should be sharing your success with others."
