World.title: Government sensible to adopt 'blank canvas' stance on Russian spying - former minister
World.content:
Former Defence Minister on Russian man's alleged spying for NZ Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The government is being sensible by not confirming or denying spying in Russia, former defence minister Wayne Mapp says.

New Zealand is being accused of spying on Russia, but experts are questioning just how likely that is and say the event seems bound to worsen relations which are already poor.

The man's arrest in the south-east city of Khabarovsk - first reported by The Moscow Times and accompanied by a video from Russia's federal security service the FSB - was for allegedly using email and instant messaging to provide information to the NZ Security Intelligence Service.

The 55-year-old man could face life imprisonment if found guilty of treason.

The government and the SIS have refused to comment while Russia's Ambassador to New Zealand Stanislav Krans refused an invitation to be interviewed on Morning Report on Wednesday.

Security analyst Paul Buchanan and Waikato University professor of international law Al Gillespie are among those who said there were good reasons to be highly sceptical of the Russian statements.

The arrest of the man facing the spying accusations in Russia was filmed. TACC

Former defence minister Dr Wayne Mapp said while he was speculating about the FSB's narrative, the footage of the arrested man "does not look like James Bond, that's for sure".

He also surmised there could be some "Russian disinformation" because of the convenience that someone was able to film it on a street.

"We are talking about a paranoid state that believes it's surrounded by enemies. I imagine they think the Five Eyes group is the worst of their enemies."

Russia was a police state and something "doesn't seem right just looking at that footage of the arrest".

It was odd to have a "visual" arrest and the man was then seen in court. It suggested "a prepared narrative".

"It might be about Russia demonstrating to its own citizens: look, we're surrounded by these Five Eyes enemies."

The government's stance was the right approach, he said.

"... not unsurprisingly, ministers and the SIS are not going to tell us anything... the prime minister said he's been briefed. He's clearly been briefed on something."

Mapp said the government needed to leave the situation as "a blank canvas" and neither confirm nor deny any aspects.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Silver Ferns remain on course to top pool after beating Uganda
World.content:
The Silver Ferns have beaten a plucky Uganda 58-50 to remain on top of their pool at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The Silver Ferns crucially beat the fourth ranked Jamaica on Monday, but world number six Uganda were never going to be an easy task.

Catherine Hall completed her remarkable return from injury when she started at goal defence and played half a game.

Hall missed the second half of the ANZ Premiership when she suffered a foot injury, which required surgery.

Despite just having eight test caps Hall was named for Glasgow subject to medical clearance, with selectors seeing her as a key part of the puzzle.

Hall's start at goal defence, saw captain Karin Burger move up to wing defence.

Coach Dame Noeline Taurua tested a number of different combinations in their third match of the Games, including starting Amelia Walmsley at goal attack.

Uganda played a disciplined game on attack with the massive target of 201cm Mary Cholhok, who plays in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball league, at goal shoot.

Catherine Hall bibbed up for the first time at the Commonwealth Games. Jayne Russell / Photosport

The Silver Ferns held a slim 15-14 lead after the first quarter but that didn't stop Taurua from ringing six changes after the break, including moving Walmsley into goal shoot.

Carys Stythe came on at goal defence for just her fourth Test for New Zealand and Hall moved back to goal keep, while Mila Reuelu-Buchanan went into wing defence.

New Zealand pushed out to a 5 goal lead but Uganda stayed within reach and the Silver Ferns led 28-25 at half-time.

More changes came in the third quarter, marked by the return of Grace Nweke at goal shoot, and Martina Salmon was injected at goal attack.

Kelly Jackson came back on at goal keep to mark Cholhok, her Queensland Firebirds team-mate.

Things started to unravel a bit for Uganda, who were playing their fourth game in as many days.

The Ferns started having a major impact in defence across the court, and Uganda's typically disciplined attack, started breaking down.

New Zealand led 44-35 heading into the final quarter, where more changes came, including Salmon to goal shoot.

New Zealand will be disappointed that they didn't put their foot down in the final quarter, which Uganda won 15-14.

The Silver Ferns shot at 88 percent.

The way things stand, the Silver Ferns are likely to meet England or South Africa in the semi-finals, while Jamaica will have to face world number one Australia in the final four.

World.title: 'Left to rot': Auckland residents say Kainga Ora ghost homes attracting illegal dumping
World.content:
Locals sceptical about plans to build 1200 homes near Arrowtown Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A resident on a central Auckland street say multiple boarded up houses and vacant lots have been "left to rot", after a major Kainga Ora project was stopped last year.

And a city councillor says the community feels "abandoned" after the government pulled the plug on the development, but the housing minister and Kainga Ora say some social homes are being planned.

Hundreds of homes were set to be built on O'Donnell Avenue, as part of the housing agency's Wesley West development.

Demolition began before the agency undertook a nationwide re-set last year.

Resident Stu Harwood said there were more than 30 empty Kainga Ora lots or houses on the street, and some had been fenced or boarded up for two years.

"They've effectively been left to rot.

"Because these houses are just degrading in plain view of everyone in the neighbourhood - it's now become a target for illegal dumping, they haven't been looked after at all. There's rubbish collecting, all up and down the street."

An old suitcase, mattress, spare tyre and mound of building materials are among items RNZ saw had been tossed onto the sections, or grass berms outside them.

An old suitcase and other items. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Stu Harwood said signs urging against dumping and regular calls to the council hadn't stopped the dumping.

Auckland Council told RNZ it had 56 call-outs for illegal dumping on the street in the last financial year.

Harwood said there was a view among residents that the street had "gone downhill".

"It's a real shame, this street's got a school on it, Wesley Primary, you know it's a great neighbourhood, and it's a real shame to see these properties not used."

Stu Harwood. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Kainga Ora's general manager of urban development and delivery, Nick Howcroft, said the agency had plans to transform 36 state house sites into 331 new medium-high density social and private market units in the area.

Residents were moved out between May 2024 and February 2025, and some demolition started, he said.

But following a government re-set of the agency last year, $72 million from the project was re-prioritised.

Howcroft said Kainga Ora is instead planning 39 2-4 bedroom state homes across four sites, predominantly for families, and had lodged a resource consent application with Auckland Council, with construction expected to start in late spring.

Kainga Ora had plans to build hundreds of homes on O'Donnell Avenue, but that was stopped last year. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Albany-Eden-Puketapapa councillor Julie Fairey said that's a fraction of what had been imagined.

"It was going to be quite a much larger scale of redevelopment. They were talking about creating effectively a new town centre at the intersection of Sandringham and Stoddard Road.

"There was a lot of discussion with council about the council facilities that would be needed, potentially a new park in the area."

The Cityvision-backed councillor said the Wesely community felt abandoned after the development stopped, while thousands of others across the city needed housing.

"There's nothing happening with these sections...so they're attracting illegal dumping, there could be issues with rats or vermin, so not only is it an under-utilisation of land, but the community feel really abandoned, and that sucks."

Auckland councillor Julie Fairey. RNZ/ The Detail - Sharon Brettkelly

Howcroft said Kainga Ora was regularly monitoring the sites for illegal dumping and doing regular ground maintenance on the properties.

"If neighbours are aware of any issues with people illegally accessing the sites or dumping rubbish, we would appreciate them letting us know."

'Big challenge'

Wesley Primary School principal Andy Crowe said he was expecting his school to grow from about 150 to 600 students.

The school was gearing up for multiple stages of development too - and in 2023 moved into new buildings ahead of major construction.

But plans for three more large hubs - the equivalent of 12 extra classrooms - ground to a halt.

O'Donnell Avenue. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

He said families in the social houses were forced to move out of the area, including to Ōtāhuhu and Karaka.

"They basically are getting shipped everywhere else but staying in our community. Transience is a really really big challenge.

"One of the key drivers for our kids success, regardless of what school or socio-economic background, is that they get to stay in education, and they get to stay in the community that's supporting them."

Crowe said it's been difficult to re-set as a school, while meeting the strategic objectives of the curriculum.

He said he was pleased to hear the new homes being built on O'Donnell Avenue were predominantly for families, and might contribute to roll growth.

Overngrown grass on O'Donnell Avenue. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Data from the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport show there are currently 9356 people on Auckland's social housing register.

Fairey said she thought Kainga Ora staff wanted the larger development to go ahead.

"I think that a lot of the people at Kainga Ora would love to be able to progress this, but they do not have support from their minister, they do not have support from this government or Cabinet."

Housing Minister Chris Bishop said while the original development was paused, hundreds of homes had been built in the wider Mt Roskill area - with state homes still coming for Wesley.

"It's a gain in terms of social homes, yes. I mean we have tried to re-focus the Wesley component of the wider Mt Roskill project towards social houses.

"The large scale projects are a mixture of urban renewal for social houses, but also fundamentally just market houses. Just private sector market sales."

Housing Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Bishop said he'd stressed to officials that empty state homes or land must be looked after to prevent rubbish dumping.

He said Kainga Ora owned 78,000 houses throughout the country and at any given point there would be demolition, sales, and vacancies.

At the end of March 2026 there were 400 empty Kainga Ora homes, down from 1300 when National went into government, he said.

World.title: 'Timely': Horticulture industry welcomes government's changes to RSE scheme
World.content:
Industry welcomes loosened RSE rules for trusted employers Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The horticulture industry says changes to the Recognised Seasonal Employment (RSE) scheme will give employers clarity and help to protect workers.

The government said rule changes would be phased in over the next two years.

They included stronger and clearer accommodation standards for RSE workers, who also would have greater flexibility to move between employers during their time in Aotearoa.

The workers would soon be able to apply for a migrant exploitation protection visa, allowing them to break contract and stay in the country for up to six months.

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford said other changes would aim to "simplify" wage deductions, while extending accreditation time for "exemplary" growers to six years.

Horticulture New Zealand said the changes would reduce unnecessary compliance for trusted employers.

Chief executive Kate Scott said standardised cost-recovery agreements, clearer rules on allowable costs and stronger complaints processes would make the system easier for workers to understand and navigate.

"This policy review is timely for a scheme that has delivered enduring benefits for growers, workers and Pacific communities for almost two decades. Practical changes are needed to keep it fit for the future.

"The RSE scheme fills genuine seasonal gaps when enough local workers are not available, helping growers harvest crops on time while continuing to recruit, train and employ New Zealanders."

Orchardist Paul Paynter, general manager of Yummy Fruit, said the changes would make complying less onerous for growers.

He said seasonal fluctuations meant growers were sometimes short-staffed, and it would be less complicated to transfer workers from one grower to another.

Paynter told Morning Report problems in the sector had been "90-plus percent with labour contractors rather than with established businesses like ours".

World.title: Qantas 24-hour test flight tracked by millions online
World.content:
A Qantas aircraft set to be used for direct flights between Australia and Europe has been tracked by millions of internet users as it completed a marathon 24-hour test flight from Melbourne to France.

The specially adapted Airbus A350-1000ULR is one of 12 aircraft set to be delivered to Qantas as part of Project Sunrise, which is due to deliver non-stop Sydney to London flights from next year.

When launched, the route will become the world's longest commercial passenger service.

Airbus said the aircraft, which boasts a specially designed extra fuel tank, remained in the air for 24 hours and 24 minutes, covering 23,075 km without stopping, before landing at the aircraft manufacturer's factory in Toulouse, France.

Flight-tracking provider Flightradar24 said the trip was the second-most-tracked flight ever on its channels - behind a 2024 flight carrying Queen Elizabeth II's coffin - with more than 3.6 million people following its progress northwards via Canada.

In 2005, a Boeing 777-200LR Worldliner flew 21,601.7 kilometres from Hong Kong to London in 22 hours and 42 minutes.

Qantas has ordered 12 modified A350-1000ULR aircraft, designed to connect Australia's east coast with London and New York in about 20 hours.

The services aim to turn what was once a five-day journey on the "Kangaroo Route" to London into a single flight lasting 19 to 21 hours, depending on routing and winds.

The first aircraft, which carries 20,000 litres of fuel and can seat 238 passengers, is due for delivery in April 2027.

Qantas expects to operate daily nonstop flights between Sydney and London from October 2027.

World.title: One hospitalised after 'domestic-related' incidents at two Auckland properties
World.content:
Two properties have been cordoned off and a person has been hospitalised following overnight incidents on Auckland's North Shore.

Ambulances attended call outs to addresses on Lingfield St in Glenfield and Seon Place in Birkdale after 8pm Tuesday.

A Lingfield Street property has been cordoned off. Nick Monro / RNZ

It is not known how many people were involved in either incident, though police told the New Zealand Herald the incidents were "domestic-related" and one person had been arrested.

"One person is in custody and police are not seeking anyone else in connection with the incident. Police can confirm there are two scenes, and inquiries remain ongoing."

St John told RNZ it responded to the Birkdale address with an ambulance and a critical care unit and one person was taken to North Shore Hospital in moderate condition.

A property has been cordoned off at 43 Lingfield Street in Glenfield following an incident overnight. Nick Monro / RNZ

They were called to the Glenfield address at 8.50pm and were still at the scene shortly before 10pm. They referred further inquiries to police.

World.title: Live: Glasgow Commonwealth Games, day five
World.content:
Commonwealth Games: Lewis Clareburt clinches gold for 400m IM Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Swimmers Lewis Clareburt and Erika Fairweather will try to enhance their medal hauls in the pool on day 5 at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

Clareburt stunned his rivals over 200m butterfly yesterday and contests his preferred 400m medley today, while Fairweather seeks her fifth piece of metal, when she races over 800m freestyle.

At athletics, Lauren Bruce qualified second in the women's hammer, while speedster Zoe Hobbs lines up in the 100 metres semifinals.

Boxer Alex Mukaka will take home a medal, if he can overcome his Namibian quarterfinal opponent, while the Silver Ferns are playing Uganda for the top spot in their netball pool.

World.title: Live: Kennedy claims silver, smashes Aussie record in electric 100m final
World.content:
We just chatted to a saturated Georgia Harris, who had the worst of the conditions for her 100m semifinal.

This photo is very much not from tonight. (Getty)

Her time of 11.80 wasn't what she wanted, but at 22, there's plenty to look forward to.

"The time isn't what I wanted and what I know I'm capable of, but ... I didn't expect to be swimming tonight. "What can you do in those conditions? I showed up and I'm a Commonwealth Games semifinalist."

She says it's quite hard to analyse her start because of the diabolical weather.

"This is not what I'm capable of but this is just the beginning of Georgia Harris, so keep your eyes out."

I let her know about that little message of support from her parents we showed you earlier and it got her a little choked up (sorry Georgia!) because her parents couldn't be there in Germany when she won the 100m at the World University Games last year.

"It makes me emotional every time I think about it. It's a special moment for them to be here and actually watch me do it live."

World.title: Country footy player charged after 'ugly' scenes in southern WA
World.content:
A country football player has been charged with assault and choking after clashes during a game in southern Western Australia.

The man was allegedly involved in two incidents during Sunday's Lower South West Football League clash in Kojonup between the hometown Cougars and the Bridgetown Bulldogs.

Footage of two incidents during the game prompted public outcry and a police investigation.

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed Kojonup Police, with assistance from Busselton detectives, charged the man, from Cowaramup, with assault occasioning bodily harm and "impeding another person's breathing or blood circulation by applying pressure to the neck".

The Cowaramup man is accused of choking an opposing player. (Supplied)

On Tuesday WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch said violence on the football field was "not on".

"You are not immune on the sporting field," he said.

"We understand there are normal contacts in the spirit of play, but if it is outside of play and a deliberate targeted attack, then it is an assault."

Loading...

Game 'turned ugly'

Kojonup Football Club vice-president Matt Marinoni said the top-of-the-table clash was a "tense and fiery" game that "turned ugly".

He said the umpires did not see the off-ball incident.

"Then there was a lot of noise in the crowd," Mr Marinoni said.

"From there there was a bit of a wrestle and melee because we saw one of our teammates was on the ground, unconscious."

That player is in good spirits and recovering from his facial injuries and concussion, but is "shaken", according to the club.

A spokesperson from the Lower South West Football League told the ABC it was aware of the incident.

"The matter has been referred to the Country Football WA tribunal process and will be dealt with in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures," the spokesperson said.

The league declined to comment further, in order to "preserve the integrity and fairness of the tribunal process".

The Bridgetown Football Club said the matter was being dealt with by Country Football WA.

"[We] do not condone the behaviour shown during Sunday's game," the club said in a statement.

"This has no place in football and does not reflect the true values of our club."

The 23-year-old is due to face the Katanning Magistrates Court in August.

World.title: Joint spares Aussie blushes on tough day at Memphis Open
World.content:
Rising star Maya Joint has spared Australia's blushes at the WTA's hard-court event in Memphis.

On a day when the Australian challenge fizzled, the world number 77 won her round-of-16 clash against wildcard Whitney Osuigwe in straight sets.

The 20-year-old needed a tick over 90 minutes for a 6-4, 6-1 win against the American.

Joint will now meet the winner of top-seed Ekaterina Alexandrova or fellow Russian Kristina Liutova for a place in the quarterfinals.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Already boasting tournament victories in Rabat and Eastbourne last year, which helped her climb to a career-best number 28 in the world in February this year, Joint lost her serve twice in the opening set but did enough to take it in 45 minutes.

The second set proved more comfortable and Joint, who famously eliminated Serena Williams in the opening round of Wimbledon this year, broke three times to advance.

There was no such joy for Talia Gibson and Storm Hunter though.

Gibson was soundly beaten by German Tatjana Maria 6-0, 6-3, while compatriot Storm Hunter succumbed 7-5, 7-5 to fifth-seeded Colombian Camila Osorio.

World number 66 Kimberly Birrell, who lost her first-round doubles clash alongside American Peyton Stearns to Ingrid Martins and Ekaterina Ovcharenko 6-4, 6-7 (7/4), 11-9, takes on China's Ma Yexin in the singles draw on Tuesday.

In the shock of the day, Swiss third seed Viktorija Golubic was eliminated in three sets by Katie Volynets of the US, while all three unseeded Russian players in action were victorious.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Embattled LIV Golf tour asks to defer payment to Adelaide golf club
World.content:
The financially struggling LIV Golf tour has asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club, raising doubts over whether next year's Adelaide event will go ahead.

Kooyonga in Adelaide's western suburbs is scheduled to host LIV Golf Adelaide in 2027 before the tour moves to a newly redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course in 2028.

But the future of the league has been under a cloud since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced it would be pulling its reported billions in funding at the end of the 2026 season.

The Grange Golf Club has previously hosted the LIV event in Adelaide. (ABC News: Rory McClaren)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said he was made aware last week that LIV Golf had asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club.

"An extension was sought by LIV as they're working through programming next year for those payments to be made in September," he said.

"That extension was granted."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas says he is aware LIV Golf has asked for an extension. (ABC News)

Mr Malinauskas indicated there would "presumably" be enough time for Kooyonga to prepare for the March 2027 event, given the club had granted the payment extension.

The deferred payment is worth $500,000, Adelaide radio station FIVEaa reported.

In a statement, Kooyonga Golf Club confirmed it "evaluated and approved" a "short operational extension regarding its initial venue payment" to LIV Golf.

Deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague said the government needed to be more transparent about the event's future.

SA's deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague wants more transparency about the event's future. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

"Those who've bought tickets, those who are committing all sorts of other ways to the holding of the event are going to be left mightily disappointed … if all of a sudden LIV Golf goes from hero to zero," he said.

"If there's one thing you need to host successful international events, it's confidence and it's the capacity for everybody to get behind something because you know that it's actually going to happen and not just be shrouded in doubt.

"That's unfortunately where we stand right now."

The ABC has contacted LIV Golf for comment.

The shift to North Adelaide has been controversial. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The premier has previously said the state government would need a "clear indication" from LIV Golf about the event's future by October.

Can the SA government justify a $45m golf course upgrade without LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

The state government has a contract with LIV Golf until 2031 and pays an undisclosed fee for the tour to host an annual event in Adelaide.

LIV Golf's success at the Grange Golf Club was also the catalyst for the government to fund a controversial $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course.

The project has been subject to protests over the felling of 585 trees.

The government has since secured the Australian Open golf tournament to be hosted at the North Adelaide Golf Course from 2028 to 2034.

World.title: The sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains
World.content:
"It's just a square."

That's the three-star review of Nelson Mandela Place in Glasgow by someone named Katie Nicholson on Google.

Katie isn't entirely wrong. A statue for the freedom fighter and former South African president is set to be unveiled in October, but for now there's not a whole lot to see at the spot, listed as a tourist attraction on Google Maps.

But the couple of street signs tacked to buildings on West George Street, not far from the city centre, sit as an elegant and understated middle finger to apartheid South Africa.

The South African consulate left this location for some reason. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 1986, while Mandela was still in prison on Robben Island, the Glasgow City Council changed the name of St George's Place to Nelson Mandela Place.

It meant that the South African consulate under the then-ruling National Party was forced not only to see the name of one of their chief antagonists as they entered the Stock Exchange building every day, but also send out correspondence bearing his name.

They opted to use a PO Box address before moving from the location in the early 90s.

After Mandela was released, he came to the city to thank the people for their solidarity in 1993.

Nelson Mandela thanked Glasgow in 1993, between being released from prison and becoming president of South Africa. (Getty Images: Chris Bacon/PA)

"While we were physically denied our freedom in the country of our birth, a city 6,000 miles away, and as renowned as Glasgow, refused to accept the legitimacy of the apartheid system, and declared us to be free."

That cry of freedom is as synonymous with the Scottish as it is with Mandela himself.

So, how does a celebration of this Commonwealth sit with a city and country that has always had a fraught relationship with oppressors generally and the English specifically?

ABE – Anyone but England

Andy Murray got to represent Scotland in the 2022 Battle of the Brits. (Getty Images: Mark Runnacles/Battle of the Brits)

Tennis great Andy Murray once perplexed some (read: Americans) less au fait with the unique rivalries within the UK when he was asked who he'd be supporting at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and replied: "Anyone but England."

Scotland isn't on its own in this regard.

In the Ashes last summer, Australia's injury-plagued men's Test team scored a triumphant professional 4-1 victory, but more Australian joy was derived from watching another epic capitulation of an England team that had declared itself the saviour of Test cricket, teaching us all how to entertain, if not actually win much of anything.

We cheered every humiliating faceplant and fumble at least as much as we celebrated the all-time world-class performances of Travis Head and Mitchell Starc.

The recently completed World Cup was another reminder of the collective glee shared by so many in watching England stumble.

The Sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

There's just something about the schadenfreude for Scots, Aussies and dozens of other nations in watching England lose.

Sure, you've got the Parthenon Sculptures and Rosetta Stone, but we've got Ellyse Perry and Steve Smith.

"There is this standard, reflexive idea of that they would prefer almost everybody to win other than England, as the most powerful part of the United Kingdom," Western Sydney University emeritus professor of culture and research David Rowe told ABC Sport.

"I think for some people it's serious, for some people it's just a bit of fun."

Loading Instagram content

There are jokes to be made, but also reflections on the very real subjugation that went on for centuries, and arguably only ended in 1997 when Hong Kong gained its independence.

This celebration of empire remains a peculiarity as calls grow to decolonise our language and our lives.

For a perfect example, the Parthenon Sculptures mentioned earlier are more famously known as the Elgin Marbles, named for the lord who nicked them from Greece and brought them back to Old Blighty at the start of the 19th century.

"I mean, the Commonwealth of Nations is, let's face it, anachronistic," Rowe said.

Flags that don't always get to fly wave prominently at the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"There are people who … don't know much about it or, if they schooled up on it, educated themselves about it, would realise that this is an anachronistic organisation based on an empire that no longer technically exists."

Although, many in the still-constituent Scotland would tell you the legacy, if not the actuality, of the empire remains in many ways.

"There are plenty of people in Scotland, including its leading Scottish National Party, who really would prefer to separate from the United Kingdom and who are mightily displeased by Brexit," said Rowe, a sports sociologist who consulted on the Glasgow Life team tasked with helping boost the city's standing on the global sporting stage.

"There are plenty of Scots who felt a greater affinity with the European Union than with England."

Strange, anomalous and anachronistic

A time machine is perhaps a fitting vehicle of entry of an event harking back to the past. (AAP: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

At the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were warmly welcomed by the packed crowd at Glasgow's Hydro, perhaps surprisingly considering the same crowd's hearty refrains of Flower of Scotland barely an hour later.

The Scottish anthem retells Robert the Bruce's legendary victory over King Edward II of England at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.

The thrust of the rousing choon, and Scotland's identity more broadly, is about how this small but mighty land of hard folk repelled the crown time and again on the back of sheer grit and pride.

So ingrained in their identity is sticking it to the English that, instead of tearing down statues of old royals and dignitaries like the Duke of Wellington, they have simply given up on removing the traffic cones placed on his head.

The Games have never opened like this – maybe they always should The 2026 Commonwealth Games are like no other that came before them and the opening ceremony was similarly unique in a way that will make it hard to go back.

And yet, twice in the past 12 years, Glasgow has gone out of its way to host what is correctly dubbed the Friendly Games, welcoming dozens of nations whose primary unifying theme is that they were once conquered by the "bastards" from that anthem.

"It does strike me as something of an irony that it's not that very long ago that Scotland had a referendum to sever its ties with the United Kingdom and the British Crown, and now it's hosting a Commonwealth Games," Rowe said.

"I think it's having a bit of fun, all the kilts and all the Scottish culture, reminding people that Scotland has its own identity and has not just been subsumed by the United Kingdom."

The Commonwealth Games has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

If you need more evidence of the strange bedfellows in effect, Rowe said you need only look at the event's original name.

It was called the British Empire Games from 1930 to 1950, the British Empire and Commonwealth Games until for the next four editions, and the British Commonwealth Games until 1972.

"So even more coded British," Rowe told ABC Sport.

"And it's a strange body in some ways, if you consider that it is a monument to colonialism and imperialism. And yet the members, most of whom were formerly under the jurisdiction of the British crown, were colonised, have now voluntarily agreed to join an organisation which was formed out of that imperial arrangement."

It also provides those in the British Isles a chance to beat England while representing Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man.

Scottish knights of the British Empire Chris Hoy and Andy Murray have won a combined 13 Olympic medals for Great Britain.

Duncan Scott is Team GB's most decorated Olympic swimmer, Mark Cavendish has won a world championship and Olympic silver with the Union Jack next to his name, but both turned around to beat the English while flying the Scottish saltire and Isle of Man's triskelion during the Commonwealth Games.

Duncan Scott has won more Olympic medals than any other British swimmer. (Supplied: Commonwealth Sport)

So how does the home crowd feel watching their sporting heroes flying those flags?

"I think it means more to them to compete for Scotland," one Glasgow local, Peter, told ABC Sport.

"You can see it in their faces when they do better. It does mean a lot more to them to represent their home country."

There's perhaps a hint of personal projection in this fan's assessment, as summed up by his mate, Pat.

"I would hope that it does [mean more] for them, because it would for me," he said.

Duncan Scott with the 2014 and 2026 mascots, the latter sporting a traffic cone for a horn. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

No amount of raucous crowd support or national pride is going to turn a 45-year-old bricklayer who's had a hot dog for breakfast into a 10-flat 100m runner. But at the tippy-top of sport, where the margins are at their finest, it's got to be worth a few hundredths of a second.

Angharad Evans swam for Team GB at the 2025 world championships in Singapore, missing the semifinals and finishing a brutal 18th overall in the 100m breaststroke as she went almost two seconds slower than her time at the national trials.

She carried those scars with her until she exorcised them with a spectacular victory at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre, winning her first international gold medal and thanking the crowd for getting her to the wall 0.12 of a second ahead of Aimee Canny.

Angharad Evans said the Tollcross crowd carried her for the final 10 metres. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"Scotland was there to witness that and that was a very, very special moment for me," she said.

"I thanked them because leading into competitions it's so easy for doubts and negative thoughts to play a part in my mindset leading up, and I walk out and they just really uplift me and give me the confidence I need and boost me up.

"They often talk about how proud they are of us bringing back gold medals and PBs, but I'm immensely proud to have the Tartan Army supporting me in the crowd.

"Wearing the blue and white, hearing the crowd, being part of Scotland just carries you to the end. I don't think I would have had the strength and the courage I did in the last 10 metres if I wasn't in the blue and white and didn't have that crowd behind me.

"They absolutely helped me get to the end and finish in first place. So it's a medal for me but it's also a medal for Scotland."

All that from an English-born 23-year-old who is still learning the words to that famous Scottish anthem.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
World.content:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Archie Goodburn did not win a medal but won the respect of everyone as he competes while dealing with brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport" they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final. But outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"[A dream] where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Seeing double? (Getty Images: PA Images/Owen Humphreys)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games that two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her identical twin sister who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow. But everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

Loading...

All it takes is one look at the comment section to see people on either side of the heated debate: from supporters saying shorter dresses are easier to play in, to those who reckon the Diamonds look "silly".

Responding to haters, Bruce says it's a "good thing we're strong … fit, and we train hard".

I mean, it's not like they aren't wearing shorts under the dress. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

5. Mollie O'Callaghan pulls out of the backstroke

Mollie O'Callaghan has withdrawn from the 50m backstroke. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Coming into this Commonwealth Games, Mollie O'Callaghan revealed she was managing a back injury, and it cost her a chance in her backup event the 50m backstroke.

The 22-year-old was worried that she might not even be able to compete in Glasgow after scans revealed stress fractures and bone bruising on her lumbar spine.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

World.title: Sabalenka, Djokovic lead mixed doubles teams for US Open
World.content:
Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic headline the initial list of 16 teams entered into the US Open mixed doubles championship.

The tournament was overhauled last year, with a $US1 million ($1.43 million) prize going to the winners, in an effort to get top singles players to compete. Many of those types of stars were listed among the teams announced Monday by the US Tennis Association.

Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud, the runners-up in 2025, are entered again, along with Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz, the Japanese duo of Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori, along with Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper.

The main draw will be played over two days on August 25-26, with all the matches set to be held in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, the two biggest venues at the US Open.

Teams can enter up until August 17, when the six duos with the best combined singles rankings at the time will be automatically entered into the main draw.

That means Sabalenka, the two-time defending US Open women's champion and Djokovic, still ranked number five on the men's tour at age 39, will be safely into the field.

Eight teams will be given wild cards by the USTA, and two other teams will play their way into the field through a qualifying tournament to be held from August 24.

Defending champions win US Open mixed doubles final Italian pair Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori accomplish their "mission" by winning the US Open mixed doubles title for the second straight year in a controversially revamped format.

The remainder of the teams that were entered as of Monday:

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev; Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli; Diana Shnaider and Daniil Medvedev; Amanda Anisimova and Learner Tien; Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime; Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe; Taylor Townsend and Alexander Zverev; Elena-Gabriela Ruse and Nuno Borges; Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori; Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten; and siblings Peyton Stearns and Preston Stearns.

Errani and Vavassori are the two-time defending US Open champions. The Italians needed a wild card to get into last year's event because their singles ranking was too low, and that will be the case again this year.

The US Open was initially criticised last year because the format of the event shut out doubles specialists such as Errani and Vavassori, but the tournament certainly seemed a success, helping draw 78,000 fans to the grounds and selling out Ashe both days.

"Any time you can bring women and men together on the same team, you showcase tennis at its best. This is exactly what the mixed doubles championship does," USTA CEO Craig Tiley said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The mixed doubles championship is an innovation that will engage new audiences and give our fans another opportunity to see the biggest stars compete together."

Errani and Vavassori were the only traditional doubles team in last year's tournament.

There is a chance for more this year — Siniakova and Patten are doubles specialists — with the addition of the eight-team qualifying tournament, which will include six direct entries and two wild cards.

The format will be best-of-three-set matches with sets to four games, tiebreakers at 4-all and a 10-point match tie-break instead of a third set, through the semifinals. The final will be standard scoring with sets to six games and a tiebreaker at 6-all, and a 10-point match tiebreaker if necessary.

AP

World.title: 'A gorgeous human' gets her solo moment and still shares it with her mates
World.content:
There aren't many legacies in sport as dominant as Australia in the women's 4x100m freestyle relay.

The first night of the Glasgow program marked the team's 19th victory in the past 21 major international finals across the Olympics, long-course world championships, Pan Pacs and Commonwealth Games.

It also marked the sixth time Meg Harris had stood on the top step of the podium with her teammates in those events, bridging the gap from the Campbells era to these Commonwealth Games and onwards towards Brisbane 2032.

But on Tuesday morning (AEST), when Mollie O'Callaghan and Shayna Jack joined her up there, they did so with her blessing, of course, after she became the solo 100m champion for the first time.

Meg Harris (centre) pipped superstars Shayna Jack (left) and Mollie O'Callaghan to the wall. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"It's pretty incredible, I've never done that before. I've never been in that position," Harris said.

"Hopefully this is just the start of my journey. I'm pretty happy with that. These girls are absolutely incredible, so any chance I get to stand on the podium with them is great."

The trials in June marked the first time she had made the team as an individual 100m swimmer.

Glasgow 2026 day four live Australia wins nine gold medals across the pool, athletics track and in the gymnastics on day four in Glasgow.

The 24-year-old admitted to struggling with motivation in the 100m after the Paris Olympics, rediscovering her love for the sport through her pet 50m event, where she won the world title in Singapore last year.

"I've always loved the [100m] race," she said.

"The 50m was something I've always loved and always known I've enjoyed racing that … but the 100m is always the one I've been working towards in the long run. I guess I need to take a step back and enjoy it for a while."

Harris's win was one of seven gold medals on the night for Australia, with Alex Perkins in the 100m butterfly and Jenna Forrester in the 400m individual medley also enjoying a breakout meet.

Jenna Forrester has enjoyed a breakout Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Forrester's victory added to her surprise 200m backstroke victory three nights earlier.

"We all really get around each other, and that's what makes Team Australia really special and successful," Perkins said.

Little did she know how true that was.

Minutes earlier, Harris had made an immediate pivot from star performer to cheer captain, stepping away from her media obligations to cheer Perkins on with every stroke as she powered to victory.

"She's amazing; all those girls are in the 100m freestyle," Perkins said.

"[They're] so successful in that event and [Harris is] just also a gorgeous human. I was really proud; it was really inspiring to watch her before my event."

100m butterfly gold medallist Alex Perkins is a big fan of Meg Harris. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Perkins and Harris are kindred spirits, two swimmers winning their favourite events for the first time after years of toil while in their mid-20s (Perkins celebrating gold on her 26th birthday).

Along with Forrester, Sam Short, Lani Pallister and a slew of other gold medallists on the night and at these Games, it's all part of a moment of transition for the Dolphins in Glasgow.

It's not so much a passing of the baton as simply getting more hands on it.

"We've got a home [Olympic] Games in 2032, we're all trying to do our best and make the most of every moment," Perkins said.

And Harris is a key part of that.

The 4x100m freestyle squad featured eight swimmers in Glasgow: Brittany Castelluzzo (25), Inez Miller (19), Jessica Cole (19) and Hannah Casey (20) in their heat; and Harris, Perkins, Jack and O'Callaghan in the final.

The jewel in Australian swimming's crown is central to the rejuvenation that never really stops for this all-conquering team.

In among the Dolphins, they call themselves "the starfish", according to the retiring Jack.

Swimming is perhaps the loneliest of all elite sport pursuits, so finding that connection is crucial to, if you'll pardon the pun, keeping your head above water.

"Meg's my roommate here, which I'm really grateful for because we do have a lot of events together and being able to share in those moments with her is extremely special to me," Jack said.

"Swimming is such an event that can be quite isolating. That's also why I love the relays because you get to share in those special moments with somebody else, and being able to go 1-2-3 tonight, it's just another moment I get to share with these amazing girls."
