Tech.title: A Two-Person Startup Has Fixed One of the Most Hated Sounds in Modern Life
Tech.content:
I behave very strangely in my kitchen. On any given day, you will find me, often mid-conversation, sprinting from one end of the room to the other. Nothing on the stove has caught fire. No pots are boiling over. I am trying to reach the microwave oven before its counter hits zero.

Why? I detest so deeply its shrill beep heralding the completion of its reheating duties that it's almost as if the appliance has trained me, through operant conditioning, to open its door at T-minus 1 second, so the grating noise is silenced before it begins. But there is another way, a means by which microwave makers can keep their margins, not change the hardware in any way, and, just by manipulating a few lines of code, change the kitchen experience sonically for the better for aurally assaulted microwavers everywhere.

Enter Joel Corelitz and Colin Coogan from Starling, sound designers who have previously worked with clients including Sony, Microsoft, Netflix, and Sega, as well as on major projects such as a sonic strategy for Ford's entire lineup. Corelitz, much like the rest of us, loathes his microwave's unbearable beeps, so he decided to see if they could do something about it.

Beep Beep

The beep has cursed humanity for a relatively short period of time. The use of “beep” to mean a short, high-pitched sound first appeared in an Arthur C. Clarke sci-fi story, The Sands of Mars, as recently as 1951. Before this, “beep” was used as a descriptor of the sound of car horns.

For decades now, nearly all microwaves have used the same technology to generate their penetrating pings: a small, cheap device called a passive piezoelectric buzzer. It's a membrane that, when electrically charged, vibrates, producing a rudimentary beep.

The piezo buzzer was first brought to the mass market in the 1970s by Japanese manufacturers. Thanks to their low cost—piezoelectric buzzers cost a matter of cents—and simplicity, the buzzers soon found their way into all manner of gadgets: toys, smoke detectors, alarm clocks, multimeters, watches, and, yes, microwaves. However, the versatility was matched by limitations. Manufacturers can set the beep's frequency and duration, but that's about it. This has not stopped the basic tech from still being widely deployed in all manner of gear.

Manufacturers can add speakers to a microwave, allowing the appliance to reproduce a cornucopia of aural delights. But the reason the vast majority of microwave manufacturers stubbornly stick with offensive beeps is, naturally, cost. Competition in consumer white goods is fierce. Why replace a super-cheap part that does the job with something pricier?

The challenge Corelitz and Coogan set themselves was this: better microwave sound, sound with some personality; but no new hardware, so using existing chips and existing buzzers. Everything had to be done just with code.

Tech.title: Can the New York Times Save Journalism From Our AI Overlords?
Tech.content:
For most companies, spending upwards of $20 million on a single legal fight with an uncertain outcome might mean the boss has some explaining to do. For A.G. Sulzberger, the publisher of The New York Times, that explanation is simple: It’s the cost of defending journalism—at the Times and everywhere else.

Sulzberger, who took on the publisher role about a decade ago and has been an influential leader in the Times’ much-lauded push into digital innovation, has no shortage of defending to do lately. Nearly three years ago, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally used New York Times journalism to train AI models. That legal case, in which motions are still being filed about discovery requests, is only one front in a broader battle: The Trump administration is waging an ongoing war on press freedoms—most recently with an outrageous attempt to subpoena Times journalists over coverage of the president’s Qatar-gifted jet to be used as Air Force One—while AI companies radically reshape the way people find and consume information online.

The Times has arguably never been stronger as a business, having recently surpassed 13 million subscribers, and its newsroom is widely seen among journalists as one of the most stable and well-resourced in the business. Still, Sulzberger believes that journalism itself is facing myriad existential dilemmas—from an administration ready and willing to target reporters, from AI companies whose products depend on the very reporting they risk undermining, and media companies being demolished by the changes they’re unleashing on the open web.

I sat down with Sulzberger in late July at WIRED’s offices. We talked about that Times lawsuit, how and where AI is transforming reporting inside the newsroom, and why he thinks journalists and media executives need to team up—even while they continue to compete fiercely. You can read our entire conversation below, or listen to it here.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: AG, welcome. Thank you for being here.

A.G. SULZBERGER: It's great to be here. Thanks for inviting me.

Tech.title: Silicon Valley’s Next IPO Billionaires Are Coming. Nonprofits Are Ready for Them
Tech.content:
A decade ago, Ryan Carrier was a failed hedge fund manager watching as AI systems began to spin out of control. Facebook’s algorithms shook US elections, a Microsoft chatbot said the Holocaust was “made up,” and Tesla’s Autopilot killed its first driver. “There was no governance, oversight, or accountability,” Carrier says. To him, the AI-filled future awaiting his children looked bleak.

Carrier went on that year to found ForHumanity, a nonprofit organization developing tools for auditing AI systems. It's raised just hundreds of thousands of dollars since 2016, and is still a minor player in the industry. But that could soon change, because ForHumanity is now among the many nonprofits around the world trying to rein in AI, get animals out of cages, eliminate poverty and sickness, or spread democracy, that are all eager to claim a slice of what’s widely anticipated to be the largest wave of philanthropy in decades.

Two nearly trillion-dollar AI companies, ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Claude creator Anthropic, are expected to go public soon, making hundreds of current and former employees ultrawealthy. Some of them are aligned with a philosophy known as effective altruism that encourages making impactful donations sooner rather than later.

Anthropic’s seven founders have pledged to donate 80 percent of their wealth, and the company has agreed to chip in one or three shares for every one its employees commit to giving, depending on when they joined and up to a certain limit.

Rough estimates by a tech industry insider suggest that Anthropic’s IPO, which could happen in September, may result in $15 billion a year in additional philanthropic giving alone. That would be enough to boost total US giving by about 2.5 percent annually—the same as adding four Bill Gates’s, one of the world’s biggest donors. Anthropic declined to comment on the total amount its employees have set aside to donate and the organizations that may benefit.

All that money is far from guaranteed. The IPOs may get delayed or go poorly and leave employees clinging onto their wealth. Industry observers are also concerned that a paralyzing number of charitable options and natural fickleness could prompt workers to keep more for themselves than anticipated.

Tech.title: Private Claude Conversations Have Been Indexed by Search Engines
Tech.content:
Over the weekend, private Claude AI chats were made publicly accessible by search engines like Google and Bing, making for a privacy nightmare for the people involved and the chatbot’s maker, Anthropic.

Privacy concerns surrounding AI have always been around, but as these tools become more capable of pushing into your daily workflow with agentic capabilities, the threat of private data exposure is more timely than ever. This latest example shows that even simply sharing a conversation with others can get it exposed to a significantly larger audience.

This latest example shows that even simply sharing a conversation with others can get it exposed to a significantly larger audience.

Initially spotted by Reddit users, the common factor in the problem seems to be that the indexed conversations were shared — a common option within most AI chats — allowing “anyone with the link” to view what had been said in the Claude conversation itself.

This feature is apparently not completely protected from web crawlers, and personal conversations, while initially shared by users with people they chose, were exposed for the entire internet to see if one knew where to look.

Conversations indexed included medical records, sensitive personal information, internal corporate data and explicit content. They could be viewed within Google and Bing with a simple search and adding “site:claude.ai/share” to the query, yielding a trove of conversations, most of which have since been removed. Artifacts — tools, visualizations and shareable apps — were also accessible through search engines.

This isn’t the first time this has happened: Last year, Forbes reported the same thing happened with Anthropic — hundreds of conversations appeared on Google search results, only for them to be scrubbed later.

An Anthropic spokesperson told CNET that its system is working as it should and that when people decide to share their conversations, they’re making them publicly accessible.

“Shareable links are not guessable or discoverable unless people choose to share them themselves,” the spokesperson said. “When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.”

If ever there were a good time to adjust your privacy settings and delete old conversations from your go-to AI chatbot, it’s now. To view your shared chats in Claude, you can go to Settings > Privacy > Shared Chats.

Tech.title: Use This Searchable Database to Locate Flock Surveillance Cameras Near You
Tech.content:
Recent media coverage of Flock Safety, the fast-growing US surveillance technology company, sheds light on the local battles over the deployment of automated license plate readers.

In South Carolina, officials have been sparring over whether to install 25 new cameras, a dispute that reflects broader questions about cost, oversight, and how much surveillance communities are willing to accept. The city of Los Angeles recently broke its contract with Flock Safety, though Flock’s CEO argues that the suspension should be temporary while the police department revises its rules.

Public opposition has fueled many of these cancellations, reflecting concerns that the system facilitates mass surveillance and can lead to harms such as discriminatory policing and privacy infringements.

To track such surveillance, journalists and researchers are increasingly turning to a free tool called the Atlas of Surveillance, a collaboration between the renowned digital privacy group Electronic Frontier Foundation and the University of Nevada, Reno. The site has become a go‑to source for mapping police technology — which also includes drones, facial-recognition cameras and body cameras — with a searchable database that’s often more dependable than alternatives.

With the Atlas of Surveillance tool, you enter a city, county, state, law enforcement agency or vendor in the US and select which technology you’re interested in tracking. You’ll get a list of details based on your search, including links to public records or news articles.

“We frequently run into situations where local councilpeople don’t even know that a certain tool is in use,” said Beryl Lipton, Electronic Frontier Foundation senior investigative researcher. “Learning about a technology we have logged in the Atlas of Surveillance is meant to help people have conversations [about] whether that tool is appropriate for local use, start asking questions, and advocate for standards around how their police can or can’t use this equipment.”

Surveilling surveillance

While other tools for tracking Flock cameras and similar surveillance systems exist, I prefer the EFF’s approach, which uses reliable crowdsourced data from specific volunteers, including University of Nevada students and staff, as well as experienced researchers. These volunteers use a variety of information, including government documents, press releases, news stories and confirmed social media posts, to create lists of exactly which surveillance technologies local police or sheriff departments are using, as well as when they were adopted.

Deflock, another popular crowdsourced app for reporting Flock camera locations, has an open-source design that leaves it vulnerable to false reports from people who only think they’re seeing a surveillance device. Self-reports are also becoming less reliable as surveillance cameras are being hidden in speed signs and cacti.

The Atlas provides sources for its information and includes records dating back years. EFF

I tried the Atlas tool with several location searches, including Albany, Georgia, where five police officers were fired and arrested in July on charges of misusing the city’s Flock system. Sure enough, I could see exactly when Albany began its Flock program, among other details about the technology it uses.

“While we may know that a police department has a tool, we may not know that they don’t have a governing policy or what is in the policy they have, like how long the data is retained,” Lipton told me.

Lipton recommends that users pair the Atlas tool with the EFF’s Street-Level Surveillance hub, which offers deeper documentation, including details on third‑party vendors that collaborate with law enforcement.

The Atlas database isn’t perfect, and the volunteers can do only so much. In my own searches, I found that my home city offered accurate listings for traffic cameras, but didn’t mention the period when it adopted Flock automated license plate readers last year, before removing them after public complaint. I’ve seen similar patterns in other cities with comparable histories, suggesting the database may emphasize active programs or exclude portions of older records.

Resources like the Atlas of Surveillance give residents a clearer view of the technologies their police departments use, information that can otherwise be difficult to obtain. As I’ve covered before, some cities will carefully omit the name “Flock” when announcing new surveillance or monitoring programs, even if they are using the brand’s drones or ALPR cameras.

If you’d like to volunteer for the Atlas of Surveillance, you can select the Collaborate option to submit a datapoint for consideration.

Tech.title: The Lego-Like Envo UPT Is an EV That Can Be a Golf Cart, ATV or Lawnmower
Tech.content:
Slate Auto isn’t the only company betting that customers want to build their own EV from a parts kit. Canadian micromobility company Envo’s Utility Personal Transporter is a modular electric platform that can be reconfigured into nearly 20 different vehicles — golf cart, go-kart, snowkart, ATV, side-by-side, cargo quadricycle, last-mile delivery rig, even a stretcher-equipped emergency vehicle.

Envo has spun the platform off into its own sub-brand, Modular-EV, with a dedicated storefront and online configurator separate from Envo’s main e-bike and gokart business.

This is an electric cart, not an electric car. The UPT tops out well below highway speeds and isn’t meant to replace your daily driver. It’s meant to replace the five or six single-purpose machines currently cluttering your garage, farm shed or fleet depot. Envo’s messaging leans heavily on the smartphone analogy: the idea that UPT should be the only thing you need in your garage, the way your phone replaced your camera, calculator and GPS.

The UPT is a very small electric cart. Envo, Modular-EV

The company already builds e-bikes, go-karts, golf carts and cargo quadricycles, so a modular electric micromobility platform is a logical next step. The UPT rides on an aluminum T-slot Base Block chassis rather than a traditional welded frame, which makes the reconfiguration trick possible. The platform’s length and width can be resized, and suspension, motors and body modules bolt on wherever the application calls for them — no welding required.

Power comes from independently controlled hub motors at each wheel, which Envo says gives it precise, quad-motor torque control rather than a single drive unit sending power through axles and differentials. (This also allows the EV to pull off zero-radius tank turns.) Buyers can spec a short or long wheelbase, 2WD or 4WD, and either a single 2.83kWh battery or dual 5.66kWh packs for up to an estimated 62 to 125 miles (200 km) of range, depending on configuration and payload. That may sound short, but we’re talking about an electric golf cart with a 40 mph (60 kph) top speed; it’s not exactly built for road trips. Keeping with the modular theme, the batteries themselves are swappable and user-serviceable, which is a nice nod to repairability.

The folded UPT chassis is small enough to fit in a truck bed or an SUV’s hatch for transport. Envo, Modular-EV

From there, it’s a matter of picking tires (CargoBike or off-road), steering (wheel or handlebars, car-style pedals or a bike-crank generator), seating and body components like bumpers and cargo boxes. The whole thing can be disassembled with hand tools and rebuilt from a parts catalog, and folds down small enough to toss in a pickup bed.

Modular-EV is selling the platform both as a bare rolling chassis and as a lineup of preset builds, each with its own model number. There’s the UP20 base platform, the UT20 utility vehicle and UT21 golf cart, the AT20 through AT23 all-terrain and mobility-scooter variants and more. My personal faves are the GC20 buggy go-kart and the LV20 microcar.

There’s also a run of ET-series work vehicles aimed at airports, hospitals, film crews, event marketers and municipal fleets, all sold on the same chassis with different body kits. Envo has also announced a partnership with autonomous-driving company Faction to bring AI-driven, self-driving capabilities to the UPT for last-mile delivery. These commercial fleets are likely to be the biggest market for the modular UPTs, not the average driveway.

The modular nature of the UPT chassis opens a wide range of possible commercial and leisure applications. Envo, Modular-EV

That said, I think the DIY nature of the builds is what makes this interesting beyond the world of fleet vehicles. Someone running an electric side-by-side around a large property, or a golf cart in a car-free community, could keep a bin of swap parts on hand and turn the same chassis into a mower or plow when the season calls for it, instead of buying and storing a separate machine for every task.

The Modular-EV UPT starts around $9,000 for the bare UP20 platform, with most finished presets priced between $10,000 and $12,000. That’s not cheap for something you can’t take on the highway, but the pitch isn’t “buy a cart,” it’s “buy a platform.” You can’t mow your lawn with a Honda Civic. With this, you could then turn around and use the same chassis to haul cargo, plow snow and then toss the whole kit in the back of a truck and take it camping.

Tech.title: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 Trail Running Test: Can It Outrun Your Garmin?
Tech.content:
By 10 a.m., the golden California hills were already baking in 80-degree heat. Not exactly ideal trail running conditions, but perfect for the endurance test I had planned — not for me, but for a smartwatch. I wanted to know whether Samsung’s new trail running mode on the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 would hold up as well on the trail as it looked on paper, and whether it could make me a smarter trail runner (or, at the very least, a better hydrated one).

Samsung is pushing the Ultra 2 further into sports watch territory with native trail running, recreational diving and a rugged design that’s built to take on the elements. For trail runners, the biggest feature additions are offline navigation, live elevation data and AI-powered hydration reminders.

Before heading out, I needed a route. In theory, you’ll be able to browse nearby trails directly from the watch — a game changer, if it actually works. In reality, the route finder handed the task off to the Samsung Health app on my phone because I didn’t have any routes preloaded. There was a “Search for a route” option, but that only yielded an empty map. Even zooming in on California, with its abundance of trails, didn’t surface any routes.

My other option was loading a GPX file from a previous run. Six months ago, I had no idea what a GPX, or GPS exchange format, file was. Since then, enough smartwatch accuracy testing has left me with a small library of exported files. One happened to already be loaded on my Samsung Galaxy phone: a familiar 5-mile loop through the regional park behind my house. Most people won’t have that head start. It wasn’t the seamless experience I’d hoped for, but it got me on the trail. Once the map was loaded on the watch, I was off.

Hydration reminders might not be such a bad idea

I wasn’t even a mile in when I hit the first climb. I knew before I even looked up, because the watch called it out through the speaker. The screen showed the ascent as a line graph that filled up in real time as I went up the hill, almost like a video game challenge. Even though the road ahead looked like an endless wall of rock, I could see exactly how much suffering I had left on the watch.

Once at the summit, the screen changed to an elevation profile with a graph showing all the peaks and valleys I had yet to conquer.

About half my run was in direct sunlight near noon, so I expected the display to struggle. Instead, one of the first things I noticed was how well it handled the glare. As I moved between blazing sun and tree cover, the 5,000-nit display adjusted so smoothly that I never had to squint or cup my hand over it. Samsung’s display expertise (the company does make TVs, after all) really shows here, and it’s one place where the Ultra 2 outshines many dedicated sports watches.

About 30 minutes into the run, after grinding through two long climbs in the heat, the watch buzzed with my first hydration reminder. I was, in fact, drenched in sweat, so the timing felt about right and I would’ve gladly taken a hydration break. But since I’d traded my water bottle for a tripod on my running pack that day to shoot some footage of the watch, the reminder mostly fell on deaf ears.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 uses AI to estimate sweat loss, pulling from a combination of biometrics including heart rate and environmental factors such as temperature, elevation gain and workout duration. It’s a clever idea, but I’d trust it much more if it used a dedicated sweat sensor to measure actual perspiration loss instead of relying on a prediction.

Still, in a summer marked by relentless heat waves, hydration reminders feel less like a gimmick and more like the kind of feature that could genuinely help people from getting into trouble when adrenaline makes it easy to ignore the warning signs. I got two more hydration reminders at different points during my run, though I wasn’t able to rehydrate until I made it back home.

Even when I’m not testing out running features, I avoid hitting the trails with headphones in my ears. Rough terrain, loose rock and the occasional rustle in the brush mean I want both ears alert. So having turn-by-turn navigation come through the watch’s speaker, loud enough to actually hear outdoors, was a welcome feature on the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2.

Even though I’d technically already run this particular trail before, I didn’t remember the exact version of it, so it was nice to have the guidance. Every fork in the road, every moment I drifted off course, was met with a polite voice from my wrist reminding me to stay on course. On an unfamiliar trail, that could be the difference between staying on course and adding an unplanned mile uphill. I could also swipe over to a bird’s-eye view of the entire route, which showed exactly where I was on the trail and how much I still had left to go.

Ending the trail run on an empty tank

By the end of the 5-mile run, I was parched, dusty and ready to call it a day. The watch wasn’t far behind. It had burned through nearly 30% of its charge — a reminder that battery life is still one area where the Ultra 2 trails dedicated sports watches, many of which last a week or more on a single charge.

Samsung increased the battery capacity from 590 mAh on the original Ultra to 800 mAh on the Ultra 2, but a demanding trail run with GPS, LTE, maximum brightness and climb tracking still took a noticeable toll. I’ve yet to reach Samsung’s claimed 60 hours of normal use, though the company says battery life improves as the watch learns your habits. After two weeks, I can wear it for longer stretches than I could when I started testing it.

The Ultra 2 isn’t going to replace a dedicated sports watch such as the Garmin Forerunner or the feature-packed Fènix for serious endurance athletes. But after 5 miles in the California hills, it made me excited to get back out on the trails — and maybe even explore a new one once Samsung’s trail-finding feature rolls out. For a smartwatch that’s also expected to handle work emails, Google Gemini and the less adventurous parts of work life, that’s high praise.

Tech.title: Want to Ditch Google Search? Try These 5 Other Search Engines Now
Tech.content:
Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Getty Images

Google announced in May at its Google I/O developers conference that it was working to combine Google Search with its advanced AI tools. That means interacting with Google Search in the future might resemble using an AI chatbot instead of an index of blue links. But if you don’t like the direction Google Search is heading, there are other search engines you can try for free.

There are plenty of alternative search engines that offer advantages over Google, such as greater privacy. But the main drawback to some of these engines is that they may lack comprehensive results. That means you might have to look through more results on other search engines than on Google. I found it helpful to be more specific with my search queries when using these other engines.

It’s also important to note that even if you use these search engines within Google’s Chrome browser, you may not get the full benefit of some of these other engines. Here are five other free search engines to use instead of Google Search.

Brave

Sarah Tew/CNET

Brave is a privacy-focused search engine that blocks trackers, and it uses Google as a fallback option. What that means is if your Brave search doesn’t return a lot of results, you can enable the search engine to anonymously check Google for the same query.

Brave also offers other features, like a VPN, a crypto wallet and its own AI assistant named Leo. And Brave said your AI usage is private and secure as well. You don’t even need to create or log into an account to use Leo.

You can try Brave for free.

DuckDuckGo

Getty Images/DuckDuckGo/Viva Tung/CNET

DuckDuckGo is another privacy-focused search engine, and it has touted itself as the anti-Google. While Google collects and stores data on you to create personalized search results, DuckDuckGo doesn’t track what you do and actively blocks external trackers.

Over the past few years, DuckDuckGo also expanded the free tools it offers to people. Now it offers tools like an App Tracking Protection for Android users, its own VPN — that our experts said was great for general privacy and streaming — and an AI tool called DuckAssist.

You can try DuckDuckGo for free.

Ecosia

Ecosia

This private, Berlin-based search engine is also a green option. Ecosia writes online it has planted over 250 million trees and produces more clean energy than it takes to power all its searches and AI queries. The company also writes online that all its profits go toward climate action.

However, Ecosia writes in its privacy policy it does use Google and Microsoft Bing to provide you with results. CNBC reported in 2024 that Ecosia and Paris-based search engine Qwant partnered to create a European search index in order to reduce dependence on US companies.

You can try Ecosia for free.

Qwant

Sopa Images via Getty Images

This French-based search engine writes online it doesn’t retain your search data or sell your personal data, making it a good alternative to Google. In addition to search, Qwant also offers a feature called Qwant Junior, which it writes online is meant to help children between the ages of 6 and 12 years old safely explore the internet.

You should know that Qwant has integrated AI into its engine in what it calls Flash Answers. But you can deactivate it from your Settings menu without jumping through hoops. Historically, Qwant has used Bing’s search API, which lets companies access Bing’s search infrastructure. But according to CNBC, the company partnered with Berlin-based search engine Ecosia in 2024 to build a European search index in order to reduce dependence on US companies.

You can try Qwant for free.

Startpage

Startpage

Startpage is a search engine that’s also a search aggregator. That means it partners with other companies like Google and Microsoft Bing to bring you search results.

Despite those partnerships, Startpage said it doesn’t share any of your personal information with its partners and it submits your search requests anonymously. Startpage said it also doesn’t use tracking cookies, and it doesn’t review or access cookies you might have from other websites. Think of Startpage as a way to use Google and Bing without either getting ahold of your data.

You can try Startpage for free.

For more on other search engines, here’s what to know about DuckDuckGo and Brave Search.

Tech.title: Return to Halo Almost 25 Years Later With Xbox Game Pass Now
Tech.content:
Bungie released Halo on Xbox in 2001, and it changed gaming and pop culture forever. I remember the first time I picked up an energy sword. It felt like I was playing something special. Now, about 25 years later, I can revisit that iconic experience with Xbox Game Pass.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award pick, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month. And with a subscription to the higher-tiered Game Pass Ultimate ($23 a month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones the day they’re released, each month.

Here are all the games Xbox is bringing to Game Pass soon.

Shift at Midnight

On Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass now.

I’ve seen people post demo videos of this game online, and I’m excited to finally play it. It’s a horror game where you work as a convenience store clerk, but you have to investigate your customers since some of them are monsters in disguise. Let the wrong customer in, and you’ve got to set traps, hide and defend yourself from otherworldly horror. Don’t forget to restock the shelves and take out the trash before you clock out. (The trailer is age-restricted, so I can’t embed it, but you can watch it from behind your sofa here.)

Halo: Campaign Evolved

On Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass now.

Step into the boots of the legendary Master Chief as he takes on the Covenant and the Flood in the first installment of one of the most well-known gaming franchises in history. This remade version of the iconic Halo: Campaign Evolved includes 4K visuals, updated animations and more. There are also three new missions that take place a year prior to the start of the game. So grab your rocket launcher and some plasma grenades and get ready to take on the Covenant and the Flood for the hundredth — or first — time.

Beast of Reincarnation

Coming to Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass on Aug. 4.

Game Freak is widely known as the developer behind the Pokemon games, but its upcoming game Beast of Reincarnation is a different kind of beast — pun intended. You play as Emma and her trusty dog companion, Koo, as they try to save a post-apocalyptic Japan from corrupted creatures in this role-playing game. This game has real-time and turn-based combat, so it should present an interesting challenge.

Heretic and Hexen

New to Game Pass Premium on Aug. 4. Previously on Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass.

Face down demons, cultists and other infernal creatures with medieval weaponry and magic in these cult-classic games from the ’90s. If you look at these ported games and think they just look like Doom but with swords, you aren’t far off. Developer Raven Software used a modified version of the Doom engine to create Heretic and Hexen, so the games should look and feel familiar.

Other games coming to Game Pass

Those are a few of the games I’m looking forward to on Xbox Game Pass, but Microsoft is adding more to the service this month. Here are the other games you can try soon.

Hell Is Us – On Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium and PC Game Pass now.

Mistfall Hunter – Coming to Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass on July 30.

Corsair Cove – Coming to Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass on July 31.

These games are leaving Game Pass on July 31

While Microsoft is adding several titles to Game Pass soon, it’s also removing eight others from the service on July 31. So you still have some time to play these games for the first time, but hurry before you have to buy them separately.

For more on Xbox, here’s what to know about the recent Xbox layoffs. You can also check out our Xbox Game Pass review and which Game Pass plan is right for you.

Tech.title: Apple Upgrade Program Will Let You Lease an iPhone Without Sticker Shock
Tech.content:
There’s now a new way to own an Apple product. Starting from today in the US, you’ll be able to lease an iPhone, iPad, Mac or Apple Watch directly from the company via its new Apple Upgrade program.

Enabled by Klarna, prices for leasing Apple products will start at $18 a month for an iPhone and $12 a month for an Apple Watch, with 12- and 24-month leasing options. If you’re in the market for an iPad or Mac, you’re likely to keep that device for longer, and Apple is offering 24- or 36-month leasing options for these devices.

You can explore the different options either online or through the Apple Store, or you can go to a physical Apple Store in person. If you have an existing device to trade in, you can also lower your monthly leasing costs.

The leasing program is likely to come as welcome news to anyone overwhelmed by the thought of buying an Apple device outright — especially right now. Just last month, Apple abruptly raised prices of all of its devices due to RAMageddon, the industry-wide memory shortage that’s pushing up prices not just of Apple products, but all consumer electronics. This came shortly after Apple CEO Tim Cook called price rises “unavoidable.”

The price rises are also expected to affect upcoming launches, including at Apple’s rumored September iPhone event. If Apple does unveil a new foldable iPhone, as expected, it’s likely to be more expensive than any existing models, just as Samsung’s foldables are more expensive than its other flagship phones.

A leasing program could well prove a popular strategy at a time when many households are struggling with the cost of living. It’s a major financial challenge for Apple to balance rising component costs at a time when people are only becoming more price sensitive, said Dipanjan Chatterjee, vice president and chief analyst at Forrester.

“Having already raised prices, Apple has limited room to push them higher without further extending upgrade cycles,” said Chatterjee. “The new leasing program is a clever response: It doesn’t reduce the price of an iPhone, but it changes how consumers perceive the cost by replacing sticker shock with a predictable monthly payment.”

Apple says that signing up for the program is easy, and can take only a matter of minutes. Klarna will perform a soft credit check on applicants that won’t impact their credit score.

At the end of the leasing term, customers will be given the option of returning their device, buying it outright for a small fee, or upgrading.

Tech.title: Sales Tax Holidays 2026: Here’s What You Need to Know

Who doesn’t love seeing a lighter checkout total? Back-to-school shopping is fun until the checkout screen (and a smiling salesperson) reminds you that those notebooks, backpacks and laptops you picked up to cater to your child’s whims (or needs) have added up to a pretty good amount. And it’s not just school supplies — your wallet gets the biggest surprise at checkout when you’re shopping for clothes, dorm room essentials, surprise gifts for teachers or household stuff. That’s why every discount, no matter how small it is, feels big. After all, we aren’t paying full price at least. Now, here comes the good news — you don’t have to wait for another big sale to save.

Sales tax holidays have returned. Many US states are giving you a reason to smile at checkout once again. During these limited-time events, participating states temporarily waive or reduce sales tax on purchases. No sales tax means a smaller checkout total. Whether you’re buying a new bottle, upgrading your school laptop or just refreshing your summer wardrobe, it’s great when paying less doesn’t require a coupon code. You get an instant discount from the state. But what exactly is a sales tax holiday, and how does it work? Let’s break it down.

What is a sales tax holiday?

A sales tax holiday is a limited-time period when participating states suspend/reduce sales tax on a few qualifying items. Some tax holidays have become an annual tradition that’s followed every year; usually before the school reopens or before the summer commences. Each participating state has its own dates, list of eligible/ineligible items and spending limits.
